title: Don't Trip
my_review: I really just didn’t feel this one at all. It’s trying far too hard to be eccentric and weird and the writing and actors suffer for it. Pulls the ‘ole ‘crazy dude might be lonely, horny or murdery’, which I feel like isn’t too hard to screw up. But most of the things they do just aren’t really at all unnerving and in turn it makes most of this movie so uninteresting. “Hey, I just met you—what if we went to a support group meeting, right now?”, “I want you to deepthroat this cheap taquito!”… like a support group could be interesting, a lá ‘Fight Club’(1999), but they don’t show it(spent too much on aerial establishing shots and the swanky house), it just skips over what could be a good scene of our protag trying to fit in because the guy keeps provoking him to do more. And ‘deepthroating a taquito’? I guess it’s sort of weird, but our guy acts like he was given a cricket to eat and it makes that whole scene awkward for the wrong reasons. This happens alot, our guy acting like such a spazz over the most benign things to create this false sensation that he’s dancing with the ultimate weirdo. That inherent failure of conveying that just makes this whole movie so very skippable. Then there’s the story—what little it has. I have to assume Chloe Cherry’s only here so they can advertise her. Which admittedly, after falling for the eye catching poster—that likens itself to the other current horror/thriller megahits, I saw her in the banner and thought, “oh neat, I recognize her, cool she did another movie”, so they got me there. But I think it was to pull some ‘Scream’(1996)-like intro—killing the girl on the poster and debatably the more popular actor of this lot(there is classic character actor Fred Melamed who shows up for almost the same amount of time, but I feel like he brings around the same star power as ‘the pornstar with the lips’—but that’s neither here nor there, cause both are pretty wasted on the screen). But that whole opening is just kinda, “okay—now what?” as it then just never really follows up stylistically or story wise with her murder. Like this Trip dude has a history, but the movie’s so much more invested in making him “eccentric” that it doesn’t really give much threat to him. There’s just a murder → a whole lot of mediocre attempts at making this have some edge → and now it’s murderous again, but not in any scary, or thrilling way, dude just tranqs everyone and threatens the possibility of something exciting happening. Then there’s just the asinine “Put my name on the script!” like what a fucking lame thing to create false stakes out of. Dude could easily do that himself, there’s not much to it and it gives the opening for our guy to create an S.O.S.—which was also beyond lame. Like they wanted to avoid so much of a more interesting movie that they made the salvation be that the dad notices the bolded words in the hour or so he read the script, cause he’s just that much of a stickler for it and it has to be brought up. I dunno, more I think on this, the less positives I have for it. It’s not great and worse, it’s not so in a funny manner. It’s just plain bad.

title: Whistle
my_review:
Pretty dumb, but some of the deaths are pretty cool in a differently inventive way than its too similar counterpart—the ‘Final Destination’ series. But why’d they stop our guy from killing the dirtbag drug dealer? Morals? Pffftt. 

Also, I’ve noticed lesbians are showing up more often as protagonists in horrors lately, which is kinda interesting. Perhaps because women typically lead horror movies and more modern sentiments have led to wanting more queer representation and the easiest route is “make the final girl a lesbian”. Off the top of my head, there was the new ‘Hellraiser’(2022) that had a gay guy survive(alongside the actual final girl), but other than that, I can’t think of another movie that’s not explicitly trying to represent some queer identity having a queer main character. Not like there’s a tally board keeping track, just an interesting observation I noticed, really.

title: Black Phone 2
my_review: Backdoor audition for Derrickson inheriting the ‘Elm Street’-franchise. Better than the first for me, if only in aesthetic and going harder into the lore which seemed a little sparse and convenient in the first. But does lack some grace as it tries to ‘swing for the fences’, doubling down more on the familial drama at play—which is handled better here, but still feels like the writing’s lacking the finesse to execute. Padding in too many characters for as intimate as this movie tries to be and building and losing momentum constantly. Finney and Gwen are good protagonists, Finney leaning more into the jaded self-conscious survivor that hasn’t moved past the trauma and Gwen the kind hearted sister suffocating in a family that’s gotten better but not healed. I don’t think either of those descriptions are necessarily showcased so well, for as slow paced as this is I don’t think it gives us much time to appreciate Finney’s character as Gwen kinda takes the spotlight initially and then usurps the whole movie by the end. And their relationship with their dad continues to be lacking, Jeremy Davies is more than capable of handling the conflicting emotions, still doesn’t really get to showcase any of them as he was just a background abuser in the first and a grateful—but still guilty feeling father here. There’s a very irksome scene when Davies shows up to rescue the siblings from the snow and Gwen just bluntly monologues(sledgehammers) exactly the sort of growth she(the script) demands her brother and father need to have by the end of the movie. Her going way too hard on Finney because he’s for some reason regressed back to ignorance, even though we’re entering the third act and he’s already on the train. And “too hard” because it’s so obvious and understandable why Finney’s fucked up. She’s not exactly saying anything he wouldn’t need to hear, but her soapboxing it and raging felt weirdly harsh. Finney not having his PTSD as enough of an obstacle or turning into abuse like his father to justify her savagery. The dad deserves it though—needed it more in the first movie, but goddamn she buries the lead so much. Dragging the scene out so needlessly when she can just take the wind out of him to start by saying she saw their mom’s murder. The whole scene is really clunky to me and the writing just not seeming good enough to sell the complexities of the family without making them all come off so poorly, in acting and character. But I think that scene’s just a byproduct of the bigger issue of too many characters here, each one extra nickel and diming the runtime away. The camp angle, Ernesto, the “not”-romantic interest for Finney…many of these don’t need to be here. • Ernesto is the easiest cut, he’s too easy going and nonexistent otherwise in the movie. His only purpose is “car” and “second person to watch Gwen while Finney can’t for whatever reason”. Finney should have driven—just give him a car, or better yet, let the dad drive them and make him apart of the movie if you want to lean on the “healing the family turmoil” aspect. And the kiss was weird just a strange context and a weird reward for just Gwen in something that didn’t seem like she was struggling/longing for. Like the Grabber never did anything to Ernesto and she never was really hindered from not being romantic with him, I dunno, it was strange. • The “couple”(?) are the second easiest. Their presence is strange and their characters are stranger. Yes the woman was kinda bitchy to Gwen, but she seemed there just to have Gwen not be so kind all the time. The two of them together don’t really have any sort of agency there for as involved as they get. They’re mostly there just to be killed(?), or at the least beaten up by the Grabber so he’s not just punishing the same two characters—who can only take so much punishment. • “Mustang” was really under utilized. I forget or missed if she was related to Demián Bichir(though they don’t really act related either way, nor does it matter), but she just kinda exists at the camp for no reason too. The obvious reason would have been cause she’s a pretty girl around Finney’s age, but there’s nothing there. They do share a glance and the dad comments on as much—but at the end right before the credits, otherwise they hardly speak to eachother. She’s just another body there to help out, but also does the least of everyone. Like she’s there helping more than any other camp character, but what does she actually do that wouldn’t work with just Finney and Ernesto(if they must)? • Demián Bichir’s character is the only one I liked—if only because he was refreshing as an adult in a “kids”-horror story. He also doesn’t quite do much besides expositing stuff for the teens and then he’s out alone so the Grabber can do stuff, but he’s fine. I think he belongs, but he’s not given much to do. None of these characters are particularly developed, so they’re not quite stealing time in that way. The way they get in the way of the more intimate family drama is the fact that they’re out there so that the family doesn’t have to be there for eachother all the time when they should have been. So wasted “minutes” on them “doing” stuff than what could have been more family stuff that goes into supporting what it boils down to. Movie also just has momentum issues in general. It’s quite slow—atmospheric, but slow. There’s alot spent on Gwen’s clairvoyant dreams which are each very simmering and eerie. When things do come to a head though, it’s quite bombastic and you think the movie’s finally kicking into that gear…but then it’s back to the simmering eeriness. In particular there’s all this build up to the Grabber finally showing up and just manhandling Gwen—in front of everyone, so everyone can’t deny the spooks like horrors do until it’s too late. And they actually believe and formulate a plan with the teens, which is fairly refreshing and felt like things would be switching up there. But then they immediately go back to everyone isolating and getting spooked individually, kinda negating any “refreshed” feeling I was having there. Again, maybe without the extra characters or focusing more on the core family, then so much steam wouldn’t be lost to give them their moments or just give the movie spooks. The Grabber is cooler here though. The icy aesthetic is sick and I was down for the “cooler” and more vengeful ‘Freddy Kruger’-stint. I could see—should they dip again, a more IT-like return of him, should there be another sequel where he’s fully a supernatural slasher now, where his schtick of the “kid predator” is amplified by the supernatural powers. Which they could as the story could turn into just hunting down the spots where he may have sporadically killed an buried kids. I will say though, he doesn’t really do much here. He killed three kids—like twenty or so years ago and he does nothing else but try to kill Gwen. He cuts other people, tries to drown and choke others, but he doesn’t actually kill anyone(unless that “couple” did die from the shallow axe swing to their heads). He’s not really terrorizing anyone, not really haunting anyone, the only reason Gwen wants to go to the camp is just cause her clairvoyance is flaring up suddenly with not terribly distressing dreams(they’re worse and more distressing when she’s already at the camp). So it’s kinda just a weird plot instigator that he doesn’t really do anything to alert the siblings—assumedly the mom’s clairvoyance and Gwen’s being the only thing to do it. He doesn’t seem to lure them there, nor does he seem that terribly powerful there in that he’s inexplicably able to interfere with the corporeal plane and moreso the “spirit” plane and not really stopped by any known means. So he’s like just chilling(🥁) there and the siblings decide to show up and that’s apparently what he wanted them to do? He also kinda gives up on Finney being the main character. He makes it seem like he’s only killing Gwen to get back at Finney—as if he can only reach Gwen, but both statements aren’t really true. He seems entirely fixated on Gwen as his adversary for some reason and he is able to harm everyone else. So like what’s he even about here, sure vengeance, but he seems real passive about it. Though I did really dig when Finney slams his head in across both planes. It’s a sequel that improves. By filmmaking standards that’s especially evident as it looks very evocative and the direction’s a bit more on point(felt akin to the difference ‘Smile’(2022) into ‘Smile 2’(2024)). But it’s not hitting quite as hard as it wants to. Maybe if it made a choice between a “full camp-slasher”—more kids to kill, more coming of age, kids have to save themselves… or an “intimate family horror”—family are the only characters that matter, they each monologue alot more to convey why they’re fucked up, big sweeps of emotions as they rescue or sacrifice for one another, the full ‘Mike Flanagan’-effect, but it kinda half-asses both. And in that it just works only enough to be a decent watch, but not an impactful one.

title: Coyotes
my_review: The first genuine jumpscare for me was realizing this movie was going to be using AI for the titular “coyotes”. I’m not as entirely against the incoming domination of AI CGI, it’s gonna be inevitable as it keeps getting better(cause like AI is how we’re eventually getting holodeck shenanigans, let’s be real.). And hopefully there’s some trade-off to where it’s not used entirely to replace passionate artists and just used at the right time and place rather than entirely for one less department to pay. So I’m not denouncing it entirely for the pure fact that it’s using AI generated coyotes, but that they thought they could get away with it. Not in the sense that nobody wouldn’t notice, but how wouldn’t people notice—they look terribly out of place.  It just doesn’t look right, as detailed as they are. They just don’t mesh with anything real onscreen and the fact that they only exist in cutaways only adds to that. When characters shoot at them, it genuinely feels like they’re just firing at both as they shoot a general space that doesn’t at all seem where the coyotes are supposed to be. And every time they have to switch between AI coyotes just snarling at nothing and characters just reacting—you never feel like they’re in the same space which is just a fundamental failure of filmmaking honestly. You can throw as many detailed clips of coyotes doing menacing things but none of those clips add anything to the story and this “world” they’ve made. Aside from all that—it’s just not very good. It’s a campy story but the movie itself isn’t nearly campy enough. They do these weird out of place comic styled character introductions(might have egg in my face but I’m pretty sure they’re also AI generated) that feel oddly timed and just awkwardly out of place. Jokes and dialogue are kinda whatever, feels as if they asked the actors to improvise alot of interactions and that rarely goes so well. Like even Justin Long kinda feels awkwardly “meh” here. Like they expected him to just be as good as he was in ‘Barbarian’(2022) but didn’t really give him anything to work with. Kate Bosworth however was pretty good for what it’s worth. It’s very mediocre and only made worse by leaning on the AI to compensate. Would be very at home as some streaming movie where the two big names trick people into watching it. Also Coyotes aren’t nearly that scary, unless it’s regarding your pet’s safety.

title: Takeout
my_review: Bit’ve a case of making the protagonist less interesting than everyone else by making them to generically protagonistic. Like maybe I’m crazy, but making the supporting character(Harper) here the main character feels like a much more interesting movie.

title: Primate
my_review: This is just pure movie fun, goddamn. It’s very much a popcorn horror movie and just a really well done one—I really had so much fun with this. Its writing certainly isn’t going to ‘wow’, with the clunky exposition, the logic people operate and act on and it’s just downright stupid at times. But that’s part of the fun with this. As much as I’ve loved the elevated horror era we live in currently, movies like this I’m kinda wowed by—specifically in the case that they aren’t dogshit. Like last year’ ‘Final Destination: Bloodlines’(2025) really impressed me. Both in being very competent, but also just an absolute blast of a horror that I feel is kinda rare nowadays. This isn’t quite as good at all, but I don’t think it’s trining to be and I love it for that. Its pitch was “monkey mayhem” and goddamn we did indeed go apeshit with it. Hell, I was even thinking of how this could be a series and just going buck-wild with it. For as much as I’m positively downplaying this, this is a pretty well done film. Scenes are tense, kills are modern-‘Mortal Kombat’-levels and it’s pretty easy on the eyes really. And I really gotta praise the practical effects of the chimp. Last year I saw the verge of AI effects and they looked horrendous. This very much looks like a guy in a chimp costume, but it’s timeless and looks 100000x better than some AI slop. AI is inevitable, but it’s not there yet garbage like ‘Coyotes’(2025) ruined what might’ve been a fun horror like this is(for the record, there’s other problems with that movie and while it’s similar to this, this movie is just so much better). It is funny though, as the pool became a focal part of the movie, I recalled—I think Chris Stuckman(maybe Double Toasted) in a review, one where he lambasted some lame horror movie, but did give credit to some very impressionable moments of direction. One in particular was a pool scene where there’s a POV of the character bobbing in an out of the water and the tense music deafens every time it goes underwater. I mention that irrelevant thought because looking up this movie’s director, Johannes Roberts, I realized it was the same dude and the movie was ‘The Strangers: Prey At Night’(2018), so that was pretty neat This is the movie to show kids at a young age and have them freak the fuck out and then have them laugh at the goofy absurdity of later on. I started reminiscing about watching the movie ‘Komodo’(1999) with my sister and dad one night. How when a komodo dragon crashed through the house ready to kill, I flipped out, mortified by it. Then at the end of the vhs there were bts bits and it showed one horrifying moment of the Komodo eating a dog through the doggy door and with the different angle and lack of editing, it looked super goofy seeing the doll of the dog yanked out by the lifeless komodo. That’s always stuck with me and this movie I feel like harks to that experience other kids might have and I love that. January horror—but I shockingly love this. Evil munkey, dumb teens, rated R gore and it’s got Troy Kotsur in it—Hell. Yeah.

title: The Strangers: Chapter 2
my_review: It’s a pointless movie. People show up just to die seconds later. The strangers just appear at the exact right time to just slaughter everyone except for our protagonist. But not for lack of trying, it’s just that our protagonist can just fumble her way through every situation just as well as they—the strangers, can cheaply get the edge on her. And then they immediately ditch the new location—cause they killed everyone there already, to return to the exact setting as the first movie? What was the point of even “rescuing” her? It’d be cheaper and less asinine to just start her surviving the day after as she hikes back to civilization. I thought the entire point of this was for hospital shenanigans but that’s like 15min and they’re back out to the woods.  And I just hate the slashers here, the strangers. For one, they’re extremely unfair. They act like Jason Vorhees, apparating everywhere without rhyme or reason, but I feel like the whole allure of “the strangers” is that they’re just random people that want to kill random people. Not supernatural entities with backstories now? I haven’t really bothered with any of the other movies in this franchise(most because I wasn’t won over by the original), but these movies feel entirely conflicting to the franchise, like they want to make the next horror icons but they’re going about it by just making them like any other superhuman slasher. Then they try to pull this ‘Scream’-like “it could be anyone” nonsense, but they literally kill everyone seconds after entering the movie, so any effect is just dull by the time they try and tease with a “maybe this person is a stranger???” Like I don’t care who they are cause there’s no fucking plot to care about. It’s just Madelaine Petsch running for her life(and stopping to make a campfire for no reason), there’s nothing more given. Especially when every outside force is immediately killed on entry, so what are we even doing here?  This didn’t need to be two movies already and it’s a joke that they’re making a third. The first is just a back and forth of the protagonist outsmarting the strangers and it not mattering because the strangers are just “better” for whatever reason and this movie is just more of the same. So just cut out so much of this horribly redundant circle running from both and merge the two movies and maybe this wouldn’t be so offensively bad.  Fuck you strangers, see you in “Chapter 3”.

title: The Long Walk
my_review:
Oddly this is somehow not the most harrowing movie of the endurance of competing in a sort of rat race I’ve seen. They didn’t even shoot any horses.

The premise is interesting and the characters—while the usual suspects(especially for King), carry the story. But it doesn’t really do much else with it, which seems dumb to say for such a movie, but yeah, it kinda felt like just watching the same thing for almost two hours. It’s hard cause I’m sure alot of the allure would be from the intense thoughts of POV and descriptions of haunting imagery that’s typical King which is kinda hard to translate so 1:1 in a movie. So for the nature of this unchanging walking marathon, it just leads to not too much happening other than hearing people have shit lives and seeing them buckle under pressure—rinse, repeat. 

Like I’m sure the book talks about how devastating their feet must feel(something I know from experience in stupidly wearing flip flops to a convention) especially to walk barefoot, but the movie conveys very little visual information to convey that aspect. And everyone keeps a good chatter up cause that’s all the movie really has for them to do, but that’s at the cost of it not seeming like such a crushing endurance test. I feel like watching Olympic walkers is more distressing. And yeah, ‘They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?’(1969) feels like it hits the same beats except it feels more soul crushing by the end rather than just bleak.

Not a bad movie though. Would probably be a good sleeper pick for a random movie night pick. David Jonsson though, I’m really glad I keep seeing more of him and hope that keeps up.

title: Obsession
my_review:
This movie got very funny for me with how bad the wish was at fulfilling itself that it’s basically felt like Tim Robinson was trying so desperately to show love and being terrible at it.
Nikki: “I just don’t wanna go home… what’s waiting for me at home is really bad.” Bear: “What’s waiting for you at home?” Nikki: “I dunno. When I get home, there’s something I’m really worried about in my life.” Bear: “What is it?” Nikki: “I dunno.” Bear: “Tch—is there really something?” Nikki: “I dunno… [my dad has cancer].”
Still actually scary at times, but just that underlying thought that I got a kick of the worse Wish-Nikki got at keeping Bear entertained.

title: The Conjuring: Last Rites
my_review: Kinda mixed on this. It’s a decent sendoff, albeit I kinda feel like adhering to the real life people’s lives take away from some better choices. Like someone should have died, honestly, especially Patrick Wilson, with his heart being so prevalent. But it’s a good “final” case and the spooks are the spookiest they’ve been(atleast in my opinion). But I really wasn’t crazy about Judy and her beau. And to some extent I don’t know of it wraps up the franchise as neatly when the montage at the end is what does it. Judy and her boyfriend just weren’t doing it for me here. No offense to their actors, but I really wasn’t vibing with either when I feel like I’m supposed to be endeared to them. In Judy’s case it’s just the recasting—though it makes sense now that she’s older here, I have no attachment to that face. She shows up and they say “care”, which I don’t. The boyfriend’s little better in his arc is entirely within the movie, but he feels incredibly bland, a common problem with the franchise, but worse when you’re not Patrick Wilson or Vera Farmiga. Judy also just really got on my nerves here. She kept withholding information from her parents—something the feels kinda wild to do when it’s so obviously supernatural and her parents are super close to her and the experts on the matter. And then when she just decides to go to the spook house on her own—demanding she and her parents stay to help, completely disregarding the fact that the dad’s heart is the entire reason they don’t work anymore. She’s just so bullheaded when her character shouldn’t really be that bullheaded. In ‘Annabelle Comes Home’(2019) her characterization is much more in line with the parents, while here she just feels really ignorant to the history of what her character would have. Narratively, I think it’d have been nicer to have the past haunts come back more in the same way they do in previous movies. Like Annabelle in the first and the Nun—though it was her first movie, being behind the haunt in the second. Actually, ‘Annabelle Comes Home’ does something like that in turning the Warrens inventory room alive. They do have a giant Annabelle, but that felt more like fanfare than what I’m looking for in a nice tied bow. There’s even a bit where Farmiga says “it’s different this time” and it just kinda plays out the same as I’d’ve expected? There were several instances even where I expected something ‘more’ to happen than what did actually happen(like the nonsense with Farmiga seeing the creeping around demon)—atleast, it felt very typical in what did play out. Maybe if the mirror had been alluded to more, it’d work better. It also doesn’t quite feel like they’re expertise is every that highlighted. They don’t really get much time to investigate and seem very unprepared(like most of these movies) for any shit to hit a fan which seems silly after “1000 cases” of experience. And then everyone else makes dumb moves around them which dumbs the movie down. Like Judy’s belligerence or the immensely dumb scene of the boyfriend driving like a maniac and crashing. But I do feel like this was the scariest movie—atleast for me. That old woman actually got me several times and they seemed to have more evocative hallucinations like the sink overflowing blood, or the giant Annabelle. Hell the dog being levitated and thrown into a wall was the most jaw dropping moment this series got from me(glad he shrugged it off like most people seem to oddly do in this series). And their haunts have been steadily more cinematic which I’m very much for, especially when they glaze the Warrens at every opportunity and drop a “THIS movie is finally the most scary case…” I actually wish the haunted family got more to do here. Unlike other movies where the Warrens kinda imbed themselves in the family, no such thing happens here. But they had a decent dynamic when established, the older sisters being highlights, but they do literally nothing else once the spirit detecting starts, only the dad helps with the mirror and they’re gone after that. But my marathon ends now. The spinoffs really steered me away initially. The first not really ever feeling worthy of getting so many sequels let alone several spinoffs. It was actually seeing a picture of DC Comics announcing that for their big event at the time—some wrestlemania for the universe or whatever that they’d have guest characters show up. Sub-Zero from ‘Mortal Kombat’, Red Sonja, Homelander from ‘The Boys’ and—Annabelle. It’s such a left field addition, still is actually(probably some Warner Bros. synergy at work), but I figured it was time to finally burn through these and see if Annabelle was worthy of all this hype(not really) and if the Conjurverse had any quality to explain the many entries. In the end I felt this series is solidly “okay”. These are all very run-of-the-mill spookhouse movies that are decently consistent and competently made. The Warrens turned out to be a bit more endearing than I felt initially, they’re super vanilla but their consistent devotion to eachother is a nice crutch of these films. I’m glad they’re finally calling it though(hopefully it sticks). As consistent as they are I think it’s too old fashioned to keep seeing pop up in this day and age. Or rather if they do insist on bringing it back, I’d hope there’s more of a flare to it, cause it doesn’t really standout at all in this age of horror we’re in. Still though, okay series about romanticizing some con artists.

title: Frankenstein
my_review: I was pretty shaky on this throughout, but I think it was winning me over, that is until the final 30min or so. It’s a long movie, maybe a little too long, but I think it’s atleast captivating. The sets and design work is top notch, which is very expectable with Del Toro. But the writing and some of the acting is what kinda of detracted me a bit. And then an ending that doesn’t quite feel earned. If anything, this is a very good looking movie to me. It’s so packed full of imaginative design and given Del Toro’s affinity for antiquated lighting themes, which give a uniquely distinct look. The costumes are also full of character and really standout here—though maybe too much at times. Like many times it’s hilarious how much the main characters stick out because their clothes are so gaudy while everyone else looks period accurate. Mia Goth’s Elizabeth, in particular looked so over-the-top and goofy. But the. There were really inspired ones, like Oscar Isaac’s Frankenstein really had such a particular look that would match his manic and broody character. And then Christopher Waltz was so overt, with the gold bottomed shoes that clanged as he walked and his ornately carved ivory handle cane, but I kinda loved it most of all. I started think how cool it was that we get two classic Victorian-Horror adaptations and they both look so inspired, with this and ‘Nosferatu’(2024). The acting was a bit wishy washy. Oscar Isaac is a phenomenal actor, one of my favorite working actors even and he’s lowkey already played a fantastic Frankenstein before with his character in ‘Ex Machina’(2014). He does have his good moments here, but for the most part he’s too out of control for me. His Victor Frankenstein is so wacky and manic—not in an ostentatious way, but because he’s gnawing at the scenery and just hamming it up. There’s very little subtlety with him—something that is one of Isaac’s strengths as an actor and has flashes of(all in his expressions), but this character doesn’t play into that strength and just goes way over-the-top in a very campy sort of way. I’m not sure if Isaac does camp that well, he’ll I’m now starting to see this very much as a ‘Johnny Depp’-type role with how much it kinda demands it’s actor to get into it—not in the typical acting way, but the “I’ve made a choice of what direction to take my performance and it’ll make or break the movie.” Jacob Elordi’s ‘The Creature’ is oddly a much more subdued role, mostly just contemplative and tragic. He’s fine for the most part, but I don’t think the makeup and directing really allow him to fully relay his emotions beyond the inflection of his voice and very “CGI Actor”-like movement. I actually really really like the character here, but I won’t deny the likes of Robert De Niro and Rory Kinnear had much juicier and more impressive roles in ‘Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein’(1994) and the series ‘Penny Dreadful’, respectively. When ‘The Creature’ starts to be more intelligent, Elordi shines more, but the movie’s also about over. Mia Goth’s Elizabeth was the only other one I wasn’t really sold on, but I’ve admittedly never been quite as enamored with her as others seem to be and her character’s a real awkward one here. Her character’s so blasé and the typical role of most female leads in these kinda stories, but there’s also a weirdness in her being engaged to William in this version. She’s so receptive to Victor’s flirting but that’s kinda out the door when ‘The Creature’ is introduced and it almost seems like she wants to be with him most of all. Showing up in a sheer nightgown, at night to entertain the the infantile wretch, getting him to choke you—Elizabeth, please. I kinda felt like Del Toro was playing into those similar queer themes as in ‘The Shape Of Water’(2017), but they were very shallow here and just seemed out of place and tropey. The ending just kinda brought it down from anything great though. Once ‘The Creature’ shows up to confront Frankenstein for the first time, it’s miss, after miss, after miss… of opportunity for Frankenstein and ‘The Creature’s development. They hardly talk, ‘The Creature’ just immediately demanding a companion and Frankenstein getting hostile towards him. Neither of them quite dwell on the fact that ‘The Creature’ is more intelligent than when they last met, or how he’s made it there after being left for dead in the castle fire(*sidenote, that was an insane fire, that also conveniently didn’t burn any pertinent papers for ‘The Creature’ to read). Instead they go right into the dynamic of regretful creator and the unwanted creation and it ends with ‘The Creature’ just running off. Then it’s straight to “some time later” and they’re still on this same level of hostility. It’s not until the boat—after both tell their stories that they seem to actually move past the bad blood as it plays into this note of forgiveness to end the cycle of bad fatherhood. But like—it just took one conversation for Frankenstein to not be such a dick to ‘The Creature’ and then ‘The Creature’s willing to forgive Frankenstein for all the hurt he caused him? They never once talked in any of their encounters and suddenly now—when they’re not even really talking, but ‘The Creature’ is pointedly telling the other side of the story to rebuke Frankenstein’s “portrait of a monster” he made for him? It’s like Del Toro noticed how much time he used on everything before and had just quickly wrap it up lest it go on for too long, truncating the buildup to the core of his whole story. My friend and I while watching, we were so fixated on the details of the original story versus the adaptations of it and the typical omissions they end up with. After the fact we finally dug in a little more and I was kinda surprised to see that the original story actually seems to have similar shortcomings, like an equally rushed endIng. But I wonder if that’s not so much the case because of how Del Toro changed the story. He’s quite faithful in a lot of way, but a big difference with his version is how tragic ‘The Creature’ is versus how malicious and vindictive he becomes in the original, being a mirror of the hate he received, but not so much a “good guy” at all. Del Toro plays more into this cycle of fatherhood. Frankenstein being raised by a man that resented him and cruelly instilled the values and lessons that made him the doctor/scientist he became and then ‘The Creature’ briefly only knowing that same cruelty as Frankenstein frustrates himself as he tries to instill greater knowledge onto him. At the end they share that moment of forgiveness to which seems to aim to end that cycle that was perpetrated, but that forgiveness doesn’t feel earned at all. They only meet three times after the castle and two of those times are just not at all on the topic of Frankenstein’s cruelty. It’s referenced and known between them, but never stated or delved in on. The boat is the only time they really talk as equals and suddenly Frankenstein is remorseful and ‘The Creature’ is so ready to grant him that forgiveness as he dies. I don’t think Del Toro properly built up to that moment which was unfortunately the bow that tied it all together. I think there’s so much good that I feel outweighs what doesn’t work here, but what doesn’t work is hard to dismiss. Del Toro was swinging big here but he doesn’t really hit very close to the direction where he’s pointing at. I enjoyed it overall, but—for me, this is another one of Del Toro’s that seems to have something great brewing in his take on the classic story, but it’s not really translated well to an equally great movie.

title: C.O.G.
my_review: It’s a dumb-fun-thriller, but it could’ve probably leaned more into that. It’s not so self-serious, but it also doesn’t come off as silly as it looks.

title: Weapons
my_review: Pretty solid, all things considered. Cregger had a high bar set for himself and though I don’t think this is even near reaching of said bar, it’s still a well made follow-up. Above all, I feel like Cregger’s strength is in writing, but that’s also not as strong here as his last outing was. He tiptoes a good line of horror and comedy, both landing without feeling like they’re sacrificing one for the other(a lá the recent ‘Halloween’ films). And the way he weaves characters into the story just really works for me. In kinda a funny instance, my friend and I initially kinda side-eyed the teacher protagonist for being so “poorly written”, that she was kinda too obtuse to the reality of her situation and it just got her in more trouble. But the slow reveal that she’s a hot mess kinda rectified a lot of those perceptions into appreciating her character a lot for being a uniquely grey-valued character(much like Justin Long in ‘Barbarian’—a character I absolutely was enthralled by). He’s thus far opted for unconventional story structure and I think it’s paid off overall, but I do think it worked more effectively in ‘Barbarian’(2022). It’s still a neat way to rope in characters that help enrich the worldbuilding. But here there’s quite a few POV characters and by the end I kinda felt a little unsatisfied with the brief closure we get for the initial main characters. If this were a book I think the length of writing all this out would smooth that sense of “unfulfillment” out, but in a movie I wished—for example, we got more time with the teacher and the dad teaming up. They just kinda show up together for the climax and they’re not really important to the story anymore. There’s also some—atleast one that really nags at me, “plotholes”(the dreaded overused/misused term) or just missed/forgotten about opportunities:  •One being the ring camera not knowing where the kids went. With all those cameras watching and seeing them run off, none could triangulate—like the dad eventually did and saw they were just going towards a suburban house, not a place lost in the woods? Set it before ring cameras and there’s no issue, but modern day with them and street cameras, security cameras, etc… someone would have noticed or atleast guesstimated. Especially when the genius plan was send a mob of kids out of the house while police searched them bring them back in, nobody saw that?! •Another(not a plothole) was what was the point of snipping the teacher’s hair? It was a Chekov’s Gun that never fired. I feel the clear path was her turning on the dad in the end, rather than the dad just getting insta-possessed and turning on her. This was more just an odd missed opportunity, or a byproduct of some rewrite where that maybe did happen but they changed it to the dad get used for whatever reason. Ehh, but nitpicking aside, it was a fun watch. Absolutely amazing ending. Something I absolutely love in media is unleashing “the floodgates” on the big bad. Like there’s one little factor the good guy has that the bad guy’s got no counter for. I.e. one of my favorite examples(I think mostly just in the movie adaptation —spoilers for this movie) was in ‘Doctor Sleep’(2019) when Daniel releases all the ghosts that haunted him over the years on the terrifying big bad and they just eviscerate her in spectacular fashion. Here, it was child mob—love it.

title: undertone

title: Influencers
my_review: I really liked how this started, I was really looking forward to this and the beginning seemed like a great start for a sequel—but man, I really felt like they squandered alot here. I feel like there’s a stack of different choices they could have taken this movie, choices that felt like they’d be bold and titillating, but this movie takes none of them and that’s really kinda disappointing. I liked that she seemed to be living a normal life, somehow getting off scott-free from the last movie. She had a cute girlfriend she genuinely seemed to like and not be playing a con with, made more evident when an influencer shows up and we really see her mood change. And then I liked how we could see the cogs turn on her disdain for the influencer. I don’t recall the first really leading you to believe there’s anything too deep with CW serial killing influencers. Half cause you can surmise a backstory with her distinguishing birthmark in juxtaposition with girls that make a living off being pretty and half cause stealing an influencer’s life is so lavish and carefree, everything given to them for just making a post. But seeing and honestly understand her disdain for the influencer. How she walks over her genuine romantic getaway that she doesn’t even really care about. She chats up her girlfriend easily which any self-conscious would be jealously-anxious over. She tries hijacking their getaway by making it a thing with her, which again, can easily see CW being super anxious about. That it’s like a compulsion the same way in ‘Dexter’ he’s compelled to kill and has honed that to a complex with killing killers, CW just has that for influencers. It was a good lead in as CW returns to her old ways, but after that I feel like the movie just doesn’t take the more interesting path. Like I for a second believed the title of the movie was literal. That CW and Diane were going to be doing the con, because their love seemed genuine(albeit a few lies) and hell, that’d make the title ‘Influencers’ genius. They even somewhat tease that’s the case but that’s for a later reveal. But from the second CW kills the influencer, I expected it to be this dual life thing where she tries to juggle getting all these influencer perks while having a close girlfriend. And then yeah, I thought “Wow, the girlfriend finds out pretty immediately, that’s cool!” thinking that meant Diane would be apart of it, willing or not. But nope. It’s kinda just a lame lead-in for the actual plot, not really mattering because CW ends up doing exactly what she’s doing in the first, so almost like “Why bother with the girlfriend?” which does become more apparent later. Then the “actual” plot starts. The influencer survivor from the first returns. We see how her life was permanently ruined by the ordeal, how CW even got off because the influencer took all these blame. Her life sucks but that leads her to notice an article and decide she’ll solve the case herself. Cool—I’m in. Influencer victim vs the serial killer, in a globe trotting chase. But again—that’s not quite what happens. It does happen for like twenty minutes, but then we’re on a new character and then right back to CW, the influencer’s investigation not really mattering for most of the movie except to motivate CW and come back at the end. That new character that was introduced, the streamer, he didn’t have the best first impression but honestly he had layers that weren’t quite expected. A cringey ‘Andrew-Tate-type-manosphere-peddling’-dusche, that doesn’t really believe it and just turns off his stream to go sheepishly listen to his curt girlfriend about how to sell that persona better. Like the clear insecurity was a good trait cause he’s desperate to put up a front but the dude’s oddly more genuine than the farce he pulls. I was worried how he’d fit in but thought it was interesting not only that he meets up with the influencer, but almost immediately finds CW in the wild and even confronts her, believing the influencer when nobody else does. He doesn’t hard accuse and he doesn’t know the whole story then, but later in a stream he doesn’t ofcourse bring it up and he’s already siding with the influencer—who’s the good guy here, so his believing her is surprising cause nothing about him seems like he would. I think the movie does use the most of his character, although I think there alot that can be cut out to make room for his stuff being more of the focal point. Something this movie’s not great at is giving a critique on that social interaction with the masses that content creators and influencers have. There was a clear one and he’s hardly seen putting on his persona and it’s not something CW exploits really which seems like the use of her character in this context—showing how phony these people can be. He plays a cool role in getting close with CW, her think she’s seducing him to get close, while he thinks he’s playing her by letting her whilst he plans her demise. And that all comes to a head towards the climax. The climax is where it just lost me completely. First the streamer’s girlfriend just kills herself cause she’s so panicked, but it seems like CW’s plan. Maybe she somehow planned to kill them, but the influencer showing up and it looking like she did it was too perfect. Then she stabs the streamer—which also feels too perfect, but okay whatever it’s mayhem. Then the strangest fight occurs, strange because it seems like CW’s intentionally trying to lose the fight. She awkwardly trips on a chair to start she hardly hits the influencer, just kinda grapples her and catches what she throws. It wasn’t until halfway through, while bombastic club music keeps blaring, that I realized this was in earnest and it’s just a bad fight scene. It’s not shot terribly, but it’s so clunky and awkwardly choreographed most of the time. So influencer wins and I’m still thinking this is somehow apart of the master plan. She only ties CW up—which I also thought was a strange thing to predict she’d do, but also weird on the influencer’s part. But then she just leaves to CW’s hideout to find her whole setup. I’m over here thinking—“Genius. She’s made it look like the influencer fucker her and the streamer up and now she’s at the hub of operations where she’ll somehow pin everything on her, maybe even her girlfriend’s death.” Fuck. No. The influencer for some reason just turns on the streamer’s stream(I’m pretty sure she does it, cause why else would it be setup for a reveal?) and lets CW convict herself for good as she kills the streamer. But that’s such a dumb ending. I can’t really conceive of why she left to CW’s place, assumedly to save Diane, but if she believed that just call the cops? She fortunately finds everything incriminating and saves the day, but it all feels so unsatisfying. We hardly see her most of the movie, so she doesn’t really do anything to really entrap CW, she just shows up. She kinda lives what CW’s capable of, but not really enough to know what she’d do. CW winning in how I thought would also be dumb cause of all the coincidences, but I don’t know what her fuckin’ game plan was there. She even calls the influencer a killer as if she was playing that angle but the influencer getting away like she did proves how poorly conceived that idea would have been, especially when the streamer just sees the texts and realizes it’s CW. I feel like the better ending is CW winning if only cause I feel like that’s what the movie kinda sets us up for. In the first movie it’s the same deal, although the influencer winning is a good twist that feels earned cause CW got careless and thought little of her and that she’d die like the rest. CW’s loss is a surprise, but it felt earned, this one just feels—dumb. Like they didn’t know how to wrap this up or rather they just wanted it to end as it did and didn’t do a good job building towards that. Plus the ending with her hacking the friend and groupies of the streamer was too silly. They just stand there and watch and she just kills more, cause she’s lost that hard. I just didn’t care enough at that point to enjoy the unleashed CW. Felt like the movie also had missed opportunities about whatever commentary this eeks on being about. The streamer being a toxic misogynist isn’t really relevant, just a character trait, which is so out of place in this movie for it to not be relevant. Maybe just in how CW tries to seduce him by playing a scared girl that wants him bad. But really the AI nonsense really bothered me. The first movie did this too, although it’s just barely enough to be somewhat believable—like I just recall the voice stuff and video generating/filters used. And maybe I don’t know AI’s capabilities, but I don’t think this is it. That she can ask ChatGPT to be a bat-computer for her and scan faces and geolocate exact spots based on corners of images. It’s too much, but what it really hurts it just the effectiveness as CW as a villain. How she easily maneuvers through the social platforms in ways the people at the top don’t even conceive of. Just giving her a bat-computer takes away her skills and takes away the commentary this might’ve had going.  I also think we didn’t need the flashback sequence at all. It was already pretty clear CW loved Diane from the opening, if you wanted to hammer that home just add her crying after killing her in the scene where she kills here. There’s nothing gained from the flashback, just weird additional tragedy for CW, but why? What does seeing her bonding with Diane give us—Diane’s dead and gone, nothing in the story is triggering her memory of her, it’s a useless flashback. A flashback that could’ve easily been cut out to add more to the influencer or streamer plotlines. It’s still looks good, some of the writing works and actings pretty decent. Cassandra Naud is still the breakout here. She’s so stunning and captivating as this role that seems(probably is I feel like) tailored for her and I can only hope that she pops off in some way. Still definitely on the “gem”-end of indie movies. I’m just so frustrated that there’s several good movies here and the one that this is—isn’t that great.

title: Exit 8
my_review: Didn’t quite expect what this turned into. I guess “spot the anomaly” was some trending idea of late since I’ve seen virtually the same plot as this in a couple of games. But I don’t think there’s much of a movie here. Second time this month I’ve brought up this movie—‘Beyond The Infinite Two Minutes’(2020)(the other time was for ‘Triangle(2009)), where-in they have a pretty fun ‘time-loop’ premise and a clever execution, but there’s just no progression of story to it. It’s just loop after loop and that’s it, that’s the schtick. There’s some loose story attached, but it’s beholden to the gimmick getting enough attention. It works for a bit, but when they have to move passed it, it feels like they never planned that far ahead and so they just keep doing the loop until it gradually finds some inelegant stopping place.

title: Dangerous Animals
my_review:
Really wanted to like this as some campy fun— which there’s flashes of, but boy is it just kinda plain mediocre at times. Maybe I wasn’t on the same wavelength, but the movie felt too straightforward for any of it to be tongue-in-cheek. Like Jai Courtney felt rightfully hammed up— and that’s what I wanted, but the rest felt so basic and aimed for a genuine horror rather than that fun campy kind. The problem with that though is it’s just kinda too weak to be genuine. Also every underwater and shark shot looked like a SyFy original movie

For some reason, I actually kept thinking of ‘The Loved Ones’(2009), maybe just the Aussieness of it all, so kinda funny to see it’s the same director.

title: Bring Her Back
my_review: Ooo, I was not a fan of this. ‘Talk To Me’(2022) was a movie I very much feel was something fresh for the horror genre and I was eager for whatever followed its wake. And while I think it’s sometimes unfair to hold a movie to a separate movie’s standards(fair game in a series) this movie wasn’t giving that same juice and unfortunately was doing worse than just being passable. Just so very annoying a movie to watch. Children in horror are inherently fickle and dubious to hold entirely against a film when it’s entirely possible that they’re being portrayed earnestly and honestly to how frustrating kids can and are expected to be in the face of high pressure situations. But boy was it just getting so very headache inducing in the way the drama built up around the boy and his sister. His lack of communication whenever pertinent(he’s so mindful to speak up when not really necessary). The sister yapping for context rather than listening to the arguments happening around her. That classic case of “he said, she said”, but betraying her ride or die after something so insubstantial. Especially when he runs off after seeing the possessed-boy in the yard covered in blood and decides to not convey any of what Sally Hawkins was doing in that scene. Aside from that though, I’m really not crazy about gross out horror. Gross looking horror is fine, but horror through gross out is just a chore and an immediate dampener on enjoyment. It can work like say in ‘Barbarian’(2022)(hairy bottle), were its not constant and nauseating, but hits when it needs to. But in this movie’s case of a constant baseline of grotesqueness that make me just see the whole movie as grimy in an “critically put-off”-sorta way, the same way you’d feel watching something like ‘Hoarders’. It’s also just not a wildly compelling story? Classic “foster parent with dark ideations for their foster kids”-type story, but with a extremely vague, seemingly “pure shock value” hidden story that’s oddly very unremarked upon outside of this “ritual and mechanic. ‘Talk To Me’ was somewhat similar in this regard, the ‘inner mechanics of how the macguffin works’ being unimportant so as much as the usage of the macguffin. But I there’s just so little context for what Sally Hawkins is up to that you kinda don’t care about all the video tape stuff— as much as they like to just play them for shock value. I got everything she was doing, but just the “how and why” were too unanswered that it was unsatisfying to just go through it all to just leave it hanging. Don’t need a whole backstory on whoever’s on the tapes but rather when Sally Hawkins got tangled with and obsessed with it. It’s fine for the most part. A bit rough going down, but inherently it’s competent. About on par with most modern-horror. *Which sidenote— I’m kinda over the shock of people maiming themselves as the only thing going for a horror movie. Yes it’s “crazy” to see someone fuck their own shit up, but like, there’s other ways to make things scary. In this movie’s case I was especially done seeing the little boy literally stuff himself with objects that tore up his mouth and protruded his stomach. ‘Smile 2’(2024) gets a pass because it’s also got the paranoia bit and I love it, unlike this one.

title: A Breed Apart
my_review: It’s pretty bad on its own, unfortunately not in the fun way I was hoping for. But the AI— the atrociously implemented AI, really kicks it down another peg. I wanted better for the ‘Fall’-girls, or atleast something bad that was watchable.

title: Final Destination Bloodlines
my_review: I do like how quickly they all become numb to any sorta of death in this “tight knit” family. All of them lowkey(well, save one lovable obvious one) being quite selfish about saving themselves over grieving eachother. They do two back-to-back funerals, then just don’t do a funeral, then just see two cousins mutilated bodies and walk away, mother bisected like it was inconvenient and then finally “dealing” with everything and still going to prom!?!? It’s almost as if this was just a bad week or two rather than an almost life crippling amount of successive traumatic events.

title: Until Dawn
my_review: I think this is intentionally starkly different from the game in an effort to spin the series in this weird franchised ‘Cabin In The Woods’-type “mystery box of scenarios”. But it’s going about it in a strange way that this just doesn’t standout very much as a movie. Not to say the videogame of ‘Until Dawn’ is all that unique, but at the time it was pretty impressive to play a bad horror movie with some notable actors. Here they got the ‘Groundhog Day’ aspect which is neat, but it’s kinda underutilized. It mostly feels like random bullshit every time that they don’t really get better from, just more on their toes. So in that regard it’s kinda silly that(seemingly) no one else has “bested” this as these guys aren’t even that remarkably capable.  But it is much more watchable than I expected. Once I realized it’s not really trying to be the game(despite some echoes here and there), its existence doesn’t feel as under scrutiny. Will say though, the water scene was kinda cool.

title: Marshmallow
my_review: It started off somewhat promising, but the longer it went the more flaws it accumulated. Wasn’t a fan of whenever something dramatic happened and we spend just far too long in a heightened moment accentuating it. Also it really didn’t help that the sound was just blaringly obnoxious at times. Both in those heightened moments and just in general, couldn’t hear a goddamn word at points. And I’m a stout advocate against subtitles when you don’t need them—so some scenes felt kinda entirely ruined by them being gratuitous with the sound. Also the writing for these kids was pretty bad. Very Stephen King in how these kids talk to eachother, like a couple’ve middle-aged adults candidly talking. Writing in general might’ve been kinda weak, cause by the end I kinda feel like the whole premise is a bit ‘donkey brained’ with how easily things could go as wrong as they do. It’s fine overall, but could’ve used alot more polish.

title: Sinners
my_review: I liked how goofy the vampires were in trying to get invited in. Deep cut, but really reminded me of the DORKLY ‘Plants vs Zombies’ vid of the walnut slowly turning into a zombie and casually asking to take a nibble of brains.

title: Locked
my_review: So much yapping, so little else.

title: Borderline
my_review: Overcompensates with just too much going on and really makes the actors have to shoulder this whole thing whether they can or not, or with what they’re given or lackthereof. Will say though, Baptista was a welcome surprise as she actually thrived quite well here. So much so though that I kinda wished she was more of the focus, especially with that random lesbian-ship that almost took off.

title: Ash
my_review: A whole movie just to reveal what you may have incidentally guessed(I did) in the first 10min as if it were some revelation. Should’ve been more straightforward, it’s nothing new, but the mild shakeup in storytelling isn’t doing anything for this. As well as the over abundant jumpscares and obnoxious rave lighting.

title: Clown in a Cornfield
my_review: Shockingly not as terrible as I thought it’d be. That title, the low coverage around this, you’d think this were from SYFY’s trenches—except it’s got Kevin Durand! It can’t be all bad if you’ve got Kevin Durand! But really, it’s actually kinda a decent slasher even—still pretty basic, but it’s got some pep in its step that kinda takes it to a pretty enjoyable level. Ending’s bad though, aside from it feeling very derivative of a certain “fuzzy ice cream cone”-from a trilogy, it leaves things very unresolved. Like they’re not leaving a door open for a sequel, but rather they’re not even installing a door to begin with. Fun comedic-teen-slasher, not the low produced slop it might seem like.

title: Slanted
my_review: Really weird movie. Strangely it’s much less strange than you’d expect with such a story. Just ends up pretty straightforward and kinda dull. It’s got interesting themes to play around with but I’m not sure it ever really does figure out how. It’s shallow and as bland as what it wants to ridicule for be as such. You know each story beat well before they come in right on cue. It’s like someone saw ‘The Substance’(2024) and thought “How can I make this less captivating?”

title: Good Boy
my_review: First off—that was a pretty cute dog and they indeed carried the movie. No notes on the dog’s performance. But there’s just not much here, unfortunately. They’re leaning too hard on the gimmick in a way that just makes this a bit unsatisfactory as a whole movie. The dog isn’t necessarily sleuthing out exposition, so you’re mostly just watching “dog reacts to thing” over and over. I can appreciate the grounded take, but I can’t not feel like an episode of ‘Courage The Cowardly Dog’(1999) accomplishes much the same and much more in short 11–20min episodes, what this movie struggled to do in not even 80min. And kinda worse is it still feels a bit untapped in how much they could have used the dog’s POV to frame the movie in a more interesting way. They’re ‘Tom & Jerry’ing it by just cutting all the humans faces off as if the dog’s in his own pocket world to react to, but that world just looks and sounds like ours. The dog just seems super paranoid because the owner is just so unaware—not that that shouldn’t be the case, but that the movie never really does enough to justify why the owner’s just not seeing these things. Like I want to know why the dog in the horror movie is barking at an empty corner(not this movie, but in the general premise). They fill that corner with a contextual jumpscare, but it’s not distinguished enough between why the dog’s spooked by it and why the owner just doesn’t register any of it. We see a dog’s nightmare and it’s full of colors the dog can’t even perceive. Like if they were going so hard into the gimmick, there’s more than just showing  “*dog reacts*” and waist high dialogue. Neat idea, very good dog—but not much of a movie here.

title: Heart Eyes
my_review: Could stand to be a bit sillier than it’s already trying to be. Nails its balance of genres, slasher & rom-com, but it’s just not satisfying enough in either to be a straightforward as it ends up being. But I think with just a bit more slapstick it could really do wonders here(or in a not entirely unwanted sequel).

title: Touch Me
my_review:
Had more fun with this than I expected—not that I really knew what to expect. Doesn’t get as fucky as you’d think with such a premise, but it’s much more than just “live action hentai”, so it’s not really trying to be so sexual and fucky with it. That exists and is out there in all the pornographic glory a degenerate could want. But this movie’s much more about the prospect of using such a wild sexual experience to unhealthily cope with past traumas and create a codependency on friends and lovers and anything else that gives a quick fix that is so easy to get addicted to. 

It’s weird, it’s goofy, but I like the originality. Kinda surprised it’s got so many harsh reviews, but this definitely isn’t for everyone. It’s a certain kinda sci-fi/(horror)/comedy that I know is just super polarizing. I myself have a few that I’m just not into at all(‘John Dies At The End’(2012)). And I can also see some adverse feelings because it’s just not nearly as horny as you’d think would be a guarantee. But it’s just a silly lil’ movie about toxic tentacle sex, just have fun with it.

title: Opus
my_review: I really didn’t care for this. There’s plenty wrong here and boy does that make the title all the more ironic. It totally is a rip of all those movies everyone prattles off(‘The Menu’(2022), ‘Midsommar’(2019), etc….) but there’s genuinely just no teeth to it. It’s got kooky quirks and a fanciful(ish) setting but just nothing behind it. Only way this would work is if it was funnier and/or a parody of the aforementioned, but no, it’s self-serious and immensely derivative. Bad movie.

title: Together
my_review: Solid. Maybe a bit noncommittal to the full Cronenberg levels it could have been(like cutting away from the saw and keeping it a bit blurry)—but still solid. It did have some oddly silly moments that felt out of place(frantically smashing pills to snort), but also some decent jumpscares carried by some unnerving sound design. Aside from Cronenberg though, the story and style felt reminiscent of a Junji Ito story. The slow dread of characters changing and especially some of the flash on the screen jumpscares—specifically Franco housing Brie’s hair(also the amalgam of Franco and Brie opening the door). Also this was maybe the most normal role I’ve seen Damon Herriman play and that immediately put me on edge wondering what was up with him. But I love the detail of seeing the wedding picture and not being able to quite place which one was supposed to be him and then finally realizing neither was, he’s just the amalgam of the two guys. It was kinda weird though that he’s the only one trying to join them together, is the whole town not in on it or rather are there no more cult members? Seems like kinda odd he’s the only person despite a full crowd being there at the wedding, unless I missed some line about what became of everyone else.

title: The Ugly Stepsister
my_review: There’s alot of appreciated style here with me, but ‘grossout “horror”’ is just something that really turns me off of something and boy did this really aim for that at times. It does go for some really ‘out there’-imagery that really makes this stick with you, but same could be said for the queasiness it started giving me. There were some odd story beats though that also kinda weighed this down for me. The other “ugly” stepsister had her own weird bubble of development going on and it doesn’t really fit anywhere in this story. And though this is from a different pov in the classic ‘Cinderella’-story, Cinderella was still oddly used at times, only really popping in now-and-then for some story beat. As a dumb sidenote, it admittedly it took me a good thirty minutes into this to realize it was a ‘Cinderella’ retelling. Wild to say, especially with that title(in hindsight for me), but I think I just started thinking about “Ugly Duckling” or something? But I was surprised to see a beautiful ‘stepsister’ appear and distinctly thought “Oh, that’s odd, the story usually has two stepsisters…” So I must have thought about ‘Cinderella’, but I guess I didn’t realize the POV was on one of the ugly stepsisters, thinking our protagonist was the “Cinderella” probably. It was a very dumb moment for me. Also the nurse was the most beautiful, imo.

title: Companion
my_review: Good-fun watch. Really wish I hadn’t let myself get spoiled after avoiding so much about it as this did a good job teasing the reveal. But overall something with the writing left me a bit unsatisfied. That for as clever as this could be, it still ignored logic just to leapfrog to some deeper meaning that doesn’t feel entirely earned in my opinion. Where Iris’ robotic tendencies are only beholden to dramatic effect and her triumph is only convenient when needed. Like I appreciate more how the robot triumph was handled in ‘Ex Machina’(2014). The android, Ava, does have wants and desires and seems to thrive on freedom when she obtains it, but she never “breaks the code” so to say. Everything she does is within her creator’s intent for an human passing android that can seamlessly pass the Turing Test. She is just that and just as desperate and manipulative as the human “protagonist” who ends up lying to and manipulating the creator into an escape plan for the Ava.  The difference it has with ‘Companion’ is she manipulates him(the protagonist) into believing that she “broke the code”, had a soul, truly was helpless enough and worthy of rescue. She’s not actually any of those things as much as she’s programmed to appear so and cognizant enough to comprehend her limitations paired either her unintentional desire to be independent as any other human would desire. She isn’t “human” but she exhibits everything a human would as was her design. Iris(and Patrick) on the other hand has all the same qualities, but is just saved by something like “magic code breaking”. Her triumph over her toxic exe isn’t so much earned as it is brute forced to happen. They pull the “toxic exe manipulations” at the end, that even though she “broke free” that “programming” was still there, but how does she overcome that? She’s just kills him in the end anyway. It’s a victory that’s only gained because the metaphor’s happy ending demands it even though that’s not usually how it happens IRL, victims being able to flip so easily on their abusers. Heck it’s a victory that’s shouldn’t have even happened because it’s also magic code breaking “love” that brings about the problem and the solution. It’s very human but that feels at odds with this movie and its lack of conveying that their world operates any differently than the real world. But honestly, even if it did à la ‘Wild Robot’(2024)— just have their robots defy their robotic nature, I’m not crazy about it when the world is made so non-fantastical and suddenly something only solved by proclaiming magic happens. I dunno, I think to movies where vehicles and other robots are given some degree of personification and that doesn’t bother me at all, maybe because those instances are usually an extension of a real person’s humanity shining through, The Terminator, ‘G Gundam’s Shining Gundam, The Iron Giant, ‘Her’s Samantha, etc… but that just doesn’t feel right here, especially when she had to be jailbroken to let the instigating moment happen.(Which the movie could lean on to explain the “magical defying moment”, but it doesn’t really seem to think of that of an issue to utilize such an explanation, so it’d only really be headcannon) I really did like it, but that landing just seems counterintuitive to its a pretty effective metaphor of objectification and toxic psychological abuse. Though maybe it’s apples and oranges as ‘Ex Machina’s kinda in a different level without much of any of the fun in ‘Companion’ and I’m just nitpicking too much.

title: Werewolves
my_review: Needed more imagination of what a “Werewolf-purge” meant for humanity. Like silver bullets distribution, “Wolf-Attack” insurances pacifists isolating themselves better, muzzles… there’s a lot that could be thought of and this just didn’t do it or even attempt to. It’s just a “A—> B —> A” story that hits all the “straight to DVD”-beats, but with ‘werewolves’.

title: Compulsion
my_review: Surprisingly dug this. It’s a fairly watchable erotic thriller with some hammy writing and questionable acting, but it feels in earnest at that level, not played up or mistakenly self-confident. Like if it had maybe some film grain and a bit more stylized lighting for every scene, it might be pretty primed for some cultish status, I reckon.  Plus it’s honestly pretty refreshing that an erotic thriller actually commits to the sexual aspect. I feel like lately I’ve seen so many (often bad) movies lately that pretend to be erotic thrillers, but end up akin to something slightly more titillating than Lifetime movies can be. That or it’s just a really bad softcore-adjacent thing or horrendous Tubi shovelware. This movie however is straight up front about it and it’s actually apart of the plot—which to me is what makes a good erotic thriller. When it’s not just thrown in for the “breasts-of-it-all”, but to actually use it as an emotion to evoke like any other genre.

title: We Bury the Dead
my_review:
I’m unsure if there’s a good name for it, but this is one of those “journey movies” that follow a character from point A–B and along the way it builds this collage of characters and locations with unique rules and laws while the main character reflects on point B in the downtime between. Basically ‘Apocalypse Now’(1979) & the only other that comes to mind right now is ‘Ad Astra’(2019). Though I’m not sure if this journey was particularly interesting nor did it ever really feel like a big build up to me? 

I never got quite into this and its unique take on zombies is unfortunately not so unique. That and it has to compete with the revival of the ‘28 [units of time] Later’-series which has come back and making big swings while doing it. It does seem like this got made well before, but it releasing now after ‘28 Years Later’(2025) kinda rocked my world—well it’s not really helping this movie that also wants to focus more on the human aspect of a zombie apocalypse.

Daisy Ridley is why I came and she does deliver, but I don’t think this is gonna stand out at all through the test of time.

title: Don't Move

It would need another lead in the mix to balance it out from just being lopsided until it's not. Like Chewbacca carrying a dismantled C-3PO.

title: Bone Lake
my_review:
This got better as it kept going. I had grievances pretty early on—Sage(off-brand Florence Pugh) being a major one in that she felt very antagonistic in her relationship with the oafish Diego. But as it kept going her character kinda flipped a switch—both of them in fact when they just finally break the spell to acknowledge how freaky the situation has been rather than keep lying about everything, which was very refreshing. And then by the end I felt like there was just substantial more style and inspiration in the filmmaking, which I really wish it started with. 

But there’s also just some awkward juggling going on. I couldn’t quite vibe out of this was supposed to be campy and/or erotic and/or thrilling as it kinda half commits to all three while never fully embracing either aswell. Like the name and marketing and opening itself felt very on the nose, but it’s surprisingly conservative with the nudity and sex scenes—despite the hung dong in the aforementioned opening. And the story kept bouncing in and out of campy romp or thrilling-mind-games, never feeling all that funny as there’s some genuine intrigue at work, but also never that serious as goofy as the villains turn out to be. 

What it turns into with the full slasher horror is what I wished it was more of and just being a bit less calm about everything. Like go all in on the eroticism since it plays so much to the narrative, keep us guessing to the intentions of the eccentric sibling-couple. This actually reminded me alot of ‘Speak No Evil’(2022)/(2024), new situations being proposed that you wonder how you’d react to, seeing these characters deal with said situations. Especially the 2024 American remake(atleast I remember it more there) where McAvoy really weaponizes his sexuality and machismo lifestyle to emasculate the Dad. That kinda being what happens here, but like I said—it never quite commits. Feel like when the whole identity of sex is apart of this movie, it’s kinda wild that none of the leads are so willing to bare all(or the movie didn’t ask of them), just the two randos in the opening. So they flirt with the sexual dynamics but only in a hypothetical sense rather than literal—which hinders its impact.

Still though, by the end it did kinda shape up nicely. Once they start going for gore it feels like the movie just flips another switch and gets much much better all around—like I gotta mention how oddly striking the shot was of them on the boat after it was all said and done. Fun watch, kinda a lighter ‘Speak No Evil’ and a less anxious ‘Barbarian’(2022).

my_review:

Because I couldn’t decide whether to make a jokey review or a real one or choose between two I’ll just leave these, lol.
