title: Speak No Evil
my_review: I’ll be honest, I did not care at all for ‘Speak No Evil’(2022). I got the “point” of it, but I thought it’s commentary stood in the way of story far too much that it became more asinine than twisted/scary. So I wasn’t at all interested in a remake going in until I heard they went a different direction. Suffice to say, I think this is just a straight up improvement of the original. For one, I think the 2024 version adds a lot of context and character which I felt the original was grossly lacking. Ant in particular was such a highlight here now that he’s given more agency and personality. Not to say it’d be “unrealistic” for the boy to be so meek and broken being in that situation, but I found it incredibly effective seeing him desperately trying rather than being a “lil’ weirdo” that in retrospect you understand him better, but he still comes off as just general “creepy horror dressing”, where in this version I was so anxious for him(mostly because I knew what became of him in the original). The daughter also worked a lot better. The bunny is still infuriating, but I thought her dependency on it in this version worked better. I also thought it worked well having Ant confide more with her and even show her the truth first. And of course there’s the major departure having a more actioney climax rather than a helpless. 2022 version was definitely more arthouse and 2024- more broadly appealing. But I found the “action” to be immensely anxiety inducing. These people don’t become Rambo when backed into a corner, they’re terrified of doing anything to fight back. And that felt so refreshing and grounded compared to other thrillers. Also James McAvoy. Very much about this remake.

title: Cloud
my_review: A cautionary tale for the rampant Pokémon TCG scalping. Since discovering ‘Cure’(1999), I’ve been clamoring for another similar hit from Kiyoshi Kurosawa, but I’ve honestly been more disappointed than not and this didn’t quite change that fact. The first half was promising, had that same tense atmosphere I really dig with Kurosawa, but once things kick off halfway through, it just kinda drops off. Really it’s about when the movie reaches the scene that made the poster that it starts to drop off. I’m not even sure if I got the point when it was all said and done? Guy’s a dick but this level of revenge feels unwarranted and quite the turn of events. That alone could be interesting enough, not having much more than an interesting inciting plot for some action, that’s pretty normal and inoffensible. But it’s that the action’s kinda “meh”, that it can’t lean on it for me. I got the vibe this was trying to go for some tense violent realism, something akin to what the American remake of ‘Speak No Evil’(2024) accomplished— tension from incapable protagonists( and antagonists in this movie’s case) trying to fight back against “real stakes”. That every turn you might expect disaster because that’s what the characters dread. But this movie just lacks any of that tension once it’s thrown up on screen. It just becomes an unimpressive action movie which is what brings me back to the point of this all? “The dickish Yoshii reaps what he sowed”, but what he sowed wasn’t that terrible honestly. We see so much of just his perspective that we lack anything tangible from the mooks that create a “I hate Ratel”-Club and why they want to torture him to death on a livestream. The story gives no real beats as to “why?” except for a random guy that claims Yoshii ruined his whole life seconds before dying himself. We kinda infer on the others, maybe a slight tidbit for the exe-boss being psychotic to begin with, but nothing that really drives their drive. Nothing for us to infer on whether Yoshii deserves this or he’s just unlucky to have slighted so many wackos. Same with his girlfriend who takes a dramatic heel turn because Yoshii isn’t pampering her enough and Sano said “begone thot”. Speaking of Sano, his role was the worst of all. Don’t get me wrong, I love the ride-or-die Sano, but what the hell was with him? Why does he care? What’s with his ‘John Wick’(2014)-like connections? Yoshii’s never particularly kind to him nor does he(Sano) seem so ill/fixated on Yoshii enough to go so far out of his way for him. The writing just can’t string these all together in a satisfying way and every new turn feels like some hacky amateur writer’s creepypasta. New elements are just thrown in and don’t really go anywhere. Hence why the action is so much more disappointing because there’s nothing else to really prop this up like I think it’s supposed to. Disappointing. I’m forever chasing that ‘Cure’-dragon the same way Yoshii’s probably gonna be chasing those Switch 2 consoles.

title: Blink Twice
my_review:
Interesting concept, but it's really only just that. This film—intentional or not, brings together an amalgamation of ideas from many contemporary films that might have some strong commentary on a social structure or just a striking look about them. It has its own spin on things, a genuinely interesting one, but if you think about it for more than a minute, the entire premise just falls apart, or rather, it just becomes incredibly superficial.

So if it's intentionally pulling from others in the same commentative genre it tries to sidle itself with, then it's borrowing so much that it glosses over a lot of the connective tissue that usually makes others in the genre so memorable. Like, it's so preoccupied with the 'twist' and 'commentary' and 'style' that it kind of feels like they expected the rest to fall into place due to how neglected the story's writing is.

Though if it was unintentional, then it's unfortunately "late to the party," especially if the party asked everyone to bring some snack or drink, and this just rolled up with "Pepsi" and plain "Fritos" after others had already brought "Coke" and "Doritos" (great analogy, I know). But it's not really doing anything clever with the ideas it's toying with that you haven't seen done better or more expansively in other properties.

It's got soft punches across the board, with the biggest strength being the distinct look of it and the stacked cast of big names. So it just feels like it's destined to mostly be remembered as some trivia question like, "What film starred Simon Rex, Geena Davis, and Kyle MacLachlan?"

title: Shelby Oaks
my_review: Hmmmmmmm, not great. I kinda dug the premise of “What would have happened after ‘The Blair Witch Project’(1999)?” but it’s also kinda doing way too much extra to tell that story. It starts as found footage, then a cheap-Netflix-shovelware-esk mockumentary about the found footage, then an actual movie, then back to the found footage and then back to the mockumentary and back.… Each one of them feeling pretty half-baked and worse off cause they take away from one another. I think this should have just been a mockumentary-full stop. So much idiocy is born of the nature of it being a normal movie where the main character is perhaps the dumbest character on film—giving so much fuel to the trope of ‘dumb white people in a horror’. If it was just a mockumentary the whole time she would never be alone doing these stupidly bold things like going alone to apparently haunted locations and possible sites of her sister’s demise/fate—all at night. There’d be at least be a small crew of people accompanying, giving a smidge more sense to whatever compels this woman to be so daft. But I also just think the movie gains little from switching to a standard movie when the storytelling and style still resemble that of a documentary. Maybe it’s that personal aspect tied to the POV of the sister, but to that end—just make the sister personally involved with making a doc, it could be she’s honoring her sister in making it. It also gives a seamless way to intercut back to footage that was found and just exposit the lore in a much less contrived way. Then there’s just the fact that the special effects don’t look great when so easily seen. Effects look well enough in the found footage, but in the standard movie it look goofy as hell at times(still better than using AI though which seems to be the go to for killer canine movies lately). But unfortunately the story’s very weak. Mia is a very bland character that’s so one-minded and stupid per the script ordering her to march forward—alone. Which is weird cause the husband’s not very dismissive of her wild musings, but still seems to runoff every chance he gets to leave her alone(also—off topic, why the hell did he and every other person she talked to, just leave her with blood spattered on her face for the whole beginning? No one said “Let me get you a towel,” as they stared her in the eyes to talk?). The motivations to get her to go places get increasingly asinine as she just seems to keep making poor judgement calls, again and again. I feel it’s bad writing when characters feel like they’re behaving only because ink on a page dictates them to, which is what the sister does the whole movie. There’s also this mix of supernatural cult and just a predatory kidnapping that feels very uninspired and starts to even get boring as we keep learning more. The monster/killer/villains are incredibly unremarkable, fat balding man with a mildly creepy smile is not at all menacing, atleast in how he’s presented, cause he’s hardly in the movie. Also keeping that baby was donkey brained, old lady literally had a demon behind her in the underground tunnel and then levitated the sister in front of Mia, just so she could complete a blood ritual—and she just looks at the baby like “Awwww.” Like you know, demons walk this Earth now, spawns of demons should not be pampered, especially when the sister who’s been in the shit says “We gotta kill it.” At the very least bring some psychic or priest in, do an exorcism, that’s not farfetch’d with all Mia’s seen, but I guess it is farfetch’d that Mia’s do anything sensible. As for the filmmaking it’s also a bit mediocre. There’s alot of influences at work and a lot of “mixed mediums” that aren’t showcasing much of a style through any of them. When it keeps jumping from what kind of movie it wants to be, you’re never really appreciating any of them because they’re never allowed that time to breathe. And then what you do see the most of is just so annoying and full of cheap jumpscares and all that “influence”. The scares worked best in the found footage, atleast most of the time—actually just the one scene with the towering figure vaguely in the window. Except then the movie kinda takes the time to basically circle it for you, so—ehhhh. I like Stuckman. He was there for me to stoke my interest when I first started getting into wanting to watch reviews of movies as I started getting more into movies myself. He’s a bit corny and fanboyish which is how I grew out of watching him, but he’s just trying to be positive and his love for movies is undeniable and I do think he sometimes gets too much flack for that(in seeing his crossover on Double Toasted, he came across so genuine and grateful). It’s cool he got to finally make one for himself—I wish it worked much better for me, but I also hope the experience will be learned from. This is his first real feature after all, so there’s plenty room to grow. We’ll get ‘em next time.

title: Trap
my_review: I love Josh Hartnett. Entertaining inspite of itself at times. Hartnett and Shyamalan's direction really make this for a fun game of "cats and mouse", but boy does the writing seem to actively work against this at times. Hartnett's "Cooper" is demonstrably super cunning and perceptive and the "bad guys"- the police have overwhelming advantages, yet the movie feels the need to give both the same amount of asspulls and convenience to help ushed them along. Nothing feels organic as some invisible force makes the police and their lame profiler know exactly where to ain their resources without knowing exactly where, so it comes off like they know exactly what to do, but have to play dumb for the plot's sake(like a man trying to sneak around a blind lawyer whose actually not blind, but they must play their part). And the same with Cooper, dude's on top of it, but there's still so many scenes of overt intervention guiding him on the best way forward rather than he just organically finding said paths. And all the while, both do shit that would never in a million years work, so you have to really suspend your disbelief at times, but Hartnett and the tension of it all really mitigate that fact from being entirely true. The story also has some crazy jumps that're sometimes hard to fully buy into. Chiefly lil' Shyamalan- "Lady Raven"'s willingness to play directly with fire and there nit being any sensible reason for the fact that she gets to "get away with it". Cooper will just turn his brain off when dealing with her and it gets more frustrating, than entertaining, in getting to see someone directly challenge Cooper with new dillemas. All in all though, it's pretty fun. They even let the bad guy "win" in the end which is always a pet peeve of mine in the story just refusing the well earned victory for the baddie for the sole reason being that "bad guys can't win".

title: A Quiet Place: Day One
my_review: Surprisingly tender for a 'blockbuster-apocalyptic-horror-prequel-sequel'. I mean thes first movie definitely had refreshing waves of intimacy showing with the family that definitely made it stand out more than just being "that really quiet movie", but I honestly think this surprisingly takes it a step further. A terminal woman's last wish for just a slice of home is such an understandably human plot to warrant what's a "really dumb" suicide mission and her meeting a woefully anxious and panic ridden man that decides to cling to her and her comfort cat adds another endearing layer atop that. I loved seeing them stick together and pull eachother up to keep going as the forge a friendship in the first days of an apocalyptic scenario. Lupita Nyong'o and Joseph Quinn really make the friendship sell this sweet friendship and they really nail the dance between terror and tenderness all through very subdued and quiet performances. I find myself enjoying their characters much more than I did the Abbott Family. The story/movie misses alot've those weird "plotholes" that happen when you keep asking questions about how the Abbott Family live their lives. And their(Eric & Samira) characters' "dumb choices" are clearly understandable and knowingly obtuse, unlike an angsty teen disobeying strict rules that she knows keep the family alive- because she's seen the ramifications of not following them which leads to her Dad getting killed.(My opinions are showing, lol). ***Though I will say that Eric's steadfast choice to follow Samira is a bit inexplicable. Just doing it for the cat is a so-so reason. Reading that he was supposed to reveal that he was down in the subway to kill himself before it flooded and he ended up how we meet him, well that's just seems like such a strong choice of character development that would've clearly and emotionally made his motivations all the clearer and made his friendship with Samira even more touching and less one-sided. In the sense that he seems so altruistic to support Samira through her reasonably selfish quest, but if he had this development it would've added another layer to their dynamic which I don't think Samira gets to fulfill until the very end. Plus it would've made Eric seem more like a Kindred spirit to Samira as they would've both been people that have resigned their lives and merely wish to do one more thing with what they have left. And then at the end, Samira's final moment with Eric would be all the more emotional as she gets him to choose to keep living rather than die with her. Mayhaps the most disappointed I've been at seeing what could've been in a movie. But as the movie is, it's human and still thrilling. Where I once kinda rolled my eyes at the prospect a growing franchise of spin-offs off of a surprise hit gimmick in 'A Quiet Place'- whose own sequel was a big step down, I'm now a bit more optimistic of the kind've stories that might come. Although I don't think I'll ever come around on the alien portion of it all, cause nothing productive comes from dwelling too much on the workings of them and even this movie did little more to mitigate that issue.

title: MaXXXine
my_review: Much like how 'X' was for me, I felt there were alot've interesting different ways this could've played out and it just didn't really choose any of them. But the vibes and acting were definitely there. There was just a little something missing for me- probably some film grain effect, that was missing to fully make this feel as vintage as it looked, but otherwise it's very stylish and nostalgic for that time. The 'Once Upon A Time In Hollywood' similarities are undeniable really, like this movie's aesthetic and story are definitely what Tarantino's "wet dreams" are made of. But oddly it's the "problematic" third act is what really made me compare the two. Like I feel if I were to see the endings of both movies switched, I'd've enjoyed both much more. Cause 'MaXXXine' definitely needed a smaller, less outlandish ending instead of the "murder cult shootout". And 'Once Upon... Hollywood' definitely edged me with the prospect of a big 'ole "Manson murder cult bloodfest" in the same imaginative way that 'Inglorious Basterds' ended, but instead it opted for a quieter, unfantastical fanfiction of a dark spot of Hollywood history. I thought for sure it'd all tie up in a nice bow for Maxine, the killer, the movies, the blackmail, but the way it did just didn't jive as well as the rest of the movie did. Overall though, it's a decent end to a strange "Homage Horror"-trilogy and solidly my second favorite probably, behind 'Pearl' and well infront of 'X'.

title: The Strangers: Chapter 1
my_review: This is a deeply frustrating movie to watch. Not only is it just unreasonably unfair for the protagonists, but the protagonists are also just too dumb to take any advantage. I don't think this is supposed to be supernatural, but the killers just teleport all over the place. They seem able to stage entire rooms with dooming imagery and writing, but they'd have to've done it in mere minutes. Every single move the protagonists make seems perfectly calculated to the tee as the killers are right there to antagonize them further, but there's no semblance of a plan on the killers part. No sense of any bigger power at work, it's just three jabronies playing with their food for an hour. They're not presented like a 'Michael Myers-superhuman killer' or a 'Jason Vorhees-superhumanly supernatural teleporting killer', they're just random jabronies. That's the whole premise of the movie isn't it? That they're just cruelly silent and indifferent killers that just terrorize people because they want to. I don't have a problem with that, but they don't move or operate as such. And then there's the idiotic protagonists. At first it's reasonable in how unfair the circumstances are for them, but once they get the car their brains just turn off as to not let them have a chance. The dude forgets his shotgun. They leave the truck there for him- it still works because that was their getaway vehicle, but the dude leaves it to "hunt" and "rescue". The girl gets a chance to call the cops but she can't muster any coherent speech all of the sudden. Then she can't hide or run and just lets herself get taken in the open. The dude remembers his shotgun and has one at his mercy and he's hesitant and squeamish all of the sudden, even as they antagonize him(followed by a completely silent sucker punch, despite being surrounded by dead crunchy leaves). The deck was stacked, but even when they were given a winning hand they just throw it away for a new stacked deal. And then you don't even get closure. You get half a movie as they have the audacity to hit you with "To Be Continued". No time to really dwell on the characters or leave some clues to the killers motives/identity, just "Well you'll have to wait and see!" as if these dumb-dumbs think they've made something worthy for such anticipation. Just asinine through and through.

title: Y2K
my_review: Oh man, this was a miss. I love ‘Brigsby Bear’(2017) and it’s a go-to ace up the sleeve when in need for a movie and I’m actually pretty stoked on his show, ‘Saturday Morning All Star Hits!’(2021), so I had high hopes going in. Maybe fortunately they were dashed pretty fast hearing my favorite movie reviewer claim this was a big letdown and on watching this— yeah, it’s not great. Biggest folly for this is just a lack of energy. It doesn’t feel have as fun as the writing’s cuing it to be. At times it feels so self serious at taking a beat too long to get across something “deep”, which was also done in ‘Saturday Morning…’, but for comedic effect, here it just feels genuine. Like perhaps this was trying to go for what ‘Eighth Grade’(2018) was— which is not at all the right vibe for this premise. I’m also a big fan of Jaeden Martell’s acting, but he matches this movie’s vibe too well and just isn’t injecting any life into it. Too often it feels like he’s at the climatic-emotional beat of a comedy(y’know, when the main characters argue and tell each other to get some character growth) and that just drags the whole thing down so needlessly when it’s just a constant “brrr…” throughout.  The other problem that really surprised me as being a problem is the characters, specifically how they’re killed off. Julian Dennison was a bit of life for the movie and filled what felt like the classic trope of “two bros learning about themselves and growing closer or further apart as the realize they’re growing up during one epic night”, but nope, bro fucking dies immediately. The bully, played by a usual suspect of teen romps, he fucking dies immediately after(I will admit that was the funniest moment of the movie to me)! And somehow the two rando bully looks hijack the movie as the tertiary main characters, monologuing and calling people out as if they’ve been here the whole time. I felt like I was taking crazy pills when the girl got a whole moment to talk about her sexuality and possibly being a lesbian, like extremely “She doesn’t even go here!”-energy, because she’s only just 10min ago gotten promoted to main cast. It’s so weird. To be fair– but also critically so, I didn’t much care for any of the characters, but I think just another run through making everyone more known would have really helped and not made it so damn jarring at the rotating wheel of side characters that nudge out the main characters. Major “oof” of a movie, unfortunately. It’s a funny idea, ‘The Simpsons’ proved that, but this just isn’t snappy enough and makes some strange choices that just make it even worse.

title: Oddity
my_review: Boy did this burn slow. What really bothered me with this was how redundant the nonlinear storytelling felt. The opening's probably the strongest part of this and I think the movie knows this as it highlights the sorta "hook" with a title sceen, but then it's doesn't really deliver on that hook by jumping forward in time and honestly having no reason to jump back. But it does and it really fucks with the rhythm the opening was building- which could've been really strong. Thinking on it, I think a bigger plot around what the opening sets up would've been more interesting than the drip feeding of new story elements. Instead this goes a spookier direction and for assumedly budgetary reasons, it really just meanders with typical horror movie spookiness that doesn't really seem to go anywhere by the end since the sister's whole plan kinda whiffs aside from making the Brother-in-law panic himself into ruin. And by whiffs I mean that the wood(?)-golem did fuck all but make empty promises at something grander to come. Really the supernatural element is entirely superfluous to what would be a decent thriller, because all the supernatural stuff does is seemingly for our "benefit" rather than the story's. Lot've interesting ideas just not connected at all. Feels like what 'Barbarian'(2022) could've very easily been had it not strung together everything into a much better package. Like "Creepy looking stranger banging on your door to tell you someone's inside your house", "Spooky twin sister out for revenge for her sister's demise through a golem avatar", "Husband has disturbed work associate murder his wife so he can trade up to his mistress- and must now deal with a probing Ex-Sister-in-Law that's onto his shit", "Ghost of a man's dead wife tries to scare off and warn his new girl so she doesn't suffer his same fate" and "Moving into a weird isolated old manor with too many creeks and squeaks in the night", all are potentially very interesting ideas and to me this movie just poorly glued them together. Disappointed, overall.

title: Chime
my_review: Boy I was most shocked by the runtime—didn’t realize this was a short when I started it. Kinda a formless story(especially being a short) and more about building atmosphere than anything else. But then there’s something that Kurosawa seems to pitfall into too often—which for me atleast, is when his stories taking a sharp dive in reason and logic for the sake of unnerving. The small story he hides in that built up atmosphere and tension has a habit of just “taking a sharp left” into something that feels out of nowhere and/or just poorly conceived  So the with this movie here, you’re left with a digestible snapshot of some seemingly spreading madness that’s left to interpretation. But it cuts off before it tries to make some logic leap to explain it without being a a exact repeat of what he’s done before(it’s all ‘Cure’(1997) but never as good as ‘Cure’). Which I think works—albeit in I think a way where you’re headcanoning all the ways it might make sense(like most short stories, I feel like). But it doing that gives extra thought to chew on, rather than conflict with the story to gnaw at, which is usually the case I find with most Kurosawa flicks. Just umbrage at veering too far off what was a good course. But this movie, as a short, doesn’t get that luxury to veer, it just cuts off before fulfilling anything and while that’s dissatisfying, it’s not disappointing.

title: In a Violent Nature
my_review: A "Clever Campy Homage" or a "Too Try-hard 'Bad Movie' Parody" or a "Mediocre 'Slasher Classic' Wannabe"? I genuinely can't tell at times. It has an interesting gimmick that seems like a clever spin on the genre of which character it follows in a slasher, sometimes to great effect, but more often it brings so little to the movie besides 'scenic views' and "runtime'. It really overstays it's welcome by just dragging it out, but even adds more confusion to the mix by not sticking entirely to it, breaking away to do what the schtick cannot- exposition. When you do get to the exposition, you're treated with more than just hamfisted lore dumpage, but some really (for lack of a better word) bad acting. The writing does the actors no favors, giving them standard archetypes of a slasher, but the actors themselves equally don't give much more. At a point I started wondering if it was intentionally bad. The gimmick and acting started to feel like they were making fun of the genre rather than bringing something new. The characters are some of the dumbest bricks in the world. If not for how self-serious and well done the gore was, I'd think this was a full on goof on slasher movies, or maybe even something akin to Tarantio's homages- "over the top but still with merit", or maybe it is and I'm just missing the mark. But it really does feel like it's trying hard to be something big in the horror game. Even the synopsis gives me that impression as they introduce the slasher as "-an iconic new killer...", paired with the goofy mask and unique mirder weapons, I totally get the impression that the goal might be to make the next big Halloween costume. But it's aping so much of Jason Vorhees and the 'Friday the 13th' films that put me back on the "this is a parody"-train. So if it's trying to be a "Campy Homage", it kinda succeeds. It's definitely playing all the right beats of a slasher film with the clever gimmick and then the kills are right out've Mortal Kombat. But it drags it out far too long, or rather it just made for a boring story overall. Or if it's trying to be a "'Bad Movie'/Slasher Parody", à la 'Sharknado', then it blends the comedy and horror too poorly to be enjoyed by anyone other than horror-fanatics. It's truly flummoxing some of the choices made at times that "parody" seems like the only excuse really. And if it's trying to be a "Slasher Classic", then I think it fails completely. Less would've been so much more here as it doesn't have much new to say and it really does ape too much from 'ole Vorhees to stand on its own undead legs. Any attempt at depth is shallow and asinine and it really could've found significance if it stopped trying too much and focused up more. Should've stuck to the schtick better and maybe not have tried so hard to make the "next Jason" with an artistic theme of "nature". Like it's so much about nature, but this killer hardly is and nothing the victims do is conducive to that theme of "inciting natures wrath", so it really falls completely flat for me.

title: Presence
my_review: Another notch to Soderbergh’s “grabbag” of a filmography. Actually kinda liked it. It actually felt very reminiscent of Zemekis’ ‘Here’(2024), which I kinda liked—but in this movie it has the added benefit of mobility that felt restrictive in ‘Here’. It’s not much of a Horror film, in fact it’s weakest when leaning into the horror aspect, which to its favor it doesn’t do much beyond the gimmick. Instead it’s a dysfunctional family drama told in a very gimmicky way that does feel very effective, but a bit at odds with the story. The gimmick being the camera being the haunting presence. I kinda love when the camera’s movements are felt in a movie—one of my favorite instances of this being in ‘La La Land’(2016) when there’s a big argument and a shove happens the camera is pushed away and you feel that push the same as the character receiving it did. Or another favorite in the show ‘Fleabag’(2026) wherein the protagonist breaks the fourth wall to chat to the viewer and in the second season a character unknowingly joins in on that breaking and you’re caught so off guard like the main character. And in this movie I felt like there were tons of moments like that, the ghost camera just being seen or felt by characters and you feel like you’re the haunting presence and that these characters are perceiving you watching them. Though I think the gimmick does restrain this from being a true horror—how uncharacteristic would it be for you, the viewer, to do tormenting like a standard horror when in actuality you’re just here to watch. But even then, it works well if you appreciate it and quickly adapt to not expecting the movie to try and scare you. It’s the family drama that really makes and breaks this though. I don’t think there’s quite enough of them—or rather the presence pulling them together, to really develop or grow. We only she quick snapshots of them interacting and then some oddly sidetracking subtextual story threads that only detract. Like the weird incestuous bit with the mom and son, or the mom doing something shady at work, or the dad worrying if he’d be better off divorcing—most feel like odd inclusions and it felt unfulfilling that nothing came of them when the movie’s lowkey about them. But then sometimes when they do try to go into the drama, it’s a bit hamfisted and clunky. Like every bit with the brother felt so weird and extra antagonistic and at odds with what we know of his status as the “favorite” child. Or the mom and dad kinda trying to make things work when it feels like they just changed moods offscreen. But I do think most of the stuff with the daughter works. And Chris Sullivan’s oddly really likable everytime I see him so it was cool seeing him as a lead here as the dad—which I did enjoy his bits with the daughter, even though they sometimes felt kinda sporadically done. What didn’t really work for me was the creepy friend/boy. He was fine before his weird serial killer bit came into play. Actually wild that he had a little parasol for a handheld saranwrap, like did this jabroni actually by a tiny parasol for quick and easy access to plastic wrap to kill people? But really that whole angle just felt odd and almost made it seem like the presence was only there to stop him—which we never quite learn of it’s one of the girls or not, it’s just very helpful I guess. The more I think about it, I’m not sure if the story makes as much sense as I thought the point of getting the house was to zone themselves to a school for the son and the boy is kinda introduced as a friend he made at the new school. But at the end the boy reveals he killed the two girls—girls that the daughter knew, so were they at the same school already or what? And then it ending with the brother killing him and himself to save the sister felt a bit lacklustre, it felt like a heroic moment that was hollow because the brother and sister never shared any reconciliation or bonding moment, he just wakes up and kills himself and the creep and the movie’s over. But yeah—grabbag. Uniquely done genre film for better or worse. Ultimately I did like it though, but I don’t see much wide appeal for it.

title: The Nun II
my_review: Pretty dumb all around. Premise alone is just kinda silly—it squeezes out another movie within the canon of these movies and it doesn’t even really end in the right spot. The Warrens do an exorcism, so what does it matter what Taissa Farmiga does to save the day so “definitively”. Frenchie walks off to a happy ending and then presumably it goes to shit again, so why bother with this rigmarole. If anything the story needed to have the Warrens show up to preform said exorcism to save the day, not some weird (literal)deus ex machina/macguffin to “save” the day. The demons are dumb. Maybe just the whole series in general but these demons are really bad at getting what they want as they seem super capable of doing anything and then just fail to trounce some scared kids with no protective means. That scene where the titular nun conjures spikes from the ground to not kill any one but just slightly entrap them—c’mon.  The church is dumb too though. They just insist on sending a singular nun to deal with this—all on her own. No backup, no “big guns”, just “you’ll be fine, stop worrying.” I presume the priest from the first didn’t want to return, but that’s not really a role to leave vacant—in a higher ranking(they’re all about rank) support for Farmiga. The novice nun joins her, but her inclusion was just kinda silly. She has no real arc of gaining faith and her overconfidence isn’t a problem at all when dealing with some supposed “all powerful” demon. It’s settled, the only way to make this work was it needed Russell Crowe to come in as his character in ‘The Pope’s Exorcist’(2023), it’s the only way to make this work. And then just the writing itself is kinda “dumb”—in the lame way. It takes way too long for Farmiga to join back with Frenchie and the whole while I just didn’t really care about what either of them were doing cause both storylines were so dull and boring. It picks up when they do meet, but at that point it’s the climax and the obnoxious haunting begins.  These movies—the whole ‘Conjur-verse’, they have pretty antiquated horror ideas. I don’t know why in this resurgence of horror and elevated horror, that they’re so complacent with the barest minimum. Sometimes it works out fine in the end and other times like here it’s just so blasé. Made worse when there are contemporary movies being made that are doing something similar but doing it so much better. Like ‘The First Omen’(2024) being surprisingly bold at times, or the campy insanity of the aforementioned ‘The Pope’s Exorcist’. It’s some weak ass story to just get to some general haunting before they save the day, rinse, repeat.

title: The Last Voyage of the Demeter
What You Wish For
my_review:
Something that really stood out to me when I felt most characters reacted understandably was how the vacationing girl comes back during this big event. 

Like for one, she wasn't invited, she just shows up expectantly thinking she can come in. Which sure, some people just think like that, or you might just end up accidentally catching someone at a bad time- especially without phone contact. But this girl can't read the room at all and by that I mean it's just kinda wild how she noses into this apparently corporate event, unbothered by whatever important thing is going on to chat up a guy. 

That brings me to two, she reads the room in a completely irrational way to figuring something sinister is happening. She meets the 'other guy' instead of her guy, but honestly his cover made sense- even having the watch. He's visibly very busy cooking and even tells her what he's cooking's not for her but she still [playfully] wants him to feed her and when he denies her she starts seeing what is still pretty innocuous- albeit weird food being cooked and starts getting the heebie geebies as she puts these two puzzle pieces together that were never there to begin with.   

I feel like if they wanted her to get suspicious and add another moving part of tension to this night- they shouldn't have made the cannibals so rational and her irrational. Things should also have been more askew, perhaps some macguffin that brings her back there to maybe return something and then make it even weirder that the guy who was supposed to be there now isn't. Or maybe less appetizing food/unprepared food that seemed more odd than even fine dining could explain. Like honestly a "blood sauce" at a fine dining event wouldn't make me blink twice, even though I've never heard of it I still could conceive it being used in cooking somehow. Or perhaps "Jack" actually tries to make things seem off but has to  do so low-key cause the boss is there or something. 

For me, her little role as another thing to go wrong was just too contrived and thus more annoying than not. You shouldn't be frustrated that the cannibals aren't getting away with it and if she was supposed to incite some worry of "Oh no! She's in the lion's den and doesn't even know it", I certainly don't think they accomplished it because it's more "You dummy, you kept ignoring the locked doors, raised fences, trench barrier and ended up in the lion's den, you deserve what happens."

title: Late Night with the Devil
my_review: I'm a little let down by this one. Going into it I had tempered, but high expectations and this just didn't quite land with me. Aside from being a pretty middling horror, I thought the premise sounded like it'd lend alot more to the experience of this, but ultimately—atleast for me, I didn't get that. I really wanted the movie to decide wether to fully commit to the schtick of being shot and edited like a live broadcast with supposed BTS footage added in, but this strays away from that gimmick pretty fast. The "Oldschool Late Night Show" feel just wasn't there for me and when it did cut to BTS it certainly did not feel like anything real. This wouldn't really bother me too much if not for the fact they made a drawn out intro to the fact that you're supposedly watching the "forbidden tapes of that fateful night...", like saying it's 'found footage' then hitting you with a drone shot or some steady cam. I was actually looking forward to David Dastmalchian finally featuring front and center, but though I really don't think he was bad at all, I felt he was a bit miscast aswell as a flippant character. For one—he just doesn't quite have that "host"-energy you see from late night television, both in look and enthusiasm, he does convey the wit and snark, but those alone don't really sell me on his TV presence. Especially when there's this pretty half-baked narrative of him stirring up shit for more views, I felt Dastmalchian was more earnest than not and definitely didn't convey the "sleaze" that I think they wanted you to get from him. Really just a scene towards the end of him with the producer gushing about ratings and the ending give any hint to his willingness to 'sell' out for some success, cause otherwise he's fully bought into the supernatural elements at play or just seems like an okay if not overzealous guy. The part seemed to require a much more ‘synthetically-affable’-personality with a stereotypically-masculine ‘American TV-host’-look, but Dastmalchian just has a ‘forever worried sulk’ that can be played up for being disheartened or having menace and neither seemed to fit here other than him grieving his dead wife. I did appreciate and notice some of the general lore included here around late night TV and the era. Such as a 'James Randi'-like skeptic or his counterpart in the first psychic who played up all the classic "psychic" tricks. But some of the other stuff felt at odds, like a case of doing too much. I don't think weird "rich freaks’ occult stuff" fit much when it's so centric to "little girl channels demon on Live TV", cause the latter's more than interesting enough of it's own. Or like why was the psychic freaking out when he never meets the demon, dude just dies "because", unless the insinuation is that the dead wife killed him- which if so, why not make her a more vengeful prescence than just a footnote to recall every now and then? I might be nitpicking too much, but it just felt a bit too unexceptional and like your common indie horror that just happened to have a premise that I thought would've worked a lot better than it did. It did have some cool effects reminiscent of Lynch and Cronenberg, but they were few and not nearly as iconic as either. Also good lord, that was an insane amount of prodcution companies at the beginning.

title: Scream VI
my_review: It’s distancing itself from the original with a new skin in the Big Apple, which is the best thing this has going for it. But it’s still got a lot of issues that run too deep for a new skin to fix. The thing this and 5 do that really miss the point is the mythologizing of Ghostface. Every movie under the original umbrella—Ghostface is a tool for a new killer to weaponize. But this movie and its predecessor treat it as some empowering “meta-force”, a birthright. Something that allows you to be unstoppable. Previous Ghostfaces were menacing and very capable, but it all felt very understandably so. They isolated people, they took them by surprise rather than head on, cause when it came to a head they’re practically tripping over themselves in desperation to try and finish the kill. Here Ghostface is like Michael Meyers playing Assassin’s Creed. They walk boldly in the open and strike regardless of how crowed a room is. The bodega and the apartment scenes in particular are very reckless and it’s kinda crazy that they win both encounters, not knocked around and run away when they can’t seal the deal in 10min. Characters don’t fight back until they’re allowed to—which isn’t right at all, because nothings changed from when Ghostface jumps a public convenience store of people with a knife or an apartment of characters that have fought back—one of which is the “tough jock dude protector”. My issue is that they’re writing scenes that are too bold for amateur slashers—which Ghostface almost always is. Why would the killer just put themselves in a spot to easily be beaten? The only reason why is because they have some superior force of power behind them only given by the writing taking away the aspect of Ghostface being anyone and also a bozo. The subway scene works for me, because it’s a car full of costumes in a city where everyone minds their own business, very similar to the second movie’s opening in the theater with a rowdy crowd that’re all wearing the same outfit. If there were more scenes like that—no problem. But they have far too many scenes where Ghostface operates like they’re untouchable, which is technically true, but only because these writers deify this iconic slasher too much. And then they’re continuing to make Sam some natural born slasher with deep murderous urges, which is just so dumb. I love the show ‘Dexter’ but I feel like if you’re leaning in that similar direction—“born in blood”/no fixing a fucked up killer, there’s gotta be more to it. I feel like Sam was a normal kid until she learned who her dad was and suddenly she’s Buster Bluth with a hook hand, running away in shame because she’s some “…Monster!” I already wasn’t hot on the Billy connection, but I’m really not hot on her just having latent slashing abilities due to some DND “Haunted One” background. The most I feel should come from the connection is the scrutiny angle, similar to Sidney Prescott’s persisting scrutiny across the franchise. For the most part, the “core four” are better utilized, or I guess specifically Mindy and Chad are. Mindy’s still a bit insufferable, but given more to do than just womansplain(?) what the plot should be(much Ike Randy—who I was never fond of either). Here she gets to actually participate in the deducing aspect with the gang rather than be the armchair expert. Chad is a bit more dimensional and more than just the “alpha bro”, that he’s still dubbed as in the movie. That said, neither of them had any right surviving. Mindy was stealthily stabbed in the subway and no one said anything until the other killer pointed it out and saves her to literally no benefit of their mission. Then she just prances back at the end, full mobility, right as rain. And then Chad was repeatedly double penetrated by two Ghostfaces, only to wheel out at the end with the explanation that he’s a main character, so that’s why he lived. Same as the Ghostface having bad planning, I’m fine if they want to let them live, Dewey lived through so much over the series, but they gave two very definitive kill moments and neither of them stuck. Tara’s kinda just there, maybe a bit too blasé about what she went through. It continues to be a little weird how underutilized and second-fiddled Jenna Ortega was in these two for how much of a budding star she very obviously is and was already when they were filming. It didn’t seem so weird when she was the opening “kill” in 5, but it is weird when they’re still doubling down on Sam. Sam’s still kind of a dud. To not harp so much more on her, Melissa Barrera is no leading woman and the supporting cast really accentuate that fact cause literally any other character has the looks and acting ability to be the lead. Her character’s kinda pulled back here though, the movie feels more of an ensemble which helps alot. They were obviously aware of her reception and kind of make that part of her character which annoyingly makes her a bit of a martyr. But yeah, the “put on the mask”, “become the monster” stuff is so lame. The legacy characters are surprisingly few for as much as they can’t stop digging it up. Courtney Cox feels more like an obligation and done in a way to give her some degree of dues that don’t really seem necessary? It felt like cheap “stakes raiser” and like a backdoor out for Cox if she decided she was too good for the pity crumbs they were giving just for the cred of her legacy status—which seemingly Neve Campbell wasn’t having. Kirby coming back was cool though, cause Hayden Panettiere’s great and Kirby was actually my favorite of the new characters four introduced. She’s given way more of a genuine role than Gale is and it’s kinda neat that she’s actually pretty apart of things. Her character is a bit lost though, Kirby in four was like Mindy(which was novel that they had a “game recognize game” moment) but not as “splaining”, but also very brash, alluring and confident. In this movie she’s just a badge with some sympathy, most of her character apparently aged out over the years. I genuinely get the impression that Gillett and Bettinelli-Olpin were biggest fans of the third movie, because so much of what fuels their movies were my bigger issues with the third. A more tenacious, formidable and impossible Ghostface, one where it’s kinda hard to believe it really was just one guy. Being haunted by your past by actual ghosts of your imagination. This overloading desire to lean so far into the meta nature that the identity of the series becomes flanderized. I don’t know if I’ve ever been quite won over by them and their two ‘Scream’ movies are certainly lowering and gluing their bar to impress me. It’s better than the last for me, but yeah, that bar was low. I think they were a bit to precious with things and it actively hurt their rather than just be a something that held them back a little. Like Sidney, Dewey and Gale never dying never quite bothered me as much as literally nobody(innocent) really dying here because half of them are characters they don’t want to kill and shoulder the franchise and the other half are killers and one lesbian girlfriend. The OG’s never felt like they had to die for me, if only because the series past the first feels kinda like an episodic show and you need your returnees to come back each week. The “core four” aren’t much different but they do seem to exist in a “post jumped shark”-world that makes it harder to buy that nobody died. It’s also not helped that yeah, nobody really died in this movie, some bystanders, the girlfriend, the killers, but nobody else, it’s fine to keep your favorites alive but some more blood’s gotta be spilt, otherwise it just becomes as ridiculous as it is, getting double penetrated by two Ghostfaces and still making it out fine into the sequel. I’d put this there with the third and just as rather skip them both.

title: Hellraiser
my_review: Gee, after the painful endeavor of watching this series back-to-back—each and every stinkin’ one of them, this movie is such a breathe of fresh air. I didn’t hate this at all, actually. It does feel a little too mainstreamed in the actual horror department. The Cenobites look fine, but the kills and gore themselves feel somewhat tame from its original roots. But the updated story wasn’t too bad. The spin this takes the whole “haunting” is even kinda captivating once they get to the mansion. I think if they really cut loose a bit more to match its reputation, this would’ve been received a lot better as a revival of the franchise. As it is I don’t think it revived it from the looks of it, but it was a decent attempt. I seem to recall some pessimism in general surrounding this at the time. From the outside looking in it seemed like a cheap effort to reboot some beloved franchise. Having since seen the original and finally powered through the rest of the series, that sentiment seems so hilariously off base. The franchise is more “bad” than “good”. Only one movie is truly inspired(the first one—duh) and every successive one degrades into something worse and worse, eventually becoming offensively terrible. I distinctly remember around the time I watched the first ‘Hellraiser’(1987), that I used to think that I really didn’t want to watch all the entries of a horror franchise—knowing most if not all of them just go to shit pretty fast. But after realizing I already had some contradictions to that point that I enjoyed—‘Scream’ & ‘Final Destination’ and then going through the ‘Nightmare on Elm Street’-series on a whim and I changed my tune. There were some real gems as that series went on and then a series like ‘Friday the 13th’ had some neat history to it aswell—seeing  horror icon evolve over the years. So finally I decided to go in on ‘Hellraiser’, see why ‘ole Pinhead’s so iconic… but all that this submerging brought me was validation to early-me’s belief that there’s no true benefit to watching the horror sequels. I don’t necessarily believe that now, but with ‘Hellraiser’—there is no true benefit to watching its sequels. What a garbage series that tarnishes a decent legacy. There’s only four good ones(including this one) of eleven and those other seven range from bad—maybe fun to to visit a lá HDTGM and then actual trash that’s just unfun and unpleasant. In a funny way I feel the Cenobites have taken a bit of my humanity from me. I’m free of this series now, but at what costs? They have shown me their pleasures and true to the films—they’re not great and I regret everything.

title: Terrifier 2
my_review: This was a DNF for me the first time around. There’s something that’s a surefire way to turn me off from a movie and that’s gross-out stuff. It’s almost ways off putting—intentionally so, but in the “I’d rather watch literally anything else”-way and this movie’s really front-loaded with it. It does mellow out, but it’s also just the aggressiveness of the gore and the trashy cinema look of it that I just wasn’t even interested in powering through 2hrs of it at the time, just to see what the hubbub was about. I did it this time though(jaded from a series of much worse movies, cough’Hellraiser’cough) and though I wasn’t as turned off as before—or rather more willing to power through, I can’t say I’m really at all about it still. This is just way too long for what it is. There is more of a story here—and it’s not a bad one honestly and I do appreciate it as opposed to before, but it’s played in full at the same time we see Art do his thing for the other half. And Art’s thing is just torture porn and gory mayhem that goes on much longer than it needs too(not in the critical way, but genuinely the bit is that he’s going above and beyond). And yeah, I’m just not as bemused with the kills in these movies as there’s just too much of it here that it just loses any impact. Even giving long inconsequential dream sequences to have more gratuitous kills but with an off-kilter cadence now. Maybe there was a tighter movie in there and this is just the result of asking too many times “if there’s more we can squeeze in”. Though honestly, I don’t even know if a tighter version of this would work better for me. At least I can in good conscience cross it off now.

title: Scream
my_review: It’s a weird case with this movie, be it lack of tact or a misstep in where the meta wheel spin landed on, but this movie really doesn’t work for me for as much as they try to try and trick me that it does. The movie’s whole thing about being a “re-quel”, ‘dredging up the original to sell the new’, it’s not really appealing in the slightest for me here. I know I’m already a bit hypocritical in loving ‘Force Awakens’(2015) so much while it’s panned mostly for rehashing the original, but the way this movie goes about doing the same just ain’t it. There’s hardly a foundation of new, it’s a rehash, but it’s rehashing atop of a pile of skeletons from the old. It’s not some things with legacy connections, it’s all things. The movie points out that this is very intentional and very meta. That this is the only way to bring a franchise back, but it’s not, nor is the way they’ve gone about it here. I really hate how much of a connection this new squad of friends conveniently have to the original. Not only is everyone related, but they’re all very attuned to their respective relation in the first movie, before it’s even a plot point. Randy has a niece and nephew who worship him and are just as annoying as he was about “the rules”. Billy had a bastard daughter that’s actually super hung up on that fact. Stu’s family home is fortunately in the family of another wannabe. The bitchy deputy from 4 has a son in the gang now. The series was honestly never that shy about surprise relationships and if I’m being more honest, I’ve never once been that crazy about them save one and they’re almost always used for cheap final reveals. But this movie is “Oops—All Legacies!” it’s way too much at once that it feels like they’re not taking it seriously because it feels like a parody plot line out of ‘Scary Movie’. As if Jaime Kennedy could show up with a bad fake beard and claim he was Randy’s never talked about twin who’s conveniently also super jazzed about “slasher film theory”. And in the same vein, I don’t really like any of these characters. I never really cared for Randy but he was a “necessary ‘evil’” for the movies’ theme, but goddamn, I really don’t care for Mindy. Always she’s not an uncool nerd like Randy, she’s a “cool” pompous one that gets away with just being really shitty to everyone but not having the benefit of being revealed as a killer. Chad is a pretty one note jock, I know he gets more development in the sequel, but here he’s a jock that chimes in to agree with Mindy. Whatever Chad’s girlfriend’s name was, she was just there to be dunked on and then just turn super crazy exe-girlfriend—an interesting idea, a crazy mean character not tied to the actual killers, but one not really used here. Amber is pretty nonexistent until her reveal, much like Mitch(Olyphant) in the second ‘Scream’. Wes I actually liked, in part cause I already liked the actor, but he wasn’t a dick like everyone else, but he also dies immediately so whatever. Jack Quaid’s Richie is easily the best new character here, if only because he’s so “Jack Quaid”ey. I only hated the reveal that it was him because that meant he’s out of the franchise. Tara I didn’t mind, though she didn’t really get much to do, she’s only fine because Jenna Ortega is a really good actress. But in that same vein, there’s Melissa Barrera’s Sam. Gonna be totally blunt about it, but geez-louise, she really drags this movie down. I don’t like fixating negatively so much, especially cause per what this movie even points out, fans can be toxic as hell, but genuinely—how the hell is(was) Barrera given so many lead roles. She’s consistently been the weakest link in her movies and I feel bad that she’s consistently put in that spot, but everyone acts circles around her. This movie really tries to sell her as the new Sidney and a Neve Campbell she is surely not. And then they go and have Jenna Ortega in an adjacent side role when she’s easily got the juice to actually be a “Neve Campbell” for the franchise. It’s also not helped that I really do not care for Sam’s character. It’s kinda fun to see Skeet Ulrich again, but I loathe the fact that they not only make her some prophesied spawn of Billy’s meant to inherit the franchise, but she also has to see him and he technically gives her strength. I hated that aspect of the third movie, Sidney being haunted by her dead mom, it felt so out of place in the franchise and I think it was a mistake to double down on it and bring that into this “requel”. Sam’s just boring and that’s not made better by Barrera making her even moreso and it’s just a bad combo that makes it wild that that she was supposed to shoulder the franchise from here. As for the OG’s, “ehh”. They each get their moments that are fine fan service but I’m not crazy about how the movie treats them as a whole. Sidney’s very passive, in part because for once she’s not the target—which is kinda wild when the killers are consistently obsessed with her story in some regard, so why go after some bastard child of old news with the actual golden goose is literally brought out to play? Dewey is a highlight, but I also am not crazy with “regressing” him. He is somewhat smarter, but he’s washed-up now cause he ruined his relationship with Gale? They literally couldn’t not keep from breaking them up again? I’m sure Arquette was probably willing to finally bow out but his death was pretty contrived. Gale was there, it’s hilariously bad writing that she and Dewey hardly interact(maybe intentional? I don’t know their current IRL status with eachother) before Dewey’s killed off. The OG character’s agency admittedly seem to keep getting in the way of any new character’s development, but this movie kinda cut all three of them loose for the new order and now they suffer for the other’s development—which was for naught cause most weren’t even that good. Points to go to this movie for the Ghostface bits, those never really disappointed. Except when you spend time to think about how most of the time it’s Mikey Madison doing the killings and she’s somehow a foot taller and tanking hits and duking out punishment left and right. An aggressive Anora is genuinely frightening, but her Ghostface acts nothing like Anora’s feral aggression, they act like Ghostface—a Ghostface that’s about 6’0” and likes to grapple people in to stab them whilst taking all the punishment possible. I know I saw some half-assed excuse that “the person under the mask doesn’t matter, they are Ghostface” but this is literally the only real movie where the person under there kinda matters because they’re tiny and not immediately outed. I don’t think she can’t kill, but logistically it’s has to be her most of the time cause Richie’s deep under cover most of the time and is too far away to do it and the way she fights is not like how someone her size would—because they’re manhandling everyone don’t want it to be obvious and want it to be entertaining, but c’mon play to her strengths, don’t just expect everyone to roll with it. I’ve ranted long enough and should rant into a closing argument. The worst part is this movie’s already been done and it was actually pretty good and that was in ‘Scream 4’(2011). The characters were better, the OG’s were better handled, the legacy character felt fine at just one and better yet the movie plays heavily on that one to great effect. This movie tries so hard to be meta that it forgoes any tact. Everything feels unearned when it’s digging up old corpses. It hitches itself to the wrong characters and sinks because of it. It’s entertaining as a movie, but it’s too into itself that it becomes a turn off. It panders to the more trending-cinema enthusiasts and it seems to work, but I think it’s getting away with too much, aswell as getting praise for more than it actually accomplished. I was hyped for this movie when it first came round, but left with a loss of interest in what more would come. And worse is the movie kinda safeguards itself from all the criticism and can hide behind its proclamations of meta commentary.  Bah—I’ve talked myself into a half star lower. Franchise low for me.

title: All My Friends Hate Me
my_review: This was the last "horror" movie I would've guessed to've gotten me to squirm so much. Really preys on insecurities and empathy for being in a familiar nightmare. But solid gem to find and definitely a horror movie for the right person.(I'm person) Though really, as much as you can surmise that Pete's kinda an ass in his own way(a lá '30 Rock' with Liz Lemon being the bully instead of the nerd), I still felt his friends really raked him over the coals a bit too much to entirely plead ignorance. Specifically in the moments when they're not so jokingly blaming Pete for Claire randomly Irish goodbying, or the expensive hunting range present for a guy who's never held a gun and Fig outright telling Pete he's really making a bad impression. Alot've the other instances- primarily with Harry, could indeed be chalked up to Pete's humor being different and more prudish, but not those where they're just outright being dicks to him, harping on everything just to be playfully dickish, but also including those instances where they're just as much to blame and I guess Pete's too paranoid or different a person to call them out more on it. I don't think of this as a plothole or hang-up with the writing as it could be just another shade to help fuel Pete's paranoia- "What if he is right and they are just bad friends?", but it certainly bothered me how high a road they all took at the reveal.

title: The Sadness
my_review: This could have very easily been a cult classic due to how fucked up these zombies are, but beyond that it’s really just a meandering mess. After the first twenty or so minutes this movie hits the brakes hard and really slow burns to let the characters develop or some shit but the writing’s terrible and acting’s porno level. And no it’s not even the fun kinda bad, it’s just plain bad. There’s such an awkward rhythm that can’t keep up with the edginess of the gore & violence, nor any good connective tissue to string together any scenes, so it’s just a sandwich of a really mediocre movie between scenes conceived just to shock you. It’s a pity, cause these “zombies” are genuinely quite scary. I don’t remember the last time I was kinda skeeved out by zombies since we’re so desensitized of them at this point, but this movie’s(especially the granny) were quite disturbing, atleast until they started getting too hammy. But alongside the other flaws these zombies don’t even really make much sense. The logic of how or why you’re infected is wishy washy and only seems to happen for plot reasons. They’re not brain dead and even plan but they flip from being cognizant or bloodlusted or horny or cruel. Aside from just the idea of zombies wanting to hurt people rather than eat them, there’s just not much more thought put into them and it just adds another degree of dumb to the movie. Shock value just don’t cover up the flaws, even if it do be shocking.

title: Host
my_review: Not the chin diaper! Woah, big surprise this one was. Went in relatively blind, just saw it was a popular horror in English I still hadn’t seen, so figured “Why not, it’s barely an hour—oh and Sean Baker liked it” but I got kinda spooked by this one. It’s a COVID and it utilizes that aspect really well, chiefly in just a bunch of bored isolated friends coming together on a call to fuck around with the occult for shits’n giggles. But it really shines when the horror kicks in and it never really breaks/bends the rules of a ‘screengrab’-movie which I always look out for with these contrived “one screen movies”(maybe the only rule bend is the ‘full screen’ing of someone’s vid being too convenient for the movie). If I had one gripe, it might be that things go so hilariously awry for this group after a pretty meager faux pas, no desecration of a burial ground, or awakening of anything, just a silly séance. I’m learning something that modern horror can really lean into as a strength is the forced perspective of an ‘in-movie’ camera. Not quite the same as normal found footage, in my opinion, where to me I feel like the cameraman-character is very much just a cameraman aiming to capture the movie. Perhaps that’s just a “me” thing, but I’ve just never quite felt that immersive feeling that I think is intended with traditional found footage(especially being far too young to believe in—or know about, the hoax of ‘The Blair Witch Project’(1999)) cause the camera element still feels like movie making. But a fixed camera, that confines you to a very unnerving angle with what eventually feels like no reprieve. That’s something that worked shockingly well on me in ‘Gonjiam: Haunted Asylum’(2018) that probably made me the most scared I’ve felt in a long while watching horror movies, where in a team of web-horror investigators have mounted POV cameras that get progressively harder to watch as their routine thing gets spooky and their entire POV. And that’s something I think is achieved here with this novel Zoom call, we’re force to their perspectives and what they perceive and sometimes it’s the poor quality and unsuredness that really draws out the horror. It’s a delicate thing though, cause I think it still has to look good and not just be unwatchable. Cause I feel I can just aswell dislike a movie for it decision to obstruct clear visual of what’s happening—for example movies I really end up hating are a good part due to this stunt—‘Skinamarink’(2022), ‘Irréversible’(2002), the ending 20min of ‘Climax’(2018). But when done right, I feel it’s very effective and very unyielding horror. You don’t get a cutaway, you don’t get a change of scenery, you gotta look at the scary thing and keep looking. Also I love the credits, very clever & charming(wrote that right before actual credits rolled, but the sentiment is still true)

title: #Alive
my_review: Oh man—bad, bad, bad.  On paper, this sounds like an interesting idea, ‘gamer boy gets trapped in his apartment whilst the zombie apocalypse happens outside’, but in execution this is just straight Garbo. Nothing really happens, or atleast nothing more interesting than a dude sitting in his apartment without much else to do. You’d think there’s something there with how ingenious a person can get when backed into a corner, but it’s just nothing until something eventually happens. But every new something added to the story just comes out of nowhere and kinda makes zero sense. Like observing a totally empty room for hours, thinking “If  I could just sit down,” and then right before you decide to sit your butt on the floor, a chair apparates nearby. And then if it could talk it’d say something dumb like “I’ve been here the whole time!” which is straight up not true at all. Basically this scenario happens several times in this movie. Couldn’t stop thinking about how similar the premise is to Willem Dafoe’s ‘Inside’(2023). How similarly interesting it sounds on paper, ‘thief trapped in a secluded apartment he was trying to rob’, but in execution it’s so painfully a nothing-burger. Though after this, I’m kinda looking back on it fondly—which is wild cause I didn’t care for that one at all. but it atleast worked with its premise better. Cause that one didn’t have asspulls like this one.  This movie is just a trashy zombie flick with a decent hook that doesn’t really matter in the end, cause it’s still trash.

Though all the “liberal elite” don’t get much time to shine in general, despite all having some character on them. Each time we meet them they’re dead I. It’s fun to see “main characters” keep dying in every scene until Gilpin shows up, but that carries on throughout and ends up short cutting alot of fun performances for constant quick deaths. Could have been scheduling and even how they got so many decent character actors, but it you feel remiss every time it keeps happening.

title: It Chapter Two
my_review: This movie’s a mess. Where I praise the first movie for the changes it made, this one is making all the wrong ones. Writing’s atrocious, there’s so many awkward scenes and beats that feel like they’re making it up as they go. Reneging alot of the first movie cause they don’t know how to do this movie. Characters they excelled developing now take a big dive here, doing this strange false development and pivots that bring an ‘off’-energy to this. At times it even feels like just a flex of filmmaking that mostly feels more ‘out of place’, rather than impressive. And maybe worst of all is it’s almost three hours of this—and it really didn’t need to be. The biggest problem with this is that it doesn’t know what to do with the story since the bisected the past and present into two different movies, rather than playing out in tandem. We spend the entirety of this just reliving their childhoods and having the exact same nonsense in each of their flashbacks. We already did the Pennywise haunts! You can’t for back to their childhoods and do all new ones! Where in the timeline do those fit? “After the fight—“ but that means the kids were getting actively tormented and preyed upon and STILL refused to help stop IT because they were made at Bill? It’d be the opposite, IT would leave the kids alone because it was getting scared of these kids’ resilience to his antics—especially cause movie IT is beholden to the whims of their imaginations, not the shine emitted from their friendship. It’s like a train(🥁—unfortunate book joke) these characters wait in, waiting to get their reminiscing and spook. Something done in the book, yes, but they changed the story format and this is just redundant. There’s also some very jarring revisions—that the first movie neglected to adapt and are impossible to exist in the timeline. I’m mostly on about Ben’s building of their hideout. This is how Ben acquainted himself with them in the books, but that didn’t happen in the first and now we get this very elaborate and random place of reverence between all the kids that’s just made up. We followed the kids so closely in the first and we’re supposed to believe in the middle of them watching a movie and hunting IT that they built a bunker and spent oodles of time there? What makes it not make sense is they wrote it so that Beverly leaves at the end of the first part. So her being in all their hangouts is just impossible. Really, I mostly just wish that this movie just adapted the adults more faithfully. Everything tied to the adult Losers’ lives is truncated to something in the background as they’re introduced. Admittedly, I’m not crazy about the crossover of their lives with the story—the abusive husband following Bev and Bill’s miraculous wife he’s cucking. But still, that’s a big aspect of their characters, especially when they come together and that’s lost because they aren’t deviating enough from the story to let the adult characters be more than older versions of the kids. Really, I think they just didn’t want to not have the kids reprise their roles and I think that’s fine. It’s just that this movie is effectively readapting the book by focusing so much on the kids whose stories don’t progress(cause that was the first part) and so it’s just a bunch of nonsense. To go on an off-topic side tangent, this lowkey it feels a lot like the problems between ‘Last Jedi’(2017) & ‘Rise Of Skywalker’(2019). To me, aside from other issues each have, there’s a core problem of there being no roadmap. ‘Last Jedi’ taking everything ‘Force Awakens’(2015) teed-up and—sometimes literally—just throwing it away. Then ‘Rise Of Skywalker just spends the whole movie re-adding everything back, making up a whole new story cause there was nothing to follow-up a conclusion for. As for the adult versions themselves, I’m kinda vibing differently with them that I did tween I first saw them. Bill is so uninspiring as an adult. The first part really toned down the leadership of Bill, but I thought It was still noticeably there. But this movie makes it pretty nonexistent. He’s crazed and passionate about saving the kid cause he reminds him of Georgie, but that really doesn’t weigh in anyone else here, which makes his part kinda useless. Mike’s the one that truly suffers here. They let him be the one with the research after giving that to Ben in the first, but he’s pretty half baked. The story’s as such to not give Mike any extra flashbacks, cause he doesn’t need to go remember anything, so in turn, who the fuck cares about what Mike’s doing. The first adaptation kids worked around this by having him and Bill reminisce about Silver the bike. But he also just doesn’t really fit in with the Losers. There’s moments where I feel like nobody even likes Mike. Like he’s the friend that everyone still hangs with but nobody’s bold enough to kick them out. Bev’s no longer interesting. She’s reduced to the hot and incapable ‘girl’ of the group. Which I found her to somewhat be in the book, I’m just glad she’s not getting passed around still, like Bill doesn’t randomly decide to cheat on his wife with her cause they just have to bang, all while Ben still proclaims his love and ends up with Beverly. Whatta downgrade. Surprisingly, I wasn’t crazy about Bill Hader’s Richie. Perhaps it’s cause Hader’s bringing his own humor that’s different than Richie’s humor in the first part. He’s funny, but I dunno, he felt so out of place here. Like a studio note to “liven up the movie more”. I actually am a fan of the change to make Richie gay. It’s unnecessary, but it does add another layer that Richie kinda lacked compared to everyone else. Something about his being that IT would prey on. They also bring back “beep-beep, Ritchie”, something book lovers seem to have a chip on their shoulder on. It’s used correctly here, the first having Pennywise be the only one to mockingly say it, but here Bev says it when Richie’s being too dickish. It’s just an odd thing I noticed, like why would Bev say it since it wasn’t a thing with their friend group. It’s such a weird thing to say out of the blue without the repetition.  Ben’s kinda just there, for me. They make him more closer to his book counter part—but I don’t really care? Ben’s crush on Bev doesn’t do anything for me and altogether he’s just another body in the room when you take away all the background and backstory. Stanley, suffers here cause they didn’t care about the adults’ lives, so his adult self has seconds of screentime, which is kinda fair. The only reason it’d be odd was cause they made Stanley more of a character in the first part so it’s weird for him to just die in seconds. I am seeing discourse of how this movie handles his death, but I think I like this version more? I see people call it ‘nonsensical’ and ‘wrong’—to make his suicide heroic. But I think that the book version is also nonsensical, especially with the argument that Stanley could have just not gone. The way the final confrontation works, you need everyone and so I think it gives good reason to Stanley’s very strange response. I did also think the letter was sweet and helped bring the Losers together more and made Stanley more of a tragic character that he didn’t have the strength in him to unite with his friends and stand strong.  And of course there’s James Ransone’s Eddie. Easily the highlight of this movie. Ransone perfectly captures Jack Dylan Grazer’s Eddie. There humor and patheticness to him which is very welcome. Honestly, Eddie across all versions has been the highlight, but I think Ransone’s my favorite one. RIP, Ransone, like in this role, I think he genuinely brought some good life to what were just “side characters”. Pennywise is a bit more sparingly used here, despite being a constant throughout. He did have that good scene with the poor girl that had the birthmark, but everything else was kinda “meh”. Mostly because there’s too many spooks of him and the Losers. I hated the entire last sequence of everyone getting put in a private hell. It felt masturbatory for the director to just do some wild nonsense. I felt much lower on this movie on this rewatch. It was always kind of a big step down from the first but this really felt like a big step down with all the problems it’s riddled with. Half the actors don’t even seem like they want to be there and the story jingles justifies that. Not like the book was flawless, but this is very flawed indeed.  The King cameo was pretty fun though.
