title: Gonjiam: Haunted Asylum
my_review: Genuinely—and I hate speaking hyperbolically so this is with heavy intention—one of the scariest things I’ve seen in a good while and I really hate it for how. Worth noting I watched this alone, so maybe that bears some weight on my experience. There’s nothing groundbreaking here—it’s found footage, ghost hunters, teens/young adults, all the usual suspects for a found footage movie. But what really sets this apart is the filmmaking here. Each character has their own face cam that over time starts to be more and more uncomfortably close and discombobulating as the movie starts using just the face cams. This is how the movie is so effective, it just makes you squirm while watching it. No reprieve, just long and slow moments at the most uncomfortable of angles. You just want the movie to get over with it—it’s earned the spook, it’s won, but it just won’t let up. The excess horror just becomes kinda unbearable to watch because the movie itself is a bit unbearable to watch. This is something Gaspar Noe I feel has tried to do atleast two times I’ve clocked, the entire ending of ‘Climax’(2018) being upside down and uncentered so you can’t see a goddamn thing that’s happening for 15min as it moves through the chaos. And I think most infamously—because I certainly detested the unwatchability of it, his movie ‘Irréversible’(2002) which almost feels like the camera guy forgot to point the camera at anything in the movie. I believe Noe is very intentional about it, but I truly think when he’s used it—I get the wrong emotional response in deeply criticizing the filmmaking at hand. This movie though, I also believe is so very intentional and I do hate it, but because it works so effectively.  One scene in particular—the one I’m seeing is the see, I just had to turn the lights up and even skip ten second intervals past it, I hated watching it so much. It’s when the girls are returning and one of them becomes possessed and just won’t shut the fuck up with this gratingly-high-whispered-tongued-chanting. I fucking hated how long it kept going. How you’re forced both to watch the possessed girl’s freaky face chanting in your ear(maybe worse watching with headphones) aswell as you’re forced to see the other girl be mortified and her uncomfortably close face full of fear feels more and more disconcerting. Especially as we keep following her and you’re just worried you’ll be hit with another freaky ass chanting girl bit. It’s annoying filmmaking, but I believe it’s done correctly here. Those fixed angles are used to the movies advantage. It both gives the general spooks and adds a new layer to it. One that you can’t really get away from because this movie’s the equivalent of a kid coloring with markers and oversaturating the paper with the ink’s moisture so many times that it starts tearing away at the fibers and making a hole. It does what many horrors don’t by just slowly squeezing harder and harder instead of leaving everything to the end, or giving spikes and calms before it’s normalized. I hate watching this movie, but I think that’s just because it’s actually scary through the most heinous of ways.

title: What Keeps You Alive
my_review: The true Hunting Wife 🥁 Liked it, but the closer to the end it got the less excusable its writing got. There’s some real potential here, but it’s bogged down so much by some really egregious lapses in judgements by the characters. I think it’s solid up until the second time Jackie tries to throw Jules off a cliff. It’s a lil’ shaky before then, Jackie boldly letting Jules exist so unchecked—but it still felt sound. Jackie was bold because she had every right to be and there was a sorta theme of abuse(that didn’t quite exist until the twist) that kept Jules subservient. But once Jules actually gets away—not killing Jackie when she could and then going back and staying to TRY to kill the lesbian terminator, well that’s were it all goes downhill fast, real nosedive. I think it was that very theme of abuse and “conquering” your abuser, or some sense of “I’m not weak!” that leads to the terrible spike in writing. But it’s more than that, it’s just bad choice after bad choice after that. The “antique” gun(in fact, where the hell did Jackie’s crazy looking gun go, I assume Jules would have been in reach of it the second she took the jeep and raced to the cabin), staying to fight, Jackie not even walking in the right direction when she hears the music, Jules losing a gun fight where she’s the only one with a gun, Jackie leaving the scene of the crime she wouldn’t leave per her story—assuming this is why she races before her stroke at the end, Jules prepping a martyrdomed insulin shot instead of literally anything else… it’s all just so contrived. It’s a pity, cause up to that point it was really working. The abrupt heel-turn of the sweet, femme Jackie. Jules trying to make the most of a garbage start. Heck Jules trying to survive is maybe the most genuine desperation I’ve seen in a good bit. The boat chase in particular felt very manic and distressing for Jules. And I liked the change in direction with the dynamic of Jackie and Jules needing to pretend for the neighbors, almost felt like that could have gone on for much longer than it did. And I kinda love thinking of Jackie as a potential slasher and think there’s plenty of opportunity to lean into that. I don’t want Jules to be the one to live, but Jackie instead, heck both of them if it gets Jackie to hunt her down. But the idea of seeing Jackie seduce, fall in love with, marry and hunt more women feels like there’s some franchising opportunity there(a lá ‘Creep’(2014)), I dunno. Cause she definitely doesn’t have the best of motivations, she’s just full psychopath and is basically a serial killer, even with a Dexter-esk trophy box. Make her a lesbian Jason/Michael Meyers, not like there’s much variety in the slasher pool outside of the collection of Ghostfaces.  But yeah, the nearer the credits got, the more the good felt a bit spoiled by the bad. I think ultimately the better parts outweigh the parts that didn’t work, but it’s just a case of failed potential that hurts more than anything. I would be down for a sequel though, should some slasher leanings take more effect, just sayin’.

title: Anna and the Apocalypse
my_review: I did not know this was a musical. Just zombies and Christmas, so what a revelation that was when the first song starts up. But I think this is an inspired idea, though I dunno if the execution is all that great. I actually thought the songs and performances were pretty good for a random musical(that can be really hit or miss), but for as good as they are, once the zombie aspect kicks in, I don’t know if the musical aspect is serving the zombie plot. Like it felt like there’s a musical happening and it happens to be with some other story of these kids and zombies and Christmas. In particular the moment where the best friend dies and per musical rules, ‘when there’s overwhelming emotions—you must sing!’ But it just played out like a normal zombie death. What I wanted a whole number of the friends singing to eachother a passionate farewell to their friendship as he slowly turns into a zombie with the zombies dancing too.  That’s just it unfortunately, a weird mismatch of themes from a hat and they don’t compliment one another much at all. Aside from the jocks singing about killing zombies I just didn’t feel much from the zombies or songs, just that both were done alright. Hell it didn’t even feel much like a Christmas movie, just has that flavor thrown in there to have things like bloody sweaters and candy canes used as weapons. Kinda disappointing, it’s an idea so wild it just might’ve worked, except it didn’t here.

title: The Ritual
my_review:
When I first tried watching this as something in the background I dunno what happened but it was a DNF for me. I just got annoyed at it, skipped ahead, saw they were still just mucking about in the forest(somehow I missed the whole Cultish Village) and thought it was perhaps a lesser 'Blair Witch'-type film before just switching to something more stimulating.

But I'm glad I gave it another shot based on pure "word-of-mouth" seeing frequently brought up as a underrated horror flick. It's an interesting mix of horror and guilt and Rafe Spall might just pictured in the dictionary next to the definition of guilt, cause it's really his wheelhouse. But I thought his arc was pretty satisfying in the genre of horror movies where 'the monster is an overt metaphor for some mental hangup'.

I do think it faltered in a few ways, like I dunno if killing all the bros before the finale was as interesting as them all just being in or around that village, cause both felt pretty unexplored. Especially when the final friend's the most annoying one where you don't even really care what happens to him at that point. And the village felt far too short and could've taken more pointers from 'The Deer Hunter' and really made it a tense game of "which of my best friends is about to die right here".

But still a good watch, glad I gave it another fair go this time.

title: It
my_review: I think this is a straight up improvement in a lot of ways to the past 1990 version and even to the book. I never cared much for the nonlinear back and forth between ‘past and present’, so just giving just the kids’ plot works for me. I feel like the kids are really nailed here, feeling like the right age to endure this sort of story as they do, aswell as being  given more personality beyond their refrains and superficial traits. I think Pennywise works better for me here. Derry itself feels better characterized. It just works for me. I really really like the Losers here. They’re more fleshed out—act like kids and actually feel like a breathing friend group. Like in the 1990 version, Richie and Stan’s introduction is so weird to me cause the two of them are much taller(a rarity for Seth Green) and look older and even speak like they’re older despite being 10–12yrs old, but worst of all they come in like after thoughts. None of that happens here. We see these kids as friends in their habitat, walking and talking through school, four of them having a very clear camaraderie and life to their friendship. One thing I think King is—to be blunt, total dogshit at is writing kids. King’s kids think and act with too much wisdom as King does not alter his style of writing characters for ones that do not operate as the normal adult ones he writes. They act and may speak on kid knowledge but they all feel like Steve Buscemi in ‘30 Rock’—adults pretending to be kids. The Losers here are juvenile, trash talking, braggadocious, meek… they just walk and talk like kids do. I feel that dynamic is essential for this story and I feel like this version really captures that.  And as for the Losers themselves, I feel like most of them get much better characterizations than they had before. Though for some the changes aren’t always for their benefit. • Bill’s really good here. I’ve always liked Jaeden Martell performances and I think he captures a lot of nuance in Bill. His leadership in the face of sadness for recently losing a kid brother, anger that something took him and fear for facing that something. I do feel like though, he’s not given as inspiring a role as the book and subsequently the 1990 version. In those, Bill is somewhat fearless and the lynchpin to keeping everyone steady. So many instances where the characters deliberately find confidence in Bill’s resolve. Here Bill’s not quite so commanding a leader, many times it’s someone else who takes initiative where I feel like in the other versions Bill would be the main one making those calls. And there’s even being some pushback on Bill’s crusade. The other kids are scared, of what might happen and angry that they can’t just live ignorantly like the rest of the town, but are pulled in by Bill’s avenging of Georgie. It does diminish Bill’s prominence, but I feel like he’s a better character for it. • This is the only version of Richie I like. I didn’t mind Seth Green at all, but he doesn’t fit with the rest of the Losers at all, looking like an older brother to any of them. He’s not insufferable, but an enjoyable lil’ shit. I never found Richie’s bits funny in any version, but the fact that his friends clapback on his constant joking make his jokes so much funnier. Also helps that with the age up, he’s swearing more, less “pure” as most of the kids come off as in the books, here he just can’t shut up about sex, which feels accurate. Also helps that he’s not racist 96% of the time, doing ‘sambo’ impressions at every turn. Easily the most awkward part of the book—especially on audiobook. Probably accurate for the time, but goddamn it’s so prevalent. • Ben’s got a bigger shift in character. He’s much more shy, awkward, desperate—just overall dorky, which feels apt to me for the loner he was before the Losers brought him in. There is a major change with him though—he’s given all of Mike’s eventual quirks. They sorta clash in the book aswell—Ben being a such huge bookworm and Mike’s becoming a librarian. Ben’s bookwormming being brought up constantly and Mike just turning into one cause he’s so curious. It’s never really acknowledged or even related to between the two, but that could be because in the book Ben reads all about architecture to signal his eventual prolific career as one, while Mike is all about history. But the make Ben all about history here. It’s Ben who digs up all the lore. This is necessary for the movie cause there’s no cutback to the present to cover those details, but it takes away from Mike’s prominence as a character a bit. It does help ingratiate Ben more into the group that he can help with the problem, especially when they’re aged up more and his ability to instruct how they build forts’n shit is a bit redundant in a more modern age and as older kids. It works, but the cost is Mike, which is kinda an issue. • Mike does get some better development here than the 1990 version(he’s hardly a character as a kid), but not as much as the book. They make an odd change about his parents dying in a fire that’s related to everything happening. It helps him into the fold I guess, but it’s still a kinda weird change, especially cause he’s still so tacked on to the story. That does make the change with Ben double edged and unfortunate that Mike is once again shafted a bit in the story. Which already feels a sort of way when all the other characters here are white except for Mike, but moreso when they all get better but Mike stays a weak link. Which he did even feel that way in the book, him being the last to tagalong and just being an exposition dump that doesn’t get to really participate most of the time.  • I really like Eddie here. Eddie felt a little ancillary in the book to me—amongst the characters I feel like you could easily cut out. In the movies I think adult Eddie is the highlight though. But in this movie, I think Eddie’s just as much a high point. I like that he claps back to everyone, adding to the rapport between the kids. I think his character is leaned heavily into just being kinda too meek in the other versions, being a product of his mother’s overbearing and selfish “protectiveness”. There’s still that skittishness in him, but I think it’s spun into more of a comedic tone which works well in the group dynamic. Also adds more to the frustration of the group at Bill, which was a plus to me. • Stan is an actual character here. In the other versions Stan hardly feels apart of the Losers, in part cause he doesn’t come to help in the present. So I appreciate that his eventual development doesn’t impede on the past development. I will say, his development might also be at the cost of Mike’s again. He gets quite a bit here and well, Mike’s still shafted. Which might be worse cause he was the character I would most cut out of the story in the first place in my beliefs that there’s too many damn characters. • Beverly is the best here, 10000x better than the others. 1990 version wasn’t terrible, but still a slave to how she is in the book and I really don’t care for how she is in the book. To me, book Beverly is treated like a sexual glue to the group, that her only role is to ignite the sexual developments occurring in the boys. It’s just a really weird dynamic, one that seemed hingent on the infamous “train” scene which was supposed to be the ultimate “boys growing up” part of the story—but is still the fucking weirdest thing King has written. I much prefer her dynamic with the boys here. She’s made more of a “loner reject” of the school, her red hair branding her a harlot because some kids bully her through rumors. That builds her into a more mature kid than the others which adds to her confidence. Yes the boys are developing, noticing girls for the first time, noticing a girl that’s defiantly confident in her own development she was thrust into. But she’s not some thing to pass around between them, she’s just a girl that notices them noticing and even taunts with her boldness just to josh and tease them. I do feel that maturity and boldness is the element that takes away from Bill though. Many times it’s Beverly who takes charge and charges in, Bill being as much a follower as the rest. Thinking about it, I don’t think that’s a bad thing as it matches her improved character and I wasn’t so attached to Bill’s unshakable control on the group.  • Henry is also an improvement here for me. The greaser Henry in 1990’s(maybe the book, I forget if he was characterized as such) was kinda silly. The trashy abused Henry here just feels more real and much scarier. Like he’s truly deranged in the things he’s willing to do to hurt others and everything about him exudes that. I even like that Patrick is given the mildest of characterizations to complement Henry’s derangement. Just the mildest though, making him a pyromaniac I guess, instead of the genuine psychopath that kills and tortures things cause he doesn’t think other life matters. All that to say I like the nod that he’s the only friend stoked about Henry maiming Ben whilst the others are disturbed. I think Bill Skarsgård is my preferred IT. Curry I feel matches the book’s version, Pennywise not being so inherently creepy, but distressing in the more he acts. This Pennywise is just a straight up freak. He uses the goofiness as a clown juxtaposed with being terrifying rather than patronizing and goading like Curry’s. I like that he maintains his clown aesthetic as he transforms, I think that helps make him more iconic. I like that he feels more otherworldly, it really lends more credit to the cosmic horror that he is. Like I love the bit where he actually gets Georgie laughing and that kinda puts him into a trance like something moved in him as he became more drawn to Georgie as a meal, drooling over what he wants to do to him. Also helps that the modern special effects can’t just straight up make him more terrifying. When he bares his teeth it’s very distressing and sudden and that works for the fear-monger he is. Also as an aside, I like that Pennywise actually has a cue to notice that something different is happening. In the 1990 version, Curry just sorta starts taunting them, business as usual, oddly being fixated even though nothing’s really changed from his perspective. But here, the instance Bill gets Richie to see through his tricks, IT stops trying to eat Eddie and is unnerved at the defiance. From there he’s tenacious and more desperate and I just like that it has a moment for him to switch gears cause the Losers are doing what no other has done. Derry is also more characterized. The town actually feels wrong and strange. People don’t act normally, they just want to look away and ignore everything. That might even be why they push back on Bill so hard because they want to just live and forget. The 1990 version has a moment where they claim this is happening and show evidence and none of it seemed the slightest bit as what they were describing. In general I think this movie does a lot to allude to something bigger happening behind the scenes. I don’t want to get into the damn turtle—the turtle's a really weird leftfield addition, even in the book, but it was kinda cheeky how much they bring up turtles in the movie. They don’t have to get into the weird shit, just allude that it might be happening. I do feel like some people get too precious about the book, though they are sometimes valid. I feel like a lot of the changes just work better here and I’ve seen some fans just pushback on those, wanting exactly what the book did. I’ve seen a few lambaste the whole line “you’ll float too,” how this movie takes it literally where as the book it’s just a thing IT gets tickled by in saying. But I kinda like that it’s literal, that IT actually has a shrine of floating dead kids and things that it’s a promises that everyone “floats” when he takes them. It feels cosmic horror-ey and adds to IT’s weirdness. I will concede though, that sometimes the literal attitude this movie takes does hurt itself. Like the way they treat and beat IT feels out of a superficial over coming of fear, not belief and “shine.” I don’t thin either movie really lends credit to the shine between the Losers and how that’s why they persist where many would just easily die. Then things like the deadlights don’t feel as daunting. Bev is taken by the deadlights and it just kinda puts her into a hypnotic state, not the pure dread of existential horror that breaks people. I also think there’s just some weird tonal shifts here. I think the privilege of nonlinear storytelling is not having to follow up some haunting experience, just getting to jump ‘later’, after the moment’s passed. In particular when they clean the bathroom drenched in blood, they get super casual and have fun cleaning it up. Then that goes into the ‘rock war’ which feel oddly fun—it’s just a weird series of events that always take me out. The movie also might go too far into “cheap horror.” Lotta jumpscares and Pennywise just flailing around to freak the kids out, it started feeling overdone the more it kept happening. I like this one though, best of all the ‘IT’s I reckon, even if it’s only “half” a story.

title: Leatherface
my_review: Covered in putrid gore from tauntauning a rotting cow carcass, you then stumble on a stream of clean fresh water. You first puke in said stream and then proceed to barely rinse just your face with a cupped hand of water to then just continue walking onward, letting the sun bake the sticky viscera onto your skin.

title: Radius
my_review: Interesting idea that’s more interested in answering itself(usually with more questions) than ever really exploring the idea fully. Have to wonder if they read that comic from X-Men, where a kid wakes up to his down all dead and Wolverine shows up to tell him his mutation is to basically kill people in a radius and that he has to put him down. Possibly just a coincidence, but the backstory of a mutation and the context of mutants adds a lot to that story, where here it it’s lacking any real context and is just part of the gimmick—which wasn’t that well explored or eventually explained why.

title: 12 Feet Deep
my_review: Sister and the “ex”-con are some incredibly frustrating characters. She gets them in there in the first place. She keeps yapping when she shouldn’t. Won’t stop making it all about her— though her “struggle” is the core theme of the movie, it really comes off as her being a very asininingly dense character. The only way they get out is when they sister decides to stop being such a dick about everything, as if the entire time they’re trapped she’s not taking it seriously and only once her sister is on the brink of death does she decide to try, made only worse by it being something suggested an hour ago. (Though these kinda flicks do all have that problem. Even one that I liked— ‘Fall’(2022) does the same shit by saving the day by just doing one last “college try” which would have cut the movie in half. It’s not that I want the movie to end faster, but maybe don’t solve the problem so quickly and just opt not to attempt it until you’ve hit feature length. Especially when the solution isn’t something dire like cutting an arm off to survive.) And then the “ex”-con can’t decide how evil they’re gonna be. Hanging around for no reason but to monologue, which sure, but don’t try make us sympathize cause what an evil move. And then by not committing to killing them— which again, it’s trying to make her a bit sympathetic, but c’mon, it’s already so evil just leaving random people trapped. You can’t have her so flippantly malicious and still expect us to walk away feeling sorry for her, because the mere act of flippancy in this context is so damning. I will say though, I had such a genuinely cathartic moment when she popped up with a gun at the very end, that the movie went there. Genuinely almost made the whole thing worthwhile, but then they skimp out on the schlock by the end. Which this movie needed not to do, embrace the schlock, cause it’s doesn’t work with as self serious as they tried making it.

title: Annabelle: Creation
my_review: Wow, these Annabelle movies are just super slow, aren’t they? The doll’s maybe not interesting enough to carry a whole movie as she just sits there—menacingly every scene.

title: 47 Meters Down
my_review: I feel like there’s just an array of easy solutions to this problem, chiefly being just to have them swim up whilst having dumped chum elsewhere. Or just biting the bullet and tanking the bends, which I don’t believe is so terribly as damning as sitting trapped in cage underwater. Maybe that’s a dumb idea, but so does the rest of this movie—seem so very dumb.

title: The Endless
my_review: Incidentally this feels a little lost at what it was going for. There's that grandiose Lovecraft mystery at hand, but it's a lite version. Watered down with persistent humor that doesn't land and very surface level "horror" that never seems all that bad. While there are interesting ideas at play, they don't seem to ever lead towards anything as the movie just sorta teeters out than ending on some big revelation- something I'd've expected with Lovecraft.

title: Tragedy Girls
my_review:
Feel like the inclusion of Kevin Durand—which I’m never opposed to more Durand, was kinda redundant? They open with an interesting hook and the  promptly just do jack shit with it as they hop on a different interesting prompt.

But it’s a fun lil’ gem. Maybe best enjoyed whilst not thinking much about it, but it’s still a fun spin on a slasher.

title: Get Out
my_review: Even after the reveal of Alison Williams being crazy... would.

title: Terrifier
my_review:
I’m not quite the crowd for these, in the same way I prefer to eat a dish whole, not eat the ingredients on their own. This is just pure gore and torture porn tethered together with the barest minimum of trashy writing and acting. Though after this I can see some of the allure, I guess specifically why Art has become such a breakout horror mascot. 

Like the moment he pulls a gat out of nowhere did get me. Lowkey he reminded me alot of Stu Macher from ‘Scream’(1996), a psycho killer that’s childish in how they don’t like when people don’t play along. Like the infamous scene in ‘Scream’ where Lillard improvises getting really hit with the phone and just has a big goofy reaction—that’s all Art, just taking everything so personally and goofily. Any time Art is beat with something, he’s just reeling and temperamental about it rather than malicious like any slasher would be. It works alot here and definitely feels like the only thing keeping you watching at times.

title: Shin Godzilla
my_review: I'd been putting this one off for a while and based on hearsay and my own speculation- this was very different than I expected. Everyone mentions "freaky-zilla"(how could they not though) but nobody mentions that it's "Godzilla vs Bureaucracy". Very different and very unique seeing a monster movie play out largely in large conference rooms in swivel chairs, than constant mayhem and panic- which is still there, but moreso an instigator for more deliberations.

title: The Untamed
my_review: I did not expect to like this as much as I do. Went in relatively blind, although I did realize pretty quick what made me add this to my watchlist—I knew it was the “tentacle porn”-movie right from the first slide away shot. All I had thought was “How’re they gonna go and make a movie with ‘tentacle porn’?” not really expecting much more than degeneracy and the whatnot. But this was a different kinda animal(pun somewhat intended). It’s a slow burn. You start forgetting there was a mystery, it takes so much time building up the four characters’ relationships. Somehow, this movie doesn’t rely on its gimmick. The prospect of “tentacle fucking” happening is actually quite sparingly used and reserved—which is a funny sentence to type out. This movie cares far more about the emotional level of relationships, how ‘fulfilling sex’ affects you and how it can destroy you. All four characters are in toxic relationships. Toxic in the same ways as eachother, be it sexual dependency, lovelessness, lack of sexual fulfillment, emotionally/physically abusive… all four of them kinda fall somewhere in the Venn diagram of toxicity. And while the tentacle monster is technically a fifth participant, I feel it’s more of what the movie describes before unveiling the wildest orgy you’ve ever seen. That the tentacle monster is a primal urge in everything, it is sexuality, in all ways. Cause how it’s fucking these people isn’t so much the story as much as how that transforms them. It is sexual-fulfillment/liberation/frustration/aggression… it is everything in a relationship and how the good can improve your life and the bad can ruin it. I gotta give props to this movie’s willingness to ‘boldly go’ and actually just go all in on the sex. I think that’s definitely an aspect of this that’ll polarize any and all watchers of it, but it feels essential to me. Incidentally I’ve also watched another “tentacle porn” movie recently, ‘Touch Me’(2026), that actually follows alot of the same thematic beats as this movie, the alien there also being the embodiment of a toxic relationship in other characters, but with a comedic spin on every facet. Though it doesn’t quite go as far as this movie was willing to go and I think that pushed boundary helps ‘The Untamed’ deliver something that—to me, felt very nuanced. Both kinda are, but this movie especially feels like it’s retracing the steps ‘Possession’(1981), maybe even going further, if only because “we have the technology” and I guess that’s a formula that really works for me.  This isn’t for everyone and I do feel there’s a maturity to it that you have to meet on its level, cause otherwise it’d be so easy to write this off as some movie that just does it for the shock value. Yeah this snuck up on me, really dug it.

title: The Conjuring 2
my_review:
Actually kinda dug this more than the first. Seems to address alot of nitpicks I had the first go around and just went bigger with it. 

Will say though, doors locking has become such a funny recurring gag here. For all their knowledge of ghosts, you’d think they’d know by now to take all the doors of their hinges when a haunt is happening.

title: Train to Busan
my_review: I’ve never been entirely won over by this movie. I always felt it was ‘one of the best modern zombie movies’, with great characters and the setting of a train—which is creatively utilized, as is the way the zombies work/are outsmarted. But there was always this throughline of cloyingly clunky character development and moral lessons that feels almost too much at times. But this was maybe the fourth time I brought it up to show someone and this time was with my friends and somehow—it’s even more cloying than I remembered. Definitely in part due to watching it with people who felt the same and also will vocalize & joke about that fact. I had no excuses to give and I didn’t really want to give and pass to the movie. What worked still does and this deserves credit for that, but it does deserve flack for what really doesn’t. I really hate the daughter character. She’s the equivalent of being spoon fed sugar to go along with your pizza. She’s just unnecessary and feels like a crutch of writing because they couldn’t figure out a better way to convey the themes they were aiming for. The daughter isn’t the only one though. There’s the selfish business man who you immediately know is gonna make it to the end by stepping on heads. There’s the grannies and hobo who serve as tokens of good karma than actual characters—lessons to “help others”. Even the father has such a black and white arc where his intentions of protecting his daughter are rooted in his business-mind and lack the humanity to actually make it through. None of these are inherently bad to have in a story, but I don’t think the writing here knows how to implement them without giving Vegas sized signs telling you what to feel. It’s not all the time that that’s the case—I’m thinking of two scenes in particular that standout. One is Ma Dong-seok opening up to the dad to say he must be a “bad father” because he’s sacrificing his relationship with her to provide. It’s a very nuanced scene cause it’s so obvious how much Ma dislikes the kinda man the dad is, but here it comes off as admiration and envy as it sounds like he wishes he could provide so much for his own budding family, but knows he won’t. It’s not black or white though, cause Ma’s also much less selfless and a better man that the dad was. Doing things because they’re right rather than savvy. I just really like that scene cause it’s both—not spoon fed, but also a good development for the dad as it kinda vindicates his doing whatever he can for the daughter when the whole first half kinda judges him for it. In that moment it’s bittersweet cause the better man wishes he could be him, but the whole time the dad’s in awe of this guy saving his ass. The other bit is when they push through into the safe car. It’s the “right thing” because it’s saving lives and the ones with the businessman are acting entirely out of self-preservation and their actions got two good people killed and would have gotten even more if they didn’t claw their way in. I do feel like the movie’s wanting to be black and white about this, but I sympathize with the safe car’s actions because there’s really so much that could go wrong having a good heart. This is once again where the movie follows up with something so clunky(for one of my friends it ruined the movie for him), with the grannie getting herself and everyone “bad” killed because her sister died. The framing feels like it’s saying this is good, but fuck that grannie. I think it being “good” is erroneous because it’s just as selfish an action as any the businessman makes and also just such a stupid one. It’d be one thing to just be something evil on the grannies part to match the “evil actions” the others incurred on themselves, but I don’t think what they did was evil, so that whole moment feels so bad to watch cause the vibes are all wrong. Truly, there’s one reason I think so fondly on this movie and what I look forward to in bringing it up to watch with others—it’s mother fuckin’ Ma Dong-seok/Don Lee. I think the “Reacher” effect kicks in with his character in just how electrically jubilant it is to watch this chad of a man just bodying zombies left and right. It’s not just the action around this character though—he’s just the most interesting part, him and his wife. They’re both so cute and playful and also so distinctly “better” than the dad which I think gives the dad an interesting arc in wanting to be as selfless and a role model to his daughter in the same way this couple effortlessly are without even having the baby yet. Ma’s also just very fun to watch onscreen and I’m glad it seems that this movie really opened the door for him(pity his big foray into Hollywood was the polarizing and flopped ‘Eternals’(2021), though he could still show up in other things possibly). He’s got a lot of charm and just a distinct look that sets him apart(only just realizing that I’m not sure I’ve seen much variety in body types in any of the Korean movies I’ve seen). There’s one thing I know people will like about this and that’s him and his character and it’s always the highlight of watching this. But yeah, there’s a lot of cheesiness that’s a bit too much for me in this movie. Sometimes it feels right in the “B-Movie” sense that zombie-flicks usually are, but other times it just feels kinda weak. It could just be I’m not crazy about Yeon Sang-ho as a director. I haven’t seen ‘Pennisula’(2020), but the reactions I saw kinda make me not want to, but I do remember excitedly going to watch ‘Psychokinesis’(2018) and being severely disappointed in that lame-ass movie. There’s high points to this for sure, but as a whole there’s a lot of low points, I’m finding on this rewatch.

title: The Wailing
my_review:
It's interesting that for me I really dug the long runtime. It's just a slowly unraveling horror akin to Junji Ito's 'Uzumaki' where the innocuous and strange becomes horrid and scary. 
Have to also give a shout-out to one of the most bumbling protagonists in horror. I really liked how shamelessly jumpy and excitable he was. Felt it really added to the horror that such a uncool guy was facing such big stakes.

title: Terra Formars
my_review: Something something, ‘…basically the roaches in Houston!’ Didn’t even realize this was Takashi Miike until seeing the initial reviews here, neat. Pretty bad, though. I saw it was a manga/anime and contemplated how much interest I’d invest in this and just thought “ahh, fuck-it, I’ll just watch it”, kinda glad I did cause I don’t feel like I was missing much. It’s just one of those “shock-fest” sorts of series where everyone dies horrifically after having “their moment” just for shock value. I don’t know who really kicked it off, but I know around ‘The Walking Dead’ & ‘Game Of Thrones’, this sorta stuff felt super prevalent in media, like ‘Attack On Titan’ being so chock full of it. Can’t say it does much by itself for me now. Paired with the roaches, bugs of it all… it’s just so very unappealing. Just bad all around.

title: I Am Not a Serial Killer
Creepy
my_review:
This movie made me mad, but I don't feel it was for the right reasons.

I was actually really digging it for the first half or so, was definitely giving me 'Cure' vibes, which had drawn me to Kiyoshi Kurosawa's other works in the first place, so this was a very good thing. A kinda 'broody mystery' unfolding in such a way that it stokes your curiosity the deeper they go. But by the time it comes round to actually "unmasking the monster", the whole movie spirals out of control, actually reminding me of another movie which is a much less flattering comparison from me. 

When the second half really starts going, it really invokes the same frustrations and annoyance that I got from 'Speak No Evil'(2022).  'Speak No Evil' left me filled with hate by the end, not because the heinous plot and violence, but because of how the movie gets to those aspects. I understand with that movie that it's utilizing a cultural behavior to fuel it's horror, but at the same time the characters acted immensely moronic so as to put the protagonists in danger. I actually believe it was Jeremy Saulnier commenting on his new movie at the time- 'Green Room', something like "-characters can be as smart as possible, but they have to be a little stupid to move the plot along." which I believe is an ideology that 'Speak No Evil' and 'Creepy' overcommit to. 'Creepy' has so god damn many instances of characters not explaining themselves, letting oddities slip by, not telling people what or where there going, not questioning the most bizarre shit and going into shady situations with reckless abandon. These characters seem to go brain dead in order to give the villain his opportunity and it's just not compelling to watch the story break immersion by continuously making characters go donkey brained.

But it was as I was getting riled up watching at peak annoyance, thinking to myself- "Whelp, looks like another Kurosawa that failed to capture what made 'Cure' so good.", that I finally realized the worst aspect of this. This movie's just a repeat of 'Cure'. It's not exactly the same, but Kurosawa just replaced "Hypnotism" with "Mystery Suggestion Drugs". 
-It still follows a detective of sorts who takes an odd interest in this mysterious case. 
-It has the villain be an eccentric serial killer who never gets their hands dirty, instead the somehow coerce an innocent accomplice to carry out their whims. 
-Detective starts to spiral from finding a truth that no one else seems to comprehend. 
-And said detective ends up caught in the very web he sought to destroy.
It does switch a bit of it up, but as the girl inexplicably carried out heinous actions towards her family, the correlation to what made 'Cure' so "horrific" is a "killer that's able to turn good and loving people against eachother or themselves" and 'Creepy' was using that very same premise to accentuate the heartless nature of the villain, but it somehow just didn't work as well. I feel it's due to the idiotic characters, but where this movie has characters act stupid just to be stupid, 'Cure' has characters acting dumb because they didn't realize they were being dumb. 'Cure' is fully supernatural with cops unknowingly finding themselves out of their depth, but 'Creepy' is not supernatural. In fact 'Creepy' never really explains much of how anything works, just that "it does" and characters seem to just walk right into danger like moths to a bug zapper. Like it's never explained why the girls do what they do to their families, never a scene of him drugging them or why Mio seemed to be capable of defiance? Or it never pays mind to what this mystery drug is that instantly makes people 'addicted putty' for the villain? Or how the professor/detective managed to beat the drug in an incredibly contrived and opportune moment? They're all good bits of storytelling, but they're just clumped together with no tact or care.

'Creepy' seemed only to work for me because Kurosawa was channeling 'Stephen King' and rewriting the premise/theme/hook of what I believe to be far and away his best film. But by the end it's the amount of logic loopholes that drag this down as it may be a "rewrite" of sorts, but it changed just enough of some elements to make the story nonsensical as it doesn't have the same context that worked the first go around. This movie asks you to ignore logic rather than set the stage for a world where logic can be bent. It squandered it's potential and instead made what could've been "good/fine" into a an unfortunate demerit for Kiyoshi Kurosawa.

title: Tag
my_review:
Actually factually unhinged as all hell. Genuinely I feel like this movie took the idea of “never let them guess you’re next move” to heart, cause there’s just so much “WTF?”-moments here. At first it was shockingly delightful, though the further along it got and the more it did it, it starts to feel unendingly repetitive. 

Somewhat similar feeling as the ‘SpongeBob’ episode ‘Doing Time’, where-in Mrs. Puff seems to go through a ‘Inception’(2010)-amount of dream levels that just kinda keep going into the end of the episode. As a kid it was always such a strange and unsatisfying episode, the more you’re tugged through this surreal nightmare, the more you start trying to stop and step back to wonder—“Okay, but where’s this actually going?” and the episode just doesn’t have an answer because it does not know itself. 

Yeah, this movie’s much the same, the more I think on it. The intrigue of what’s happening is supplanted by the absurdity of the next scene and it just gets old. By the end when you get an explanation, it’s as satisfying an answer as your dad’s excuse for ‘not getting ice cream’, is that it’s too cold outside and the machines freeze. Sure, it kinda works, but it’s also just so very nonsensical and/or so outta leftfield(though the entire movie is, so not completely unfounded logic).

I do kinda like it though. The beginning’s probably the better part of this, but it’s not a bad watch at all, just a bizarre one. Could have used more Aki though, especially with the strange development with her. Also just actually chomping on that queerbait, though I might take pause on that cause maybe it’s for narrative reasons not to take the bait. Also, the title’s bit strange, really doesn’t fit this at all, I feel like, especially for the in universe explanation.

title: The Final Girls
my_review: Fun somewhat meta spin on a camp slasher(‘Friday the 13th’ in particular). There’s some good acknowledgements of the typical tropes and how the typical beats land in a slasher, but it never quite goes as hard as it could. It’s all very surface level nods as it plays it super straightforward rather than making it all about the gimmick, save one or two moments(flashback and final girl-status, obviously). I do feel that’s somewhat due to having so many characters that don’t really have anything to do but exist. Like Alexander Ludwig for example just doesn’t really fit in this movie—not the actor but the character. He’s usually just there, reacting to things and not really falling into any notable role, or one the movie cares much about. There a big moment in the movie and he’s there, but like a piece of furniture, doesn’t even get a reaction shot or anything, so when they show him again I was just like—“He’s still alive?” Same with Alia Shawkat, she’s just kinda there for fodder. Hell, her and Nina Doprev just die together in a pretty uneventful way as if they’re just trying to skip all the steps that’d been putting off. Probably would have been much tighter if there were like only three interlopers. Especially since they don’t do much with “we can die too” besides ousting Middleditch a little too early. There’s something that caught me way off guard here though. I was genuinely quite surprised how damn emotional this got me. For as goofy as it is and as clunkily handled some aspects are, there’s an unexpected through line about grief. Grief between Taisa Farmiga’s character and her ill-fated mom, Malin Åckerman, who returns “from the dead” as the movie character she was most known for. Like goddamn, if anything their scenes were so endearing, seeing Farmiga’s character squeezing this bizarre opportunity for all it’s worth. Then they got down to this theme of finally letting go and then the not-mom easily was willing to die for her not-daughter, whom she barely knows in this context—that just got to me(goddamn, even tearing up now as I write it). Farmiga sells the emotion and Åckerman gives the mom such charm that makes it easy to mourn over her too. It’s a bit frustrating though that the movie doesn’t seem to appreciate the anguish Farmiga would be/is going through. Her thing with her mom is kinda a sidearc on the way to dealing with the slasher, where characters keep ignoring her feelings with the “keep your head in the game”-attitude. Like Ludwig just keeps dismissing her investment in her “fake-mom” so that they can survive and he’s even there to see her have such a heavy moment and he never mentions it. He just pops in like an award and makes out with Farmiga after she slays the evil, as if she would not be reeling from having just watched her mom die in front of her again, or rather, would still be working through the intense emotions of finally letting go. There’s also no real subtext of Farmiga blaming herself which seems like a missed opportunity? She was the one to incite the accident and typically characters would blame themselves and there her mom is dying “because” of her again and that’s not brought up as a parallel? It still hits hard, but I think it goes to show that they weren’t as attuned to the strongest aspect in my opinion, as they could have been. All that said—fun movie. Funny enough and a good pairing for any seasonal watches for as much as it pays homage to classics.  Was kinda funny that they do a blooper reel at the end and it’s literally just Thomas Middleditch and Adam Devine spitballing jokes.

title: All Cheerleaders Die
my_review: Somehow this wasn't nearly as schlocky and campy as I had expected going in. It's just a real fun lil' supernatural revenge horror.  But as much as I liked it, I kinda felt like ‘Witch-Ex Leena’ kinda hijacked the movie from Mäddy, who I was far more invested in. Like I was really getting into the “lesbian cheerleader” route with Mäddy and Tracy that was hitting all the classic beats you'd expect, even the bit where the romantic interest finds damning evidence of the MC lying about their initial intentions. But throughout that—Leena’s just there and won't leave and the movie won’t stop making it about her and Mäddy. Like if that was their route, give the two of them a little more interaction, give credence to their relationship. Cause what was there is just Mäddy feeling justifiably weirded out by Leena and then Leena stalking her until she gets to save the day. Hell, Tracy just stops being actively into Mäddy, just so Lena can creep about and ‘win’ her at the end of the day? Wack. Then there’s just too much they didn’t do because it’s short and Leena starts to become the MC. Like Mäddy hardly even gets to cover why she's doing what she's doing, she doesn't even really get revenge on Terry—Leena does for her. Hardly any schenaniganrey with the sisters who've been "Freaky Friday"ed. And then yeah, Tracy just kinda does whatever—which is apparently not following up on any previous loose ends from the beginning. She doesn't even really get a moment with Terry despite their baggage with eachother, instead she goes off killing random jabronies(Sidenote, felt bad for the one football player that was actively trying to help/make amends and Mäddy seemingly just kills him for no reason, cause she certainly didn't get a power-up. Did he just have to die because he was a footballer and just inherently bad by proxy?).   But Leena gets everything she wanted: powers, the hot ex-girlfriend she obsessed over back with her and all the big beats in the story. Like she's the one to save the cheerleaders, she's the one to provoke the reveal of Mäddy being raped then is the only one to react over it and then she gets to beat Terry. I don't even think her and Mäddy had that as good of chemistry as Mäddy and Tracy did. Almost felt like a self insert or she was in some relationship with the director but that's apparently not the case. It's just wild to me cause she's written so as such a "she doesn't even go her"-type of character. Or rather like 'The Simpsons' Poochie-bit I think alot of where Poochie is introduced out of nowhere and inexplicably gets shoehorned into every plotline to the tune of "What does Poochie[Leena] think of this development???". It's odd to go so scrupulously critical of a "rompy comedy/horror", but it's just because I liked it so much and wished it just nailed it a little better than it did. Cause this really was surprisingly fun and well done instead of the "poorly made, but goofy and schlocky"-movie I was expecting. Cut Leena out entirely, have them just get buried on ‘Indian Burial Grounds’ and let the cheerleaders bang and murder together.

title: The Conjuring
my_review:
Feel like I should like this more than I do. I’ve come to learn I’m quite enthralled by “spirit detective”-type horrors, though South Korea seems to be the best proponent of that—‘The Wailing’(2016), ‘Ex Huma’(2024). And that’s the realm I think this movie lives in, but that’s itch just ain’t scratched.

Always love seeing Patrick Wilson and Vera Farmiga always a welcome addition—though their characters are kinda bland here. Like a bowl of oatmeal without the strawberries or cream, they just kinda feel like the sneaky clean when biopics are made of living people. I don’t know if that was at all the case when they made this, but regardless—the end result here is just two very well-to-do “spirit detectives” that live an idyllic and boring life. I’m not saying I want one to be an alcoholic or to portray them as sleazier opportunists, but more than just “Dick & Jane”.

But the other reason I don’t think that “itch” got scratched is maybe the nature of this kinda horror? It’s all very bog standard—well done, but still, the boggiest of standards. There’s some of that investigative face off with the paranormal, but it ends up in the same pitfalls you usually see. The knowledge of what’s happening never counters the spooks, just leads to more spooks. But what I want is that “Oh, see this isn’t spooky at all, this is just a classic case of blah blah blah…” Their competency is there, but it never really feels like an asset other than knowing what’s happening next, which they never mitigate, just deal with as it comes.

Still though, it’s alright. Nails all the horror beats that crowd please, can’t fault it for that.

title: Texas Chainsaw 3D
my_review: I don’t believe for a second that that family had the genes on any immediate branch to produce someone as hot as Alexandra Daddario. It’s so crazy an idea that it just almost works. Something I really hated off the rip with the recent ‘Scream’ films(5 &6) was this contrived way they forced new blood into the franchise while incessantly hammering in how much they were within the “formula”, so if you don’t like it that’s on you. Same thing happens here with Daddario’s character being “apart of the family” and oddly I didn’t hate it? I have to think it’s definitely alot to do with the fact that this movie doesn’t take itself as seriously as the newer ‘Scream’s, but also that it’s not really trying to force some narrative into a series with rigid narrative. It’s just hitting the ‘reset’ button like most every sequel in this franchise has done—so yeah, go buck wild with it. That said—do they make it work here? Not entirely. I’m more remiss this ended up a one off that didn’t get the chance to get wilder with it like the 00’s got to. One way it kinda botches it, is how unbaked Daddario’s secondary background is. Like there’s her backstory as an adopted child, but then what’s her deal coming into this random inheritance? There’s not really anything that really leads you to understand why she sides with this murderous family. Leatherface literally—brutally—murdered all her “close” friends and suddenly she’s ride or die with him? There didn’t have to be much, but something to the tune of her not having a place where she belongs or whatever. Now there is some of that and I did just say it didn’t need much, but I lied and it needed more. Like I feel a clear reason for her to turn bad would be that her friends fucking suck donkey dick, but that never comes up and she never seems to think more about them once she’s taken to the police station—which is weird cause she’s the ‘kindly final girl’. On that note, the friends are so goofy here too. Not like many of the other movies have fleshed out friends, but two thirds have just enough meat on their stories to make it weird how unimportant they end up being, then the other third’s just sorta inexplicably there and then a bonus added one is just a rando that instantly gets killed off without a care(still don’t understand why they’d just leave him at her house and not be afraid of a stranger messing with her new shit). But yeah, very glad to have both Daddario, but also Tania Raymonde(as a kid I was always a fan of Cynthia on ‘Malcolm in the Middle’) and their fan service moments are obvious, but like I said, with Raymonde, there was an unhinged choice to have her support her friend and then brazenly lure her man into cheating with her, when she invited herself to be supportive of her friend—just garbage behavior. But that’s such a good motive for Daddario to not care that she or the boyfriend die and yet it never comes up. No horrible realization, or angry lashing out, or sad unwanted cuckquenery, just nothing comes from it except  Raymonde showing some skin. And as sensible as that might be alone, it’s just silly to not connect those dots. But it’s also even worse that the boyfriend dies from just the car wreck and Raymonde gets dragged off screen, to only then die horribly by a dumb cop who was coming to save her.  Maybe those two were done as so for the explicit reason as their blood wouldn’t be on Leatherface’s hands, but c’mon. Bro still sawed whatshisface in half and he’s the whole reason they were put in danger to start with. Also as an aside, that third friend as just so odd. Was he supposed to be… gay(?) or like the stand in for the not romantically available to anyone, ‘stoner/nerd’-archetype? Cause he looks so goofy and I don’t think we’re supposed to buy him being with Raymonde, so yeah, who is he and why does he look like he’s starring in a gay porn? I didn’t mind him, but there’s too much going on that you can’t not address. Ultimately I think if this channeled more of ‘The Texas Chainsaw Massacre 2’(1986), it’d be much more solid. This is a nutty premise and one the demands Daddario going full goofy cannibal by the end as she runs the hellscape estate of ‘the family’. The way this goes, it almost gets there—as awful as the “cuz” line was, that’s the schlock I wanted—but it’s mostly too much plain bad writing to carry the “good” bad writing. Like Leatherface is somehow pitied and made a victim and that’s kinda wild when he still so readily massacres whenever the opportunity presents itself. Inherently not good, but I do like it.

Cause like, Bell’s just one note and the couple believe his lie and still want to go out just the same, so there’s no real point to trusting or doubting him cause the movie says “right or wrong, he’s still such an ass they’d rather risk dying outside”.

title: The Skin I Live In
my_review: I don’t know why, but this is the first Almodóvar film I’ve really dug. Admittedly though, of not many seen. I’ve struggled want to watch Almodóvar with my reluctance to indulge in his penchant for the most toxic romance you could imagine—but played in earnest and without acknowledgement. That and in general just didn’t make his filmography that appealing to sift through and flummoxing to see such reverence. But I think his spin and style work very well here, actually.  It’s fucked all the way up. Twisted, sci-fi, erotic, thriller… just harmonizes well with Almodóvar. It’s still very weird and characters still act with a casual acceptance of the taboo, but maybe—for me, it’s that there’s no sense of skirting around obstacles. It knows what it is and it’s not supplanted by a sweeping romance(not inherently atleast, in this case).  Unfortunately I was actually very aware of the twist. I’d actually always wanted to sit down and watch this—I think when I was younger and…hornier, I tried but for whatever reason tapped out early. But somewhere along I learned the twist and always saw the poster and thought “I wonder how they explain/treat the fact that she was a man”. It is always amusing though to watch such a movie with a big twist and think “is this when [twist] happens??” Pretty great though. The most I’d knock it for was it felt very unfinished by the end. The interaction with the mother I looked forward to and wondered about Vera/Vicente’s acclimation to life or the turmoil of whatever emotions festered in captivity. But no, just cut it there. I’d almost wished we never saw them reach the dress shop and just cut from the escape if that’s where it was gonna stop.

title: Scream 4
my_review: Best sequel/“reboot” in the franchise. I think perception kinda coming around on this, but I still feel this isn’t given near the amount of dues it’s owed in the series. It does what the past two weren’t able to and juggles in new characters with the old. New characters don’t really live(until the actual soft-reboot), but they are given some more substance than previous sequels. It genuinely does feel like a new, younger cast to potentially carry on the torch which adds more value to their meta-fixation on “New Vs Old” as they die off and suffer for trying to surpass the OG’s. Especially the actual killers though, whom in each sequel they opt to just not show as much and pretend it’s as good a reveal. Making their twists tied to newly revealed context that add some “shock”, but not really a replacement for developed characters being outed as villains. Here the killers actually come and mingle more with the good guys. With Emma Robert’s Lily in particular, she’s very much a “victim” like the rest, which is why for my money that makes her’s the best reveal in the series and leads to a very cool twist of her “winning” and the last 20min being an “epilogue” where she learns that she failed to secure her victory. I still love Billy and Stu more for classic status and just the Lillard of it all, but Jill’s probably my next favorite Ghostface. Entirely due to I think her character actually providing more than a twist but a neat subversive ending unlike any other ‘Scream’s, which harks very much back to what the original did in its time. Also, I think maybe the best at leaving clues for who the killers are. First time I had a pretty decent idea at who was Ghostface at what point and when Jill makes her breakaways. With others you either don’t know to expect two or they’re just not really that central of characters to have “outs” and “opportunities” to suit up and kill, they just do and show up in a later scene. I also like the returning 3 here. Sidney is forever my favorite. And Gale’n Dewey have a bit more of an arc than the previous movies. Actually getting development now and now bearing more desire to solve the case than just the sake of good. Gale—purpose again as an “lead” and Dewey—fulfilling his role as the protector of not just his friends, but the town. Sidney doesn’t get too much, but she doesn’t entirely need it anymore. The most I could want was Sydney dunking on Ghostface which she does again and again. She’s the constant here and one I don’t want or think can ever change honestly unless they can back it up with something actually good(foreshadowing for ’Scream’(2022)). And I kinda love how outlandish the opening was, very self-deprecating.  Aside from the good though, there’s alot that feels more corny than not. Cops are horrendously bad at their jobs here, how Ghostface eluded them so blatantly is wild. Anderson and Brody were funny, but they’re more fitting for a jokier movie. Here they serve as a comedic presence that doesn’t fit and seem far too lax about dying. They’d fit far better in an opening with how campy they’ve gotten in the series, in the actual movie they took me out of it, especially in how lame, easy and inconsequential their deaths are. In general the whole town’s not nearly as on top of this as they should be. First movie was one thing, but allowing parties to happen under their noses and low security on all potential targets is wild. Sure “it’s a movie” but it’s pretty contrived while at the same time they’re so good at explaining and poking holes in other things. Low security could’ve been another easy meta point, that they could atleast address. Good movie, reason why I got into ‘Scream’ in the first place as I wanted to hop in whilst this was premiering. Hope time is even better to it amidst the…later sequels.

title: The Roommate
my_review: I like both Leighton Meester and Minka Kelly alright, but I couldn’t figure out why they’d go and cast two women who look near identical. I though “surely this’d be a plot point”, they even went down the ‘trying to be a replacement for a dead-sister’-route, but even still, like it’s never really acknowledged how alike these two are and I don’t think you can star both of them and not draw any attention to that fact. I came in expecting a very ‘obsessed [not] lesbian’-thriller since that’s very much the vibes I remember trailers for this being—like almost erotic thriller territory, like I vaguely recall the trailers hinting more towards something more sapphic, only to realize it was a side character that was offhandedly gay whom Meester merely pursues just to get her off the board. But seeing it now, I felt like that was very much not on the menu. I came in expecting my thoughts to be “would’ve been better if they committed more to the lesbian-angle”—which isn’t untrue, but the dynamic between these two did feel a bit more platonic than I expected. Like Meester’s genuine goal was to be the bestest friend and “sister” to Kelly—a role with no room for any other friends or sexual partners, but still a role that seemed mostly platonic. Which is fine, but once again, the two look so similar to me that it’s strange there wasn’t a leaning in more in the likeness they shared. That Meester’s motivation wasn’t birthed of their looking alike and/or her character always wanting a sister and/or especially her wanting to be Minka Kelly. Like she impersonated her twice here yet neither time had her actually masquerade as Kelly, but rather just go “Hmmm” as the other person thinks Kelly is who they’re talking to. It just feels like a waste and a distracting one at that as it’d both be more compelling a dynamic, I feel like and it’s just weird not to really bring it up. But then again, I almost lost it when the exe showed up and he looked identical to the active boyfriend—like what was the casting for this even thinking when the story just doesn’t seem to address any of the doppelgängers. It’s okay though, maybe a bit too mellow to really enjoy. It’s mostly the hat Kelly sported in one scene that threw me and I started realizing how good this would be as a ‘HDTGM’-movie. But at the same time, it’s also a movie they’ve done several times over before and the ones they’ve done are just so much better than this one because they’re so much more unhinged despite—most all that come to mind being tv movies(like the entire ending of this, In sure totally happened in a Lifetime movie almost verbatim). It’s something to throw on, maybe invest some fun in with friends to offshoot how unremarkable it feels—like not bad and not quite fun bad, but also not really close to “good”, it’s just there.

title: The Strange Thing About the Johnsons
Let Me In
my_review: In a vacuum, I could see this being more appreciated as a movie, but having now seen the two, I can understand why this movie hasn’t been as lingering in the zeitgeist of horror as I feel ‘Let The Right One In’(2008) has been. It’s not a bad remake at all, in fact I’m quite appreciative of the changes it’s made to set itself apart from the original—which is something I want in a remake. But it does also does change just enough that as a whole it doesn’t land as well. Be it how Owen here comes off more weird and childish, versus Oskar feeling innocent and boyish. Or—and admittedly this was something I wouldn’t have really clocked otherwise until I read that the book definitively goes that direction—the de-queerifying of the story, having Chloë Grace Moretz just play a little girl that’s a monster, which is how I interpreted the line. But regardless, the story does lose a twinge of how the relationship bloomed in the original in making it just a kid noticing girls for the first time. But at the same time, I do really like the change of the two having a date of sorts , which I liked all of that segment. Not every change is bad, cause I think this movie’s best when it is changing things, but I just feel like the changes were made without thinking about how they might play differently with the general themes at hand already. An “American Remake” of the more derogative variety, but only cause I think it might stack itself too close to the original at times. Such as the insane pool scene, it’s plain inferior here and—maybe it’s cause it was in the book—trying to redo it feels like such a misfire on this movies part. But again, in a vacuum, like this being the first of the two someone saw, I think this’d work as well and they’re both doing enough differently that I feel both are worth the watch if the curiosity is there.

title: Triangle
my_review: Not bragging or tooting my own horn, but I did unfortunately guess what was gonna happen genuinely around the 10–15th minute mark. Some combination of context clues of seeing the movie on a random post for “underrated movies”, then seeing the poster with a masked killer, glancing at reviews/comments and seeing people gush about going in blind—which satisfied me enough to “approve it” for being added to my Watchlist on here. Incidentally, it got fast tracked to getting watched on the same day, since it was so fresh on my mind. And finally, I pop it on and our main girl, Melissa George, is already out’ve it and suddenly a freak storm is brewing and I just think—“it’s gonna be flippin’ ‘Coherence’(2013), isn’t it”. Then each additional minute just made me think time shenanigans. There was still like a 13% chance that it was ‘spooky eternal ghost ship’—something à la ‘The Shinning’, or I think some ‘X-Files’ episode, but I was pretty on the time shenanigan train early and there’s quite a few common moments that just made me more sure. Again, not much of a brag, cause if anything I wish I’d gotten surprised by the twist, but my over awareness and paranoia can really put two and two together pretty fast with some nominal clues. I even have some movies on my Watchlist that I hope I eventually forget whatever prediction I had about them based on some random clues. Like not quite a prediction, but just steel trapping cultural references, but I have some pipe dream of finally watching ‘Citizen Kane’(1941) and totally forgetting what the big reveal at the end was—which is probably a lost cause at this point. Anywho, with this movie, it wasn’t earning any brownie points from me for the sharp turn it takes into a very confusing plot. I think the idea’s cool and the execution is serviceable, but it’s kinda what it ultimately amounts to that lets me down. I clocked the idea pretty quick that the masked killer was our girl the whole time and that all these loops would eventually turn her into a cold killer. So the whole movie is just following one of her all the way through until the loop restarts. But that’s kinda all there is to it, the novelty of realizing she was pulling “time turner” shenanigans gets a bit old, up until the movie unveils what it was going for. It reminded me very much of a Japanese movie, ‘Beyond The Infinite Two Minutes’(2020), which—spoilers—features a very short window into the future by way of a tv screen which is very meticulously executed in I think one-shot. It’s a cool idea, same as this, but there got to a point where you’re just watching the same thing “over and over” and the story’s hardly moving cause the whole movie is “character sees time window, tests it, is wowed and finally pulls another character to test further” for 70min. That’s about what happens here, our girl finds out about the loop and we just see everything keep happening until she finally starts at the beginning that we weren’t entirely privy to. The cast of characters is incredibly redundant here. Our girl just sticks her foot in her mouth at every interaction and never really ropes them into this phenomenon. So they all die relatively quickly and whatever background time shenanigans that happen, they’re minimal at best. Michael Dorman seems like he’d be a pretty important character but he’s both killed pretty fast and he doesn’t really do anything inbetween. It’s Liam Hemsworth that gets alightly roped in, but not really in any meaningful way. Then there’s random elements that break the loop logic, like a more evil George popping up and killing the friends in a different manner than the way the main George kills them, which adheres to the loop’s logic. I almost figured it was a ‘Primer’(2004) situation where there’s like multiple variations that feed into the same loop but each is a different level of how many loops they’re on. Like the George that did the loop five times is the George that goes crazy while the George that did it three times is the one that kills the five loop George. It’s all very convoluted and I just don’t think the movie quite does it justice by keeping thing a so simple with just George involved with the loop and those random elements that add tension, but make no damn sense. That’s kinda where I thought this would follow ‘Coherence’, where different loops are different realities and each group has its own selfish agenda to return to normal, or steal someone else’s place and return to a better life. But no, cyclical loop that infinitely repeats and each loop has the friends just not matter in the slightest. There is the ultimate goal of this though, that does very much require a closed circle. That’s in George being revealed as an abusive parent. To me it clicked that this whole thing is about how an abuser will hurt, feel bad, ask for forgiveness, treat you better and then go back to abusing. That it can be a sadly consistent cycle and it’s destructive as hell. We see our George fight tenaciously to get back to her son only to find her old self whom she’s so enraged by that she kills her to save their son and raise him “right”. We then get that cherry on top moment of the dead seagull where George goes to toss it and only sees a flock of dead seagulls thrown down in the same place. She’s been here before, she will be here again and it always ends in the same way because she’s not changing anything, just running the loop back again. And it’s actually only occurring to me now that they did totally make a ‘Sisyphus’ reference George evidently being Sisyphus and trying to break her cycle of abuse being her boulder, which does maybe give some good explanation to a few factors that I felt were random, i.e. ‘The Driver’ showing up as a strangely involved character after her big accident, that he’s probably that stand-in for Zeus for this story. Or there’s just the whole reason why this is happening, that it’s some eternal punishment for her. So that does kinda work pretty well for me. In all, this is fine. Not done aswell as it could’ve been, but the idea is rock solid(🥁). I wish the bow was tied nicer and I don’t see any reason why the story couldn’t be a bit more involved with the other people—if anything to not make this a “picture of a picture of a picture…”-movie, but that that fact was hidden at the very end when she goes back to the harbor. I dunno, I was kinda middling on this, but now I’m kinda wanting it to be just a bit better because it almost really worked. Either way, this’d be a good random pick for a movie night.

title: Eden Lake
my_review:
As well done as this is, it's a deeply unsatisfying movie. It escalates needlessly, the antagonistic teens are nauseatingly capablr and nobody really gets their comeuppance. And that's not even a deal breaker for me, but the fact that Kelly Riley doesn't really accomplish much other than killing the least culpable teen and the most annoying one. But the leader and the two more proactive teens- they get off scot-free. Maybe the dog dying is karma, but even then it's still on the teens(though Michael Fassbender was an idiot for escalating it so much rather than just taking the slight L). 

By the end though you just wonder why bother? It doesn't really condemn the town or the violence, it's all very senseless and just sorta happens in the teens favor. Narratively it all pans out as if the teens were the main characters and "woefully two the innocent town kids are murdered by the evil city folks". Again, I'm not opposed to the bleak ending, but it's very much told in a way that makes it so very unfulfilling as a movie.

title: Let the Right One In
my_review: I was very much in the mood for some ‘quiet atmospheric’-vibe of a movie, what luck that this fit the bill so well. I felt a bit remiss to watch this only in September—a Texas September that’s still so warm outside, but maybe the cold empty winter vibes were still what I was yearning for. Really dug this. Story’s(atleast in the movie as I’m coming to believe) vague and full of needing to infer on how you see the story yourself. Cause this can either be a sorta darkly sweet and endearing story of childhood, if you see Oskar’s friendship with Eli as fortuitous as they both seemed in need of one. Or it’s just dark and twisted, Eli is the kind of immortal that has aged beyond their appearance and they’re quite aware on how to manipulate vulnerable children into servitude. For myself I see it as sort of a blend, like ultimately Eli is a dual predator in this context, but I don’t think they’re so indifferent towards him. Oskar has successfully been groomed and will probably serve Eli until something in their relationship must change, but at the same time I do think Eli likes their friendship with Oskar. Though I still flip flop over being more towards one way or the other and that lingering debate has been what’s been most enjoyable, I think. Also, maybe through vaguely hearing about the remake’s pool scene from a friend long ago relaying what that movie was about, I atleast was aware that there was some carnage in the pool to happen. But goddamn, that whole scene is quite brilliant really. Almost feels kinda a shame that the movie wasn’t more about the horror cause that whole scene’s so well done yet so ‘out of the blue’ for this relatively subdued movie(barring the kinda hilarious cat swarm scene).

title: Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street
30 Days of Night
my_review: Really dig the setting and premise (and Josh Hartnett) for this, but I don't feel like it really utilized anything super well. What's supposedly "30 Days" feels like a single night- quite literally, but I never felt a big sense of time and exhaustion from the humans after enduring this nightmare for so long. Though this movie has surprising restraint, it doesn't spend any time in any creative way. Like right off the bat I was disappointed as the vamps just start slaughtering the town on day one, which is kinda funny, cause after most everyone's slaughtered then the vamps just stop being efficient killers to let the humans huddle up for the next hour or so. And I really hate these vampires. Their design's ugly, their paper thin backstory might aswell not have even been there and above all they're just kinda mindless fodder- a bit too similar to zombies. Like they have Danny Huston as the ring leader, but he's forced to speak gibberish language and monologue to seemingly nobody but himself. Imagine if the vamps were actually not brainded, but instead had some character, that their plan wasn't just "eat people fast" but round up people to feast over the month and maybe have Huston chew the scenery as he taunts Hartnett about that fact. Towards the end when Hartnett has to go save his wife, I thought "oh cool, Huston's gonna find her first and use her to force the remaining people out", but then I remembered that these vamps lack that sort of tact and they'd just eat her and the kid immediately and boringly. There's a pretty cool horror movie in the DNA here, but this movie ain't tapping into it. Maybe if-and-when they remake this they can remedy the clichés it struggles with and flex the ideas it actually brought to the table.
