title: 28 Weeks Later
my_review: Better than I remembered, or rather gave credit for at the time, but still pretty wishy-washy. Like in some ways it feels a somehow more iconic than its well revered predecessor, taking bigger swings in place of the slower burn the first was(i.e. helicopter mowing, dooming good people for survival, true hordes of infected…). But then it goes and makes true idiots of its characters—not in a sensible or endearing way, but just totally brain dead actions to justify the next page in the script. Characters are far more lacking here as well, most existing to exposit and die, do a cool thing and die, or do a stupid thing—and die. And it’s that lacking that makes the lower ebbs feel even worse. Topped all off with that early 00’s chaotic editing which I wasn’t crazy about in the first one and much moreso here since there’s so much more of it. Still more decent than I remembered, though. I maybe would have wished it was just more tonally resonant to the first. I feel that’d alleviate a lot of what’s not working while uplifting what was. Like seeing much more of the reconstruction and life after a “burp” of an apocalypse would’ve been pretty interesting. Play less into the bad and goofiness of “all gas, no brakes” and build up these characters more until there’s an explosive final act mirroring that “1–>100” opening.

title: Dead Silence
my_review: Nice surprise to see Jason Stackhouse, didn’t know he started in this. Kind of a dull movie, though. Not terribly so, but there’s not much going on and time it could’ve used to. Hold things up it just chooses not to in favor of this boring investigation that could’ve been condensed so much more than it was. Cause the ending is straight nonsense—I knew pretty immediately what it’d be, but it was nonsense. Amber Valletta kinda stuck out too much to not be suspicious of, the question of “Why make his mysterious stepmom so hot?” being secondary to “Why is this character even here?” But also—this might be on Letterboxd, albeit I do vaguely recall promo stuff featuring the same—but the ghost-ventriloquist bore some resemblance to Valletta I thought. Also the dad just casually wearing a tuxedo, I knew he was a puppet of sorts from the rip. But yeah, I surmised most all the ending, but when it happens it was just so wild and out of leftfield, Valletta’s hardly in the movie to think much about so that her reveal is shocking, but also there’s a huge “why?” that follows cause it just makes everything make so much less sense. Why would she send him on this goose chase to go burn her shrine of power—what benefit is that for her? Why not just kill Ryan Kwanten at literally any point in the movie? She’s clearly a bit sadistic with it, but she’s pretty quick on the draw to kill others, why not Kwanten when she has every opportunity, especially when she controls his dead father and has him right there several times? When did she even “build” this puppet, I’d been thinking she was an ancestor aswell, but nope, she’s a puppet too? “the perfect one” at that. I feel like even though it was a good start, you can’t kill the wife off the rip. Kwanten and her should have been returning home to meet his weird dad and his new wife and then maybe the wife dies shockingly to kick off the second act. There should’ve been a reason for Kwanten’s involvement, needing him to do something for her to finally…do her plan to kill him? Maybe something like she needs a piece from all the Ashens to build her perfect puppet. Or she wants him to burn her shrine down so she can live entirely in Valletta. I do think it almost had a great gimmick though, but I think sound design needed to be insane for this movie and it didn’t quite deliver in that. Like I actually thought the way the haunt starts, with everything muting, was kinda inspired. But it just wasn’t as dramatic a shift enough to entirely love. Like ‘Blow Out’(1981) comes to mind with how strongly silence and sounds affect the vibes. Instead it’s just kinda the typical scares just with puppets. It’s ok, but there’s maybe a much more fun movie in there somewhere.

title: Bug
my_review:
Judd and Shannon really flex their stuff here, but the writing for this really screams "An actor's dream role" and after a while it gets more tedious than not.

It's mostly playing into metaphors of paranoia, but aside from that I don't think there's too much more to this movie. Any 'depth of story's non-existent or shallow as I don't think there's any question of "what you saw" as much as "what it means". Which I kinda think works against this movie and it's themes of conspiracy and shared paranoia. That you're not really wondering about where the truth actually lies because the movie never really instills and distrust of what you're seeing or what people say, which seems like a big shortcoming to me.

title: Behind the Mask: The Rise of Leslie Vernon

my_review: Oddly a bright spot amidst my marathoning of this series. Even odder is this is the most stacked cast(thanks to the passage of time). But they’re finally past the obnoxious twisty turney gimmicks the last few loved to just pile on, but even what they do have here is still completely aimless towards any sense of direction for this franchise. Maybe these movies are just supposed to be bad-bottom of the bin horrors. Like not “bad” in a greasy fast food burger or indulging in some questionable frozen chicken nuggies. But “bad” in the “I burned my food but I’m gonna power through and try to eat it because I wasted some good ingredients in this” or “it’s my birthday but my headache is so bad I wanna crack my head open”. Like nobody wants that experience, but they just sorta end up happening eventually. These movies just exist to potentially get lumped in with some unsuspecting person and just ruin their day.

title: Hellraiser: Deader
my_review: I’m so convinced now that the latter entries of the ‘Saw’ franchise took inspiration from these latter entries of ‘Hellraiser’. Aside from this sort of “education” of the main characters, there’s so much weird convoluted storytelling in these movies that are predicated on some sort of twist and reveal. And that seems oh so familiar with how the ‘Saw’ franchise became so engrossed with the “twist” that it just seemed to be nonsensical and obnoxiously forced. Unlike ‘Saw’ though, these ‘Hellraiser’ “sequels” are barely recognizable from the “plot” that the original—I’ll say up to “3”, movies have. Pinhead is a classic movie slasher/monster with an utterly iconic design, but this franchise is maybe the worst horror franchise. It definitely deserved better.

title: Van Helsing
my_review: Maybe my biggest blindspot in movie opinions…or maybe I’m dead wrong and in wise words once said—“Am I out of touch? No, it’s the children who are wrong.” I love this movie. It’s certainly not a flawless movie—see I can be rational, but goddamn it’s fun. This came out at the perfect time in my childhood and really ignited an affinity in me for Gothic Horror/Monster Tales such as this. I genuinely can’t comprehend the disdain I’ve seen for this movie, it’s inspired, it’s camp, it dope as shit, it’s good! ‘How Did This Get Made?’ is my favorite podcast—many many nights are lullabied to replays of their episodes, but when they did this movie I felt offended. That they finally did a movie I genuinely felt was unworthy of such ridicule, it’s the one episode I can’t bear to rewatch since there’s no voice of reason, just a dogpile on my beloved. And to see it so lowly rated here feels like another offense to my character. It’s my favorite Kate Beckinsale vampire movie(favorite Beckinsale movie in general, but for added emphasis). It’s what I think of when I picture all these iconic monsters. Richard Roxburgh’s Dracula is one of my favorite villain performances. It’s the reason why I’m always confused when Van Helsing shows up in other media as an old copy and not a sexy-brooding-Victorian cowboy. It’s my favorite version of a werewolf with the the coolest transformation to boot. It’s basically flawle—ahem, it’s truly inspired and a marvel of how it world builds and handles all these icons at once. It’s not quite as tight as ‘The Mummy’(1999) was, having so much ambition at once that I can only wonder how they imagined to follow this up. But goddamn I wish I could have seen that follow-up and this franchise given a proper chance. I’m not a stupid fucking idiot, this is a good movie and I’ll always stan it.

title: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre
my_review: Jessica Biel’s incidentally a pretty awful  protagonist. Makes it everyone’s problem as she altruistically steers the group into their doom. On several occasions just ditches a friend—until she’s allowed to help(just so she can ditch them later). That or she just watches her friends get horribly offed while…’petrified’(?) in fear, not even using that opening to do anything—only when she can help does she choose not to. And worst is just go non-verbal at the function to tell everyone they’re about to be murdered. Like I can excuse the “hitchhiker” girl at the start, but because I feel like she’s assumedly gone through more, Biel not speaking up is just donkey brained. These problems don’t really fall on the character’s shoulders though, they’re just a series of choices to motivate the story and all of them make her so terribly unrootable, in my opinion. All she has going for her is that she’s Jessica Biel, but dat don’t make her a good character. It’s alright though. Thus far, it definitely feels the most earnest emulation of the first, as I go through the series and it does so with some real inspiration behind its choices. Its only problem is just how it goes about them, or more plainly, just poor writing. I was promising enough that I was curious about the director and it just made alot of sense that it’s the same guy behind ‘Friday The 13th’(2009), another horror series entry that felt inspired in its attempt, but riddled with such poor writing. Better than I thought though, but I feel like that’s each movie I’ve seen of this series. I feel like expectations were really understandably lowered, but it’s turning out to be one of the more consistently “ok at worst” horror franchises I’ve gone through so far.

title: Pulse
my_review: Kurosawa's 'Cure' was a hauntingly gripping experience that really set the bar beyond "high" for my expectations and I wonder if this films suffered a bit because of that. 'Pulse' has a similarly passive structure of a story of "mere mortals" confronting Lovecraftian-like powers beyond their understanding. But there's a number of things that for me that prevented this from reaching similar heights I found in 'Cure'. --------Semi-Spoilery rantings below-------- I don't like pointing to "age" of a film, but I kinda felt it in this. Many scary moments kinda felt unintentionally goofy to me from some combinations of the effects, or the sometimes cartoonish acting, or cliché reactions from characters. Sometimes the build up was totally there, but I constantly felt "Oh, well that's not too scary at all". Where-in 'Cure' you come to understand and feel anxious over this inevitable hypnotically grip that pulls victims in, here I feel more inclined to roll my eyes and yell at the characters to "stop doing stupid things". But especially towards the end the story starts developing in a very ambitious way that starts to buckle the movie under the scope. Either by not being able to portray scale or the dramatic effect of what was happening.(I specifically even recall being able to hear lively highways when such a thing shouldn't've been possible) I think if the film stayed more bottled to a single character's storyline and utilized more've the Internet being the "only connection" to the happenings, it would've easily curbed any of these issues. Cause this just feels too grand for as quiet and "small" as this felt. Writing also kinda faltered for me. There felt like a strange lack of depth to any of the characters and whatever little they got wasn't really enough to feel attached to. For such a story as this I think the complex thoughts and emotions should be a bit more on display. But their singlemindedness really just fueled some of my exasperation with these characters just gawking and magooing their way into danger. Overall I did recognize alot've the same things that made 'Cure' so gripping for myself, but the more overt proactive-horror and story kinda steered this too far off the trail for me. And I know there's more to it than this, but I couldn't help feeling like this was the most artsy musings of a Boomer ranting about the dangers the internet and how in their day "people were way more connected", etc, etc...

title: Urban Legends: Final Cut
my_review:
Surprisingly not terrible, considering it being a cheap sequel of a so-so ‘Scream’-knockoff. In some ways I think I prefer it to the first or even something like ‘Scream 3’(2000)—which going by the timelines, this is even more of a rip. 

An odd moment that stuck out to me was with Eva Mendes. Mostly stuck out because I forgot she was in the movie, which feels like a whiff(same with Anson Mount, especially when the other lead is this bland ass Matthew Davis), but there’s this weird moment where she got jebaited by a forged love letter that they hardly really bring attention to. Maybe I missed the part where she was a lesbian to begin with and or was into Jennifer Morrison, but also it’s just sorta thrown in there as a “whatever” to lure both of them there, which for Morrison that felt like coincidence since she happened to notice and want to go alone to investigate while Mendes got a whole forged letter. Was just such a weird moment to me cause it felt like it had me asking way to many questions for such a throwaway scene.

title: What Lies Beneath
my_review: I got really really annoyed with the climax. I didn’t like how right when she saved herself, she could then move willy-nilly. That whole scene was great. Harrison Ford dropping the act(after he had a stint of what I felt was terrible “sad” acting as he recounted the story of disposing of the body, which I choose to believe was a choice of his), coldly dooming Michelle Pfeiffer while she has to just sit there and take it, a fantastic jumpscare with weight to it because Ford himself is scared & incapacitated by it and even though he’s out cold, Pfeiffer still slowly drowns, struggling to save herself by wiggling what little she can. All that great tension just undercut by her being able to move so liberally five seconds after saving herself. If she was that strong—just climb outta the tub, but that’s lame, so why did they make a stupid choice by having her be able to do that and just not. I feel like that whole climax of a lethargic Pfeiffer & concussed bleeding Ford should have happened in the morning, like atleast an hour or two after that tub scene. And he’ll, I would’ve loved if it was a race to see who could muster the strength first. You could still have that silly bit of Ford disappearing from the bathroom, but I wanted both of them inchworming their way against eachother. Perhaps in a race to stop the neighbor or tell the first story. Perhaps not quite as exciting and maybe it’s just me, but to me that nightmarish inability to function(the ‘ole weightless punch and whatnot) being a life or death faceoff would’ve been so much more anxiety inducing. But no, they have her being able to walk and get to the car shortly after almost drowning in the tub, the she was so immobile and in general that whole clash felt a bit cliché, even though I feel like it could all play out similarly, just in inchworm speed.

title: Scream 3
my_review:
Just a shell of its former glory—though from a few line, I wonder if that’s kinda the intention? To be pretty mediocre on the third film of a horror franchise.

It’s just such a downgrade in so many aspects. The look feels cheaper and passionless. The characters continue to be pretty shallow in lieu of continuing the core three’s stories(although I do like Parker Posey’s character quite a bit). Story’s just bad and so is the new Ghostface. It feels like an obligatory entry they never wanted to make rather than something they were enthusiastic about. Also Courtney Cox’s hairdo.

Also introduces the first bit of “supernatural-ness” to the franchise with Sidney being “haunted” by her dead mother. It’s weird, I’m sure it’s all psychological, but they also make it seem like Roman’s doing—like he’s some Mysterio, conjuring illusions with his movie making skills to haunt Sidney. Except Roman’s genuinely not capable of doing most of it, he doesn’t even know where she is when it starts. It’s all in Sidney’s mind and it’s happening out of nowhere except when she’s conveniently getting a half-brother to stoke her guilt. It’s also just a pretty direction in story, adds nothing to the movie and like I said, kinda breaks the grounded nature of these movies into something “supernatural” which I don’t like at all for this series.

Low point of Craven’s tenure in the series. Can totally see why the series was confidently laid to rest for ten years after. Still follows a formula that works, but not one that entertains.

title: Idle Hands
my_review: Pleasantly surprised how fun this was. I think I vaguely recall seeing some movie of Seth Green being a stoner zombie the whole time, but otherwise I don’t think this was at all on my radar. I could see this very nearly achieving a cultish status that of other great “dumb” adventure movies, a lá ‘Bill & Ted's Excellent Adventure’(1989) or ‘Dude, Where's My Car?’(2000), but for me there’s one factor holding this back. It’s Devon Sawa. He’s easily the weakest link of this movie. I don’t think he’s got near comedic chops to pull off how physically comedic this role demands him to be. He matches the ‘greasy stoner that does nothing’-aspect, but aside from that, he feels out of place with the oddball nature of this movie. Could possibly be poor direction, but I feel like this is plainly Sawa being miscast while everyone else doesn’t. Can’t say I’m a terribly big fan of his to start—despite being a fan of the movie and franchise, I only reluctantly like him as the lead ‘Final Destination’(2000). I don’t quite see how he got the lead roles in that or this case, but while he did do well there, he’s just straight up not good in this. Not to say he’s “bad”, but yeah, he’s just not the right choice at all. Aside from that, it’s a pretty great movie. Does maybe also suffer from not neatly folding in all its parts—like Vivica A. Fox is just sorta there, or why his friends became zombies(their explanation was so half baked I kinda expected a more legit one to follow up, especially when at the end, Sawa allegedly does the same and he’s not a zombie. But I still had a blast. Also—hot damn, Jessica Alba.

title: Ravenous
my_review: There's genuinely a great horror-western in here, but I felt it couldn't decide if it wanted to be a pulpy comedic one or a tense atmospheric one. Either would've been better and have made this much more've a hidden gem.

title: eXistenZ
my_review: I genuinely can’t tell sometimes how aware Cronenberg is of himself. I’m sorry but this was straight up goofy. The world building was weird as hell, characters kinda speaking in just exposition. The story itself just on no level worked—especially with the end reveal that “it was all a virtual reality dream”. The very foundation of this movie feels nonsensical, in what world would people actually want to play these kinda games? Everyone popped outta the game and we see all the characters were players and we’re led to believe Jennifer Jason Leigh & Jude Law aren’t the protagonists of this game, which is just wild. Like a guy was just stuck being the waiter for the whole game is a player? Or Willem Dafoe just at “[Some] Country Gas Station”(that did get a fun reaction outta me) doing who knows what—waiting for something to happen? Like the congratulate them as if they earned the win, but like was anyone else trying to win? There’s some action in the plot—but action as if this were on a shoestring budget with no intention of doing anything extravagant. Even when there’s a big explosion and shooting everywhere, there’s like hardly anything happening. The only alluring thing might be just having the ability to bang in the game, but that really doesn’t feel like much of a selling point to me. Genuinely the game could be just jacking in to watch this movie in a fake reality and that’s almost the equivalent of what the fuck around doing for an hour and a half. Like this movie throws some insane curveballs—so I have to assume Cronenberg’s quite aware of how silly this is. I lost my damn mind when they pulled off the fur of the dog to reveal a hidden vest holstering two guns. Like this is straight looney tunes at times, but is that intentional? Cronenberg’s always directing with the intent for the viewer to meet him on his level. You’re give a straight bananas plot with even more kooky world logic and he wants you to be 100% on board with it. •“But of course, these typewriters are bugs and they do make you horny” •“Why yes, there is an underground illegal sex ring of the horniest people that get so fucking off on car crashes/surgeries” •“Are you stupid? These fleshy thriving tumors are the state of the art gaming system that you jack into to play the least exciting game ever!” When it was over and they keep pulling twists out, I just couldn’t believe this was actually happening. I don’t know what it’s really going for, there’s some rhetoric of “games are too immersive,” but I don’t really think it works at all? I didn’t know this was gonna be Cronenberg going in, just wanted some obscuring horror for the night and saw this well rated. But I don’t know how the hell this is at all that high. Though I also wasn’t crazy about ‘Crash’(1996) and that’s one of his highest rated. So maybe I just don’t get Cronenberg on his “weird” level.

title: The Faculty
my_review: It’s standing on alot of shoulders, besides the obvious ones, ‘Scream’(1996) really feels aped here. The story oddly fashioning itself into something meta—that doesn’t really go anywhere and just seems like alot of speculative nonsense for the sake of sounding like Randy prattling off the “rules of a horror movie”. Doesn’t really make it worse, but it does sometimes just work against the movie rather than for it or just as an homage. Like ‘The Thing’(1982) references that lack the integrity of good special effects despite being made over a decade later. But I can easily see how this could be a cult hit though. It’s got some of that classic 90’s teen flair and the cast is totally loaded with eventual stars.(Even decided to finally watch as I’ve been big on Shawn Hatosy’s recent breakout with ‘The Pitt’). And somehow it’s one of the least hokey Rodriguez movies I’ve seen.

title: Devil in the Flesh
my_review:
There's a kinda odd transition of main characters that I think kinda kills the momentum a bit. Like we're fully seeing a troubled teen cross more and more lines and suddenly it's about the teacher she's pursuing romantically. Like it turns from something like 'American Psycho'(2000) into 'The Crush'(1993) and that kinda squanders a lot of whatever they were building up. to me, it's almost a tragedy how fucked up Rose McGowan's life is here and the cycle of abuse this family has being passed down and I think that's something the movie seems aware of, but when it shifts to the teacher, McGowan becomes a full slasher and really amps up the villainy(when did she bring her friend in to kill and stage a suicide??). It's like we missed some part of her arc and it's a bit unsatisfying as she just looses the 'tragedy' of her character.

Still fun though, in the same way any thriller usually is. Not quite a full on erotic thriller, though I think it likens itself to one. Like I said, most of the beginning is showing a kinda sympathetic origin story, versus something like McGowan in 'Jawbreaker'(1999) where she's fully a maneater/sexual-villain. Was almost a jumpscare to see a sex scene with nudity all of the sudden and it not be McGowan. I feel it's that McGowan didn't want to do nudity, so they just threw in a scene with someone who would do nudity, just so it could be more of an erotic thriller.

title: Scream 2
my_review:
Better than I remember it being, but still suffers a bit from sequelitis. It likes to talk about the stakes for the sequel, the reception of them, what usually goes into a good sequel, but it never quite digs into the pitfalls the same way the original did. Cause those pitfalls just make the story much less bottled.

The first wants you suspecting everyone—and so does this one, except most of the suspects aren’t really given a chance to build up any credibility, or even character for that matter. They point fingers at the veterans, but honestly there’s never a moment where I ever really suspected them, so that leaves you with background characters that don’t make a big splash when the reveal comes.

That said, the Ghostface aspect is pretty well done here. They’re aggressive and seemingly more effective than Billy and Stu were. Not to say they’re better, but the OG’s were all about the theatrics and story while this one—Mitch, for the most part I assume, he’s a real deal killer, not an aspirational one and I think that kinda bleeds through in how capable Ghostface can be. I only wish he was actually around more, especially cause Olyphant is top tier. 

Sidney is also still a great character, although there’s some questionable choices and moments with her. Her being a drama-girl is a little convenient and within the series seems like an outlier. Her also having a boyfriend she also flip-flops on trusting is an odd thing to do again. But I do still love her very much “no bullshit” attitude when dealing with the killers, part of why she’s my favorite ‘Final Girl’.

Basically the horror/thriller aspects are good, but the story and characters falter quite a bit. A sequel that had a really hard task of following up the legendary first and maybe not the best successor, still pretty entertaining.

title: Cure
my_review: I think I finally figured out why it’s called ‘Cure’(maybe it’s already out there, but I myself never really looked it up and just finally arrived at this point after talking about it with a friend whose first viewing this was). That this rewatch I really took notice of the scene when Takabe picks up his dry cleaning. How while he’s waiting, the salary man next to him is just grumbling nonsense. We never return to that salary man and nothing more comes of it, but I think it’s a cue into that underlying layer of annoyance and irritation there is in everyday life. After piecing that, every scene kinda seems less vaguely unnerving and now more evidence of that ‘festering suppressed rage’ that bubbles underneath everyone and that’s what Mamiya/Mesmer is exploiting. Like there’s the policeman who shot his partner. He seems just kinda broken, seemingly just a byproduct of the hypnosis. When they ask him why and he’s just like “I always hated him…”, I chalked it up to just nonsense as the man’s clearly on some sort of auto pilot. But now I think it’s genuinely true, that policeman genuinely—atleast in some capacity, disliked his colleague. He describes some of it as reasons why and it sounds petty and benign, but I think they’re authentic reasons—like hating how someone chews, or how they yawn, or how they talk about the weather. All these things you just kinda ignore and move on in everyday life, but they don’t leave, they stockpile. I don’t think that policeman necessarily hated the partner at all, but he hated all those things about him and Mamiya pulled that resentment out into a “release” as his next victim-perpetrator. More obviously with the doctor. Before it just seemed like it was just the hypnosis, that he was giving the doctor a reason(which he maybe still was), telling her that men belittled her endeavors to become a doctor and that makes her go kill a man. But like the policeman, it’s probably true. Maybe just an educated guess as I don’t think Mamiya can quite read minds, but a woman in a male dominated profession would definitely have trudged through some pushback and who wouldn’t resent that? And that’s exactly what Mamiya honed in on to trigger her urge to kill. Heck that’s probably why Mamiya is such an annoying person to talk to. Like a good negotiator he’s throwing people off, stoking that rage they bottle up cause he’s about to throw kindling onto it. He loops around in circles until they just kinda sit on that annoyance and move on—cause he’s knows it doesn’t leave. All that’s pent up is never released. But then with Takabe, it all felt more clear while also adding even more layers. We see Takabe’s home life is kinda miserable. He doesn’t have that benefit of a “housewife” because she’s schizophrenic. He ends up coming home to maybe: nothing but an empty plate, food—but uncooked food, a lost wife, an empty but still running washing machine… all on top of a stressful job. A job that’s probably the only gratifying thing for him, since his home life is so nonexistent and his salary only goes into supporting that nothingness. We feel bad and empathize with him ofcourse, but atleast for me, I never quite grasped that he’s probably just been a pressure cooker that whole time. When he blows up at the raw meat dinner, I would chalk that up to the stress of this case and a home life that doesn’t alleviate that, but I believe it’s more than that, it’s just rage at everything. Dude’s been sick with this resentment for so long, like a cancer, just eating away at him. That’s why he needs a cure. The ‘cure’—is probably moreso for the next avatar of Mesmer, but this liberation from that life of misery. Mamiya/Mesmer enchants people through dredging up those feelings and offering them a solution, but for Mamiya himself and Takabe now, the promise is even greater. Mesmer wants Takabe cause he seems so “powerful” a will, resisting him several times over before finally succumbing to some degree of enchantment. The thing I debate over—even still with all this revelation, is “Was Takabe acting as himself or as a hypnotized agent?” Cause to me, Takabe wants the ‘cure’ by the end, that’s why he goes to the spook house. I initially believed Takabe was still aligned good and his detective work just took him into a trap wherein that Mesmer converted him. But this viewing, I think Takabe is desperate for this ‘cure’. After all the mindfuckery with Mamiya he kinda loses composure—I don’t think he’s hypnotized at all, but he’s starting to act on curiosity to this sense of freedom that Mamiya and his psychologist friend talk about. Takabe is corrupted, but he’s still himself, just acting as if he’s already decided on an outcome. That’s why he’s kinda indifferent when his friend seems to be hypnotized and ends up dead(I don’t think he killed the friend, contrary to what I’ve seen theorized). He has a nice meal at the diner—but smokes now(maybe a bad clue, I felt like he didn’t smoke before but picked it up cause Mamiya/Masmer did). And I think he kills Mamiya just cause he hates Mamiya, dude was annoying and a killer and I think he kills him out of apathy and just wanting to be done with him as a cop. Takabe to me acts not on someone else’s command, but like someone knowingly taking the bait. He’s got nothing to lose now that he’s decided to try Mesmer out, certainly influenced by Mesmer toying with his emotions, but still himself, just now let loose cause he’s deciding to go down the rabbit hole. Fuckin’ love this movie.

title: I Know What You Did Last Summer
Wishmaster
my_review: It’s a poorly conceived ‘Hellraiser’-rip with an evil Djinn granting literal wishes by way if “monkey’s paw”, instead of the iconic sadomasochistic Cenobites. Except there’s not even much of a reason that a Djinn is the slasher/movie monster, cause they just kinda do whatever they want with the vaguest hint of “careful what you wish for” to taunt their victims with. Rarely does a character say “I wish…” and earn some deranged version of their wish, as the Djinn just sorta pranks them after either he or they bring something up and he just makes it fucky. Like if he’s that magical and lawless then why downs the just magic every situation into his favor? There need to be rules and this movie refuses to abide by any for some cheap kills and that kinda just makes this even dumber than it already is.

title: Nightwatch
my_review: Why’s everyone act so goddamn weird in this? It’s as if aliens made a mystery/thriller, cause there’s just not a damn human in any of this! Josh Brolin’s such a freaky lil’ guy. He does all that weird machismo posturing that always crosses the line into lunacy. Then when McGregor accuses him of framing him, he just sorta laughs and never really tells him anything cause McGregor storms off. And then it gets even weirder because McGregor calls home and Brolin’s back to being his friend and McGregor doesn’t really seem at all like he ever suspected him a few scenes even though he hasn’t really been cleared yet(nor tried to defend himself). Patricia Arquette doesn’t seem to remember to think until prompted. She reasonably spazzes out over the accusations at her boyfriend, though she also just believes everything she says. Like after the seventh call you’d think it’s super weird how relentless this lady seems.   The prostitute, Joyce, might actually be a robot. That scene at the restaurant where Brolin weirdly keeps demanding of her and she kinda just keeps following along as if she’s strung out on something and isn’t like consciously present. Brad Douriff’s weird, but he’s just doing his thing. And then Ewan McGregor’s just compliant to everything. Everyone keeps doing and saying weird shit to him and he just sorta takes it. Even as weird stuff keeps happening, he kinda lets it, continuing to be horrible at his job. Just letting things happen without really trying to stop them. What a terrible main character. There’s fuckin’—John C. Reilly, who constantly has an inquisitive face like he’s onto—something. But that scene where Arquette just suddenly pipes up that she was actually at the crime scene and Reilly’s just like “Really?! Oh that’s weird.” like does that not make her a lil’ more suspicious. The scene that takes the cake for me though is when he and Brolin—buddy cops they are now(thinking on it, why weren’t they with Arquette) they show up to the morgue and Nick Nolte greets them and not a single bell goes off that something’s weird. Reilly, the cop that he is, he looks an actively psychotic Nick Nolte with a bat, whose face is bleeding & sweaty and he just talks to him like a normal person. When Nolte ordered him to arrest Brolin and Reilly just does it—I just started waving my arms it total bafflement. Then there’s Nick Nolte who’s shockingly not the strangest character. Like it’s so painfully obvious it’s Nolte and somehow, he’s the most normal one for most of the movie. But he’s also reasonably insane when the twist happens, cause yeah, he’s the crazy killer guy, so what’s everyone else’s excuse. Like holy shit, this whole movie’s was just so weird for no reason. I am seeing after searching for it here, that this was a remake and it does seem better reviewed. But I have to wonder if they’re just a freaky in that movie since it’s the same director. Aliens exist and they made this movie, apparently.

title: Scream
my_review:
Ghostface is genuinely such a perfect a design. Iconic, but cheap and made of very obtainable pieces. Kinda spooky and still goofy enough not to take seriously. Perhaps the clumsiest and most jukable slasher, but entirely lethal and very cruel. Where most slashers move slow and methodically, Ghostface flails and dashes so fast that they crash into things. Everything about them adds to the nature of why they’re scary, a costume anyone can wear and plenty do without murderous intentions, but that all leads to the paranoia of the whodunnit-nature of the series. It spills into real life because it’s a familiar costume, you’ve seen it before and now you’ve seen it do murder. It’s another part of the meta foundation that makes the movie so groundbreaking.

Plus they have that cool knife wipe maneuver.

title: Tender Loving Care
my_review: Seems like it’d just be some lowbrow campy nonsense, but goddamn, it’s pretty intense. There’s still some of that camp DNA in it, with those silly moments of characters monologuing to the player some overt exposition just like the Pedro Pascal Hot Ones-meme—“…You should hear this too.” But there’s some real depth to this story. Even when you can see where the breadcrumbs are leading, it doesn’t matter cause you get so skeptical about what’s really happening. Like the horny moments aren’t just thrown in there for only the sake of getting to be titillated(🥁) by Beth Tegarden, they serve a purpose here, testing the characters and the player/watcher on where depravity might mislead them. And then the actual drama is quite twisted, sometimes hilariously so, but often kinda disconcerting, really makes this far more compelling that you’d’ve expected. Made me wish this form of storytelling took off a bit more. It’s a bit different than just the TelltaleGames, the ‘Until Dawn’s, the ‘Bandersnatch’s, I enjoyed all of those and others on their own, but the variation and way the story really weaves the choices in feels more substantial in how they ultimately serve the story—not in the “good/bad ending” way or totally branching off, but that choices & influences feel integral to how this story wants to be told. Like a smaller, movie scale version of what ‘Disco Eysium’ does so ground breakingly.

title: The Return of the Texas Chainsaw Massacre
my_review: Feels like a watered down version of the third one—which was already a watered down version of the first movie. Oddly, in that “watering down” this does somehow skew a bit more towards being less mainstream feeling than how ‘Leatherface: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre III’(1990) felt. Like how the last one makes ‘the family’ a bit more norma than before, it’s even moreso with this one—to a sitcom level, even. But in doing so it does feel a bit more like the original and just feels too “offputting” for general audiences. Mostly in Matthew McConaughey being so unhinged—felt like a precursor of what he’d go on to be in ‘Killer Joe’(2011), but also how he and the whole family plays off eachother, feeling chaotic like the original. Like to me Tonie Perensky was another standout alongside McConaughey, her character having this weird ‘lesbian/woman’s woman/big sister’-vibe with the girls while also being very content that these girls are on the “chopping block”. Almost like some of the cast brought in their own characters from other things to play here. It’s a weird aspect of this to contextualize, I’m struggling even now to attempt to do so, but it is the biggest thing this movie’s got going for it, I’d say. Like I dunno if it even works entirely, but it is certainly unique.

title: Angel Dust
my_review:
In the beginning I was very bemused over how similar this movie felt to ‘Cure’(1997), both in mystery and atmosphere. So much so I was wondering if ‘Cure’ was gonna turn out to be more of an imitation than I’d’ve preferred thinking of it as. But no, this movie takes a pretty sharp turn, that atmosphere broken up a bit, the mystery made a bit more convoluted than it ends up being… it just feels different than what ‘Cure’ maintains and becomes. 

Possibly hypocritical to say after those thoughts, but I did prefer that first half more. Story just starts getting very hard to follow—atleast for me. There’s some choices with the editing and the multiple storylines and an excess of characters that all become a bit’ve a chore to track. Then there’s what is an interesting direction with our investigator feeling like she’s unknowingly involved(a lá ‘Ex Machina’(2014) bathroom scene), but in addition to everything else, it just adds a bit more to the confusion.

It’s alright, but maybe a bit too all-over to enjoy it casually—which would be the camp I feel this would be falling in for me.

title: Jason Goes to Hell: The Final Friday
My Boyfriend's Back
my_review:
I kinda loved this. It’s so campy and plays all the right notes of a good coming of age story, just with a morbid twist. Felt very ‘Heathers’(1988) with the temperament of a John Waters film. It’s so unserious while actually having some heart to it. It was also fun to do several genuine double takes in this, each being more shocked than the last, “Oh hey, a young Matthew Fox, that’s cool,” hilariously being what I thought would be the biggest surprise actor in this movie. *Even just had a double take realizing who this director was, wow.

By the end though, it does kinda feel like it’s been beating a dead horse, just repeating beats over and over. Like it finishes a scene and just does it again in a different location. Whole fun scenarios kinda left by the wayside as they to those roundabouts. And then I wanted it to go even further into the morbid nature of the story and commit harder to its story, but it rears away every time it might go in that direction. Or it annoyingly just saves it for dream sequences that sometimes you’re not even sure are happening or are just part of the quirky style of this. I wanted this to be just a smidge more fucked up, like full ‘Tammy And The T-Rex’(1994) with Denise Richard’s loving her boyfriend animatronic body, or not. Like it’s too much for Disney Channel, but not by much.

Still, what a gem this is.

title: Alien³
my_review:
Boy I didn't enjoy this. 
While I like some of the unique atmosphere and look Fincher brought, I ultimately felt it was never utilized super well. There were some scenes I thought were coming and I was on edge with anticipation for, but they never came(-a Xenomorph lit by candlelight??). Even if what I'd guessed/hoped for to happen- didn't, the film didn't do anything in it's stead, leaving me more "unsatisfied" than "content".

But My real issue is just with the writing- specifically the usage of characters. This movie just had a real problem utilizing good characters, quickly offing them and replacing them with very generic and bland space fillers. Like of course there's the "Newt & Bishop" waste- which was just tripping right at the "Starting Line", but it's Charles Dance's 'Clemmons'- that I felt was honestly a bright spot not just of the movie but the franchise, was so horribly wasted in the end. My shock at his premature death wasn't of "Wow, I'm surprised this character died", it was "Fuck, He was the best character! How on Earth is it going to pay-off?"(It never did). I was just so charmed by Dance's performance and how he got on with Ripley and hoped to see more of a "them vs us vs alien" scenario play out, but nope, killed at the apex of his development for cheap shock. I understand how the series kinda started with a shifting protagonist"-gimmick to great effect, but here I just felt like too much of the fat was trimmed off and the remaining was just too dry and chewy to enjoy. Especially when, IMO, Ripley isn't quite the badass she became in 'Aliens', which I believe makes for a better protagonist than just a final girl constantly running from their monster as they fail to convince others to do the same.

And for the replacements, it's all just a bunch've "nuthin'". Like a "Space Prison"s a pretty interesting idea, especially one with a group of "religiously zealous" prisoners. But my problem stems from the fact that they're of a religion that "shaves their head" and the fact that most all the prisoners are 'British-White-Dudes' with very little distinction between them, so when the good characters are shaved down to "Ripley and a bunch've no-name jabronies" then it's just not very captivating at all. Maybe if some had more demonstrable qualites, good or bad, then the problem wouldn't bother me as much, but as it is, it's no different than just copying and pasting the same character model in a crowd to make the group look bigger. Like the bits in ‘South Park’ when the kids’ hair or clothes aren’t there to distinguish them so they constantly get confused over who’s talking.

There was 'Dillon', as a mold breaker to the crew of "skeevy white Brits" and voice of reason, but even then, Dillon just yells alot. There's very little more to him than some very basic beliefs that don't make for a very dynamic character. He was promising at face value, the "strict shepherd that keeps his flock of wolves in line" is interesting enough- or atleast I thought so. Cause in practice, Dillon was like a tertiary character that somehow got promoted to "supporting role" and he never developed more because of it.(He failed to achieve the same merit as LL Cool J as the revered chef 'Deep Blue Sea', in which his character is almost the same as Dillon and is promoted just the same, lol)

I dunno, for every credit I tried to give, it just wasn't enough to outweigh the bad, especially when the first half is so much stronger- and that's before the titular "alien" is even involved. Not bad for hacky reasons, just bad for making all the wrong steps.

title: Twin Peaks: Fire Walk with Me
Misery
my_review: This is some pitch perfect casting, I tell you hwat. Kathy Bates truly makes this movie cause she completely embodies ‘Annie Wilkes’ in her performance. She timid, eager, innocent, cute & bright eyed—but at the same time she’s a pressure cooker, ready to be set off in rage at the mildest change in her mood. Ready to unleash a frightening wrath that seems hulkish in how indiscriminately she breaks things, but even more terrifying when she does hone-in, focusing her wrath into the cruelest punishments. She should be up there with the greats of ‘killer’ performances with Hopkins’ ‘Hannibal Lector’, or Perkins’ ‘Norman Bates’, or Bardem’s ‘Anton Chigurh’… she just nails every facet of Annie so perfectly. And then the perfect pairing is with the miserable James Caan. The man never seems happy, always embittered and serious. Yet now that man has to appease the most temperamental woman’s fanciful delusions about him and his work. Tiptoeing in every conversation so that his dickish attitude doesn’t bleed through and get him into more trouble. Much like the pairing of Caan and Will Ferrell in ‘Elf’(2003), the character’s misery plays so well off Caan’s miserableness. Every step of the movie you can tell he wants to let it out but has to watch himself so that The scarier Annie doesn’t let it out first. Perfect cold day watch. Classically tense and twisted. Truly just damn fine thriller. Such a wild whiplash to go from the a mega comfort film like—‘When Harry Met Sally’(1989) to this suspenseful flick, but very impressive that both work so well at what they do. Reiner effortlessly jumped genres  like very few others could, whatta legend. RIP.

title: It
my_review: Mixed bag for me, but I actually really vibe with the nostalgic and old school—sometimes straightforward filmmaking here. The 2017 version was my first exposure to the ‘IT’ story, truly not knowing much beyond the “killer clown”-reputation this movie became popular for as even just word of mouth. But I’m fresh off the book now(latest in a since greater acquaintance with King’s writings than I had then), motivated to finish with the new show ‘Welcome To Derry’ coming out(to good reviews??) so I figured now would be a great time to go back to watch what I never did. Though to preface, I was not stoked on the book much at all, perhaps due to knowing the story and already liking the sifted adaptation of it, either way I just didn’t jive at all with it. Off-the-bat though—this is definitely the more faithful adaptation by far. They keep King’s story structure, interconnecting the past and present, giving moments direct references to experiences. The characters are similar given almost the same prominence as in the books. And IT in general just behaves much more in-line with how the book envisions ‘Pennywise’—not so much as a clown at all, but an entity that happens to torment in a clown skin. I’ve never been too jazzed about nonlinear storytelling. I feel ‘Dunkirk’(2017)—a fine movie, has done some real damage in storytelling with the prevalence of imitating it lately. So many times it’s needlessly convoluted and doesn’t really add much at all to the story, much like when a movie does a long one-shot-take a lá ‘Goodfellas’(1990) that feels trivial rather than immersive. The only time I was thoroughly enthralled by it was in the TNG finale ‘All Good Things’, otherwise I can’t think of many instances where it was memorable for that structure in a ‘positive light’ for me(I did just think of ‘Arrival’(2016), loved it there and in ‘Slaughterhouse, Five’). So to say that I feel pretty biased towards the book and this movie for it before it’s even started. That said—I’m still not crazy about it here. I think the book had a more “epic” intention behind it, both stories converging on a final confrontation and how it impacts the characters. This movie despite doing it, it actually finishes up the past story at about the midway point, almost like it didn’t want to commit to it like the 2017 version, but also wanted to still be faithful to the book’s structure. The entire second half of the movie leaves just sporadic flashbacks to moments before and shortly after, which I think still lines up with the book, just not having those moments happen before the climax. So it just kinda feels weird in moments like Beverly bringing up the bloody bathroom with like thirty minutes left. In general I don’t think there’s much gained from it, but the way this movie went about it was probably the worser way to implement it, not really gaining much that it was intended to give. I do kinda dig when a character reflects on an experience and jumps back to their childhood, but per King, those moments are overabundant and longer than I think they should’ve been, so yeah, just not into regardless. Though I can’t entirely criticize the structure without discussing the characters, since that structure is made worse by the amount of characters operating on the same shifting scale. I think there’s far too many characters in this one story. The only reason the book’s as fucking long as it is, is because there’s so many damn characters given big stretches of thought and prominence that keep adding up and never really condensing down. Maybe over a series of books it’d be fine, but as it is it feels excessive. The act of juggling characters is tedious for both King, the movies and the readers/audience. I feel like two main(ish) characters could easily be cut out of the story and it would be all for the benefit(Stan & Richie/Eddie). This movie though does take the time to give everyone their time. Mike(shout out to the dad from ‘Sister, Sister’, Tim Reid) for example is given more of an actual role as an adult, though he’s still a pretty neutered version from the book(which Mike in the book also feels like he’s in a different story of his own tangential to the rest of the Losers). Bill—though he’s feels much less like a leader here, he’s still given the most drive for seeing things through. Ben still being a weird pseudo-main character who exists only to be fat, ridiculously smart(although the aged up and more mature one here doesn’t feel so off) and obsessed with Beverly Marsh. Eddie and Richie feeling like the most one dimensional, although like the 2017 version, I think Eddie is the most compelling adult character, almost to the point that he feels like the main characters. Richie’s weird though, I fucking hated him in the book per King making his character spout egregiously racist caricatures in most every scene(though it is probably accurate for the time). He sometimes works comedically otherwise, but also seems like the movie lies to us and makes everyone laugh at something that doesn’t even seem the slightest bit charming. Stan’s the real ‘loser’(🥁) here, you hardly notice him in the group and he’s pretty uninteresting, not quite given depth that the other versions of the stories give him. Henry Bowers is maybe the worst adapted character here. For as focal as he is in the childhood-half of the story, he barely seems like a character here. I don’t entirely blame the movie for how weird his inclusion is in the present though—it was always a wonky part and ultimately felt redundant for what he accomplished, though maybe flack given for trying nothing to remedy that. Beverly Marsh is just a whole can of worms to me. I really don’t care for how her character’s treated in the story. Something King seems pretty bad at in general is women characters, often they’re just shallow and boiled down to a super desirable damsel that’s very sexual(ly “liberated”). She is very much the stereotype for what people think of a “guy’s girl”, being one of the boys but also treated like the ‘town bicycle’, to be blunt. It’s much worse in the novel, beyond even just the infamously “wtf” train scene where she takes the initiative to ‘fuck the boys into men’. But she also just seems like a “freeuse” figure that is at the ready for anyone’s use. It’s really really weird to me and this movie didn’t do much to curb that aspect of her character. They did remove the casually sexual aspect of her interactions with everyone, but she does still kind of flirt with everyone, being both their maternal figure and a the one they’re all still hot for. I think I prefer this Beverly over the book one by quite a bit, but I’m still not crazy about her at all. They did skip one of the worst scenes in the book of Bill inexplicably cheating on his very caring wife with Beverly—something that felt so odd when King won’t shut up about Ben being in love with her and then having Ben end up with her, like “not until Bill gets his last taste” sorta dynamic, it’s just weird even in context. It’s undeniable that Tim Curry is a large part of why Pennywise is the most culturally impactful character Stephen King has created in his long and prolific career of creating characters. Pennywise is what mythologized this movie. Like before seeing the 2017 version, IT existed as word-of-mouth. Something everyone loved to bring up as scary—“that killer clown movie where he eats children.” I can’t even entirely comprehend how big this role was, remembering some of the names it attracted for what I felt would be just another horror remake. Keeping in mind and appreciating that value Curry brought the character—he was fine for me. There is some scariness maybe lost to time in how goofy the scares play off. The iconic sewer drain scene ending with a weird static image of Pennywise with teeth—something I’m sure some people were got by back in the day, but to me, made the scene sillier than was intended. There’s some great imagery I think is still quite evocative, like Pennywise stretching the shower drain to pop out, but often Pennywise just felt like a creep rather than a scary monster. A scary creep, but not something I’m terribly unnerved by. Like he comes off as a malicious Bugs Bunny most of the time. This movie is also faithful to the books and just makes IT fully shapeshifting, doing the werewolf and the spider, but personally I think that diminishes the effect of using Pennywise as the face of things in the first place. Like this is probably on King—but he’s all about balloons, “You’ll float down here too!” and all that jazz, but then IT’s a spider that hangs people up in webs? IT isn’t even a spider, but if that’s how they finally fight IT, I think a more spider-like motif should have been felt than the goofy tauntings of a clown that wants to ‘salt you with fear’ so it can eat you. And I think an unintentional byproduct of that “watering down,” of the “clown” aspect is there’s just not that much of Curry here for as iconic as he makes this movie. So without the eyes of an impressionable watcher, Pennywise does have much “teeth” to him for myself. Feels sacrilegious to say, but I think for me—this is the second clown role I think I much prefer the other casting of than Curry(semi-famously he was cast as the Joker in ‘Batman: The Animated Series’, doing a few episodes before being recast with Mark Hamill—who I think defines the Joker more than any other actor). For all that criticism, I did really resonate with what was maybe an unintentional aspect of this movie. Something about that empty feeling, late 80’s/early 90’s ‘tv movie’, with a synthy score… it just feels so cozy to me. Like wrap up on a cold rainy day and pop this on. Like it makes me imagine catching this on a crt-tv on a glaucous day—like fuck that just feels blissful. That high of nostalgia I feel like I yearn for. To go slightly off topic by bringing up ‘Twin Peaks’ and certain episodes of ‘The X-Files’, shows I dream of watching in a northwestern cabin in the rainy cold woods bundled with a fire and warm chocolate milk—this movie kinda gives that vibe. I think it’s a vibe maybe inherent to King, perhaps the ‘Maine’ of it all, but there’s a few movies that maybe win me over more than they should because of “vibes”(I know ‘Secret Window’(2004) is one). I don’t think this movie knew that it was giving that off, but I love that it did. The camp of the tv movie—like an adult [original] ‘Goosebumps’ tv show episode, it really works for me and I think it really works for King. Glad I got around to seeing it(🥁), though I prefer the 2017 movie, I think there’s merit here and it does work better for me than the 2019 sequel did. But if accuracy is the goal, I think this does an admirable attempt at that behemoth of a book(whilst glossing over the bad parts). Also it was pretty funny seeing “—Epstein” as the first name in the credits for this movie of all things, even though it’s not the infamous one.

title: Leatherface: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre III
my_review: I’m aware there’s a few “hard reboots” in this franchise and I know the reputation for them isn’t kind—but I was kinda surprised how much this was working for me. It’s definitely a much more conventional spin than the first two, but in some ways that makes it work pretty well, I thought, though just as well, it does take away a bit from the magic the first two had. Like honestly, the premise of this was a bit more interesting than teens stranding themselves and mucking about and wandering into instadeath—here there being a hunt of sorts as they trick and herd drivers off the main road into their territory. Made the family feel more proactive and understandably capable, where the original family—atleast in the first movie—it kinda feels like they just luck out on these teens stumbling into their land and being so dim as to walk themselves into danger. Like they had a whole routine here and that’s kinda frightening in itself cause it’s an effective one. I think I do feel the original family is still more iconic and terrifying to face, but this one felt more effective. Leatherface is probably the most clear change, he being the most clear thing lifted from the original(obviously), aside from “grandpa”. He’s much less “freaky” here and I feel this’ll be a trend going forward. That he’s becoming more of just a standard slasher, which I guess was inevitable and to be expected. I will say, one way it does really fall short though is how cowardly this movie’s made. We have so many tee’d up kills and every one of them is never shown or heavily hidden. Like goddamn, maybe the most frustrated I’ve been, watching moment after moment get undercut by a cutaway, right before it was about to really deliver. Definitely felt like a more mainstreamed attempt on the story and in that regard I think it really holds this movie back. Overall though, it’s surprisingly enjoyable—I guess since I was so prepped for it to be utter shit. Maybe the rest of the franchise will also be surprisingly decent if I maintain this attitude. Especially because I honestly struggle to comprehend how any franchise could be worse than the ‘Hellraiser’-series, my bar is low and so these have a real shot at being decent, maybe.

title: Manhunter
my_review: Some other about this movie to me, it’s really strange. Not terribly familiar, nor much of a fan of Mann admittedly, so I’m operating on a limited scope, but this felt a lot like ‘Thief’(1981), which incidentally has been my favorite of Mann’s movies thus far. ‘Thief’ had just such a vibe about it, specifically how entrenched in night it was and this movie I feel somewhat follows suit. Like there is a vibe about it, but more like a dream. It’s really nagging at me how or even why it feels like that to me. Is it the cinematic approach, or intentionally so? It doesn’t really feel like it plays out as similar thrillers do and I can quite pin why, other than how much this focuses on its protagonist, Will Graham’s, sanity and perhaps in doing so it lends itself to a more surreal vibe than a more grounded one. I’m finding it just so unique, a feeling I guess I don’t normally associate with the kinda movie this is. Whether it works as a whole for me—there’s highs and lows. Vibes are good, great even, but—maybe this is to my modern sentiment and internet-fed curiosity of the world—it feels kinda plain, which might be why it’s so flummoxing to me? I quite love the show ‘Mindhunter’ and this slow amalgamation the FBI form on the minds and personalities of serial killers, but it’s highlighted the fact that we didn’t really understand serial killers the same way then as we do now. So I’m wondering if with this movie—being made around the time ‘Mindhunter’ takes place—if there was a different perception of “a serial killer”. Cause there’s one immediate thing you notice between Brian Cox’s performance of Hannibal Lector(Lecktor, per this movie?) & Anthony Hopkins’ more infamously iconic performance of Hannibal Lector and that’s their entire demeanor and presentation. Hopkins opts for a more eccentric one, but within it you feel like it’s someone playing a game with you and winning, but you don’t even know what game it is. Like Hopkins’ Lector feels like a performance of a man who thinks himself better than others and knows a little flair just fucks with them and proves his mentally superior power over people. Cox’s Lecktor feels much more tame and mild mannered. He speaks pretty casually and proves to have a sharp mind, but he feels quite normal. The same goes for Tom Noonan’s portrayal of the Tooth Fairy—is he a weirdo? Very much so, but there’s not at all a presence that Ralph Finnes has in the remake, ‘Red Dragon’(2002), wherein that movie Finnes’ Tooth Fairy is outwardly frightening. Both Lektor & the Tooth Fairy have some strangeness about them, but the comparison to their later interpretations is night and day. So I wonder if perception of serial killers plays a part in this. The prospect that Lecktor is both a literal predator of man who’s feasted on human flesh is just nowhere in this movie. I think that’s deliberate nor do I think it’s entirely on Cox being the one to do it, but it feels quite tame to me. Same as Noonan’s Tooth Fairy, the reality of his murders is never really confronted. Despite this being rated ‘R’, it feels very PG-13 in its more sanitized depiction of killers. I think there’s merit in the subtle portrayals, but for the movie to harp so much on Graham’s pyche suffering from “getting into the heads of the killers,” well it just doesn’t really translate how heinous these killers are or why this guy feels on the brink of something. I think there’s more Mann could have done to convey this in either of the killer’s scenes. All we understand is people fear them and there’s some novelty in not knowing in Lecktor’s case why Graham is so damn shaken up by this guy. But it’s constantly brought up and it does hurt the movie cause Graham’s mind state is kinda at the forefront here, so if that’s not nailed, then does the movie work as well? The other big thing to me was the needle drops—just kinda felt outta nowhere and odd. But the longer they went, the more I was kinda feelin’ it. It does at to the dreaminess of things and does add a lot of personality to this. They do last quite a while though and especially towards the end it’s kinda constant. I’m not great at listening to music and comprehending the lyrics, so when it kept happening it wasn’t ’til way too late the thought occurred that the songs were pertinent to what was transpiring on screen. Though the more it kept happening the more the movie did start feeling like a music video and in someway—just didn’t know quite what to do for the climax. Very unique movie. I wonder if there was much interest in Cox’s Lecktor. As different as he is, I do think Cox made an impression, especially when his character did feel like there was a lot more to him. Honestly without ‘Silence Of The Lambs’(1991) & the rest of the Hannibal Lector craze soon after, I think his part in just ‘Red Dragon’/‘Manhunter’ is really weird. Perhaps the book digs more into him, but he’s a huge character that barely gets any attention here, even after he’s meddled with things and it’s odd that he just kinda teeters out of relevance despite his big shadow.

title: White Dog
my_review: It’s a bit hokey and over-the-top at times, but when it clicked for what this movie was going for it felt a lot more poignant. Hate is a learned evil and it robs lives of their innocence the more it’s continued to be taught. Is it better to sever the problem out or to reform it? Can you even reform it? Is it worth the effort? This carries some real weight to it, much as the melodrama makes it seem on the sillier side(still is at times). Even its ending while delivering a strong gut punch, it does so through a kinda goofy sequence of “who’s the dog gonna hurt?” I don’t know if at the end it’s saying that the racism prevails as much as that violent hate will. As I interpreted it, the dog goes to attach the person that looks like the man that taught him to hate. It’s a bit comically dramatic, like after rehabilitation, the dog thinks “You! You’re the one that taught me to hate Black people!” as it now turns on the old White man. But yeah, I do think what it’s saying is that learning runs deep, that even though the dog learned to not attack skin color, it’s still aggressive enough to redirect that hate. I’m not sure if I entirely agree with it, atleast if the metaphor is for racists in general. I would agree that with a dog, it might just be a lost cause to rehabilitate as there’s always that chance it could snap back for reasons we can’t really comprehend, not having the minds of dogs. But I do think people can change, hell there’s an overabundance of stories in media showcasing just that. But it’s perhaps just that this movie’s more concerned with the teaching aspect. That this innocent dog has been tainted with hate by a racist man and that pervasive teaching is just pure evil. But solid movie overall. I can see it being a topic of discussion for comedic & academic discussions as it works for both and I think that’s kinda the charm of this movie.

title: Invasion of the Body Snatchers
my_review: Alot've good build-up here, but it just really doesn't go anywhere for like forty minutes and it's kinda riddled with inconsistencies. Once you get past the "scary" part, you're just kinda scratching your head at how it all works. Like as good as the horror and machinations of the 'Pod People' are, the actual "logic" behind them is very odd and very wishy washy. It almost feels as if they're making it up as they go as they keep coming up with new mechanics to how the "Pod People" work, even if it might contradict something earlier. For example, there's a moment where Donald Sutherland's calling for help after they failed to snatch the lot of them and as he gets the operator she immediately calls him by name—so how do they know his name? Like I get it when they assimilate Goldbloom and Nimoy, cause apparently the snatching just copies them onto an emotionless pod-drone so they retain all the knowledge, but just lack any sort've humanity—but how does the operator know who Sutherland is? I would assume "hivemind", but then the whole thing of them pretending to be Pod People makes no sense because all the drones would already know they're taken. It plays it both ways of "one arm not knowing what the other does", but also "they're all one collective". They seem to just do their own thing, but also seem to respond to some unknown shared call to group up—such as the ending when Sutherland sees all his coworkers mindlessly standing there, halfheartedly doing their jobs. But then a second later they without utterance, they start to all leave the building, passing by Sutherland whilst he's doing his own thing and they just pass him by—even looking at him, but never really caring. And if it's to be believed he is a Pod Person already at this point(I personally don't think this), why is he the only Pod Person doing weird shit? He does very distinct movements that aren't drone like and so then the revelation that he was a drone that whole while, it betrays the rest of how we know the Pod People act. And then there's the odd passiveness of it all. The Pod People just don't seem at all enthusiastic about assimilating everyone, assumedly because they can't really tell(but they can, as stated above), but they also pretend to be normal, even when there's overwhelming odds in their favor to just swarm people. There's no 'in-universe lore' for why they don't just force people asleep, so if they have the numbers, why pretend? There's even the bit where Sutherland and Adams are jumped by a bunch've them(mostly named characters oddly) which happens completely unprompted, so why do they act then, but not while they just walk among them. It's like they operate on some weird ‘stealth-game-mechanic’ of proccing NPC's to be alerted to their location and remove their ability to hide—which just doesn't really make sense when the Pod People seem very much competent and aware of everything. They're very similar to zombies, but you overlook when there's similar instances in zombie flicks because you know the zombies are brainless and reactionary, but the Pod People are not that. They're a well oiled machine as they systematically organize a takeover and that's why these outliers are flummoxing to make sense of and take you out of the horror of it all. I also don't know what's up with the pods, lol. They seem to make new copies and somehow sap the... essence(?) of the human. We don't realize this until Adams shrivels up and while a new Adams stands up born anew. But my wonder is both where do the pods even come from and why are they just hauling pods everywhere throughout the movie? There's the thought that the pods are being hauled around to set up another assimilation of a new person, but then there's the moments where pods spring up out've nowhere ready to assimilate, thus making the hauling of all these pods redundant. And there's also the thought of the pod sucking up the husks of people and to that end I can only wonder "Why?" what benefit is there in that and why would the movie get into it if there was a genuine lore reason. There's thousands of pods by the end of it but the Pod People are the ones moving them, so if that's how they do it then the "sleep anywhere and become assimilated" stuff is impossible. And goddamn if the answer’s "Both." then why even bother hauling pods when spontaneous pods work just as well. I'm not usually so "nitpicking" as I feel I'm being here, but this movie just kept opening cans of worms, the reason for which seems to be because "worms are scary". But it just makes you spend too much time trying to justify the movie like a bad Christopher Nolan-pic. You try to make sense of it but it just doesn't—because here comes a dog with a human face—because that's scary. Hell, even the scariest thing in Brooke Adams' freaky "eye trick" is unexplainable. It's a well made movie with great effects and directing, but it's merely a mask for cheap horror attempts akin to the much criticized "jumpscares" of today. Writing be damned, things only happen to scare you in the scene and that kinda weighs it down too much for me by the end.

title: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre
my_review: I don’t know how intentional alot of this movie is, since alot seems like they’re just a bit out of their depth, but this really a marvel of horror cinema. The lack of frills and artistry add such a layer of uncomfortable realism that makes this truly feel nightmarishly less farfetch’d than the average horror movie. Cause while it’s callous and freaky and twisted… it’s also oh so uncinematic for the bulk of it—that it just feels conceivable. It’s a morbid setting of death, but it’s messy/junky like someone’s lived there, the Sawyers just being trashy weirdos that happen to indulge in human harvesting. Like you know you’re irrationally afraid to sleep cause “Freddy’ll getcha”, but are you being that irrational to think this can’t happen Texas? I think that’s the brilliance this found—intentional or not. It makes what’s ‘outlandishly scary’—grounded.
